23174-a-good-for-nothing-1876:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published A Good for Nothing in 1876, a work of fiction centred on a boy named Ralph. The opening follows Ralph from babyhood into early childhood. His mother reads deep meaning into small habits, taking his thumb-sucking and quiet corner-sitting as signs of a poet's brooding mind.

By age five, Ralph has become the ruling force in his own home. Boyesen tells this with gentle irony, letting the mother's proud reading sit beside the plain facts of a spoiled small child. Readers get a wry portrait of family pride, early character, and how adults can build large hopes on very small evidence.
abridgement-of-elements-of-phrenology-18: Abridgement of Elements of Phrenology, 1876. The abridged elements. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
account-of-an-alchemical-roll-on-parchme: Account of an Alchemical Roll on Parchment, 1876. The Cromarty roll. This book preserves that account. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Volume V of the Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica appeared in 1876, the halfway point of Allen's ten. The symptoms of each remedy stand in strict anatomical order, a habit that lets a busy reader land on the right page fast. Sources are cited, so claims can be traced.

Some entries run for pages, proof of how often a drug was tested in that busy age of provings. Others stay brief. All of it feeds the same craft: choosing one remedy whose proved picture matches the sick person's signs. The volume keeps the archive's standard of full record over fine writing.
arxiv-2511-20376:
Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller recover hidden cliques from messy random graphs. Their 2025 paper studies random intersection graphs, a network model. Many cliques of roughly size k are planted at random. Each vertex joins each clique independently with some probability. Vertices can belong to polynomially many cliques at once. That overlap defeats simple and even spectral methods.

The authors give the first efficient recovery algorithms here. Both exact and approximate recovery are achieved. The methods tolerate noise and monotone adversaries. They even survive an optimal number of corrupted edges. Recovery works once cliques exceed roughly the square root threshold. The proofs-to-algorithms route runs through sum-of-squares optimization. Certificates must prove no large clique hides outside the truth. Modified biclique certificates supply that ingredient. A sharp concentration property keeps false positives away. The same ideas certify that the recovered clustering is optimal.
arxiv-2511-20576:
Lin, Anand, and Brown cut the measurement rounds quantum error correction needs. Their 2025 paper introduces local single-shot checks for toric codes. Syndrome measurements detect errors but are themselves noisy. Standard schemes repeat them many times per decoding round. That repetition costs heavy time overhead in fault-tolerant machines.

Single-shot correction uses one round, but usually needs heavy checks. Heavy checks wreck circuit-level performance in practice. The new checks cap their weight by acting on small lattice patches. A dynamic measurement scheme rotates which checks run when. Required rounds shrink by a factor tied to patch size. Simulations used sliding-window decoding under circuit-level noise. Local checks beat conventional ones at reduced window sizes. Fixed-width checks preserve the effective circuit distance with bare qubits. Variable-width checks won under phenomenological noise instead, with higher thresholds.
arxiv-2511-20776:
Hiroyuki Yamase and colleagues build in 2025 a strong-coupling theory of plasmons, collective charge oscillations, in bilayer materials like the cuprate superconductors. A bilayer supports two plasmon modes where a single layer has one, and earlier work described them only in the weak-coupling regime, ignoring the fierce electron correlations that define cuprates. The team's t-J-V model, with no double occupancy and a long-range Coulomb term, treats them head-on.

The two modes survive, resembling their weak-coupling counterparts. One twist: particle-hole excitations are noticeably suppressed, so the plasmon modes stay sharp across a wider range of momenta. Superconductivity in these materials emerges near 5 percent hole doping and peaks around 16 percent. The authors propose that plasmon signals in yttrium-based cuprates correspond to the lower of the two modes, and call for experiments to test the claim.
arxiv-2511-21076:
Aaditya L. Kachhadiya introduces in 2025 the Deceptron, a learned module that helps solve physics inverse problems, where the unknown input must be recovered from measured output. Such problems are ill-conditioned: plain gradient steps crawl and depend touchily on step size. The Deceptron learns a local inverse of a forward model. Training adds a supervised fit, forward-reverse consistency, and a Jacobian composition penalty. That penalty pushes the product of the two Jacobians toward the identity.

At solve time, its D-IPG algorithm steps downhill in output space, pulls the step back through the learned inverse, and projects, under the same safeguards as baselines. On recovering the initial condition of a one-dimensional heat problem, it hit the target tolerance in about 20 times fewer iterations than projected gradient. A damped oscillator problem needed 2 to 3 times fewer, rivalling Gauss-Newton in cost. A 2D variant, DeceptronNet, previews image-space corrections.
arxiv-2511-21176:
Retractions were once rare embarrassments; lately they arrive by the ten thousand as paper mills and sloppy work flood journals. Zhengyi Zhou, Ying Lou, Zhesi Shen, and Menghui Li study global retractions in 2025 through a topic lens, asking which subjects, not just which fields, carry the problem. They assign topics to roughly 46,000 of some 55,000 retracted papers and pair them with Web of Science publication counts from 2000 to 2024. A relative retraction rate then compares each topic against the global background.

Retracted papers grew from 140 in 2000 to over 11,000 by 2022, far outpacing overall publication growth from 785,000 to about 2.8 million papers a year. The year 2023 set a record with over 14,000 retraction notices. Electrical engineering and computer science alone account for more than 9,700 retractions, about 31 per 10,000 papers. Some low-rate fields hide badly hit topics, and some topics show suspicious publication surges alongside high retraction rates, flags the authors offer for targeted integrity checks.
arxiv-2511-21276:
Sutirtha Biswas and Kshitij Kumar Yadav blend physical law with deep learning to predict how buildings shake in earthquakes, in 2025. The standard finite element method is accurate but too slow for large-scale or real-time seismic analysis. Purely data-driven networks are fast, yet they often fail on new shaking patterns because nothing forces them to respect mechanics.

Biswas and Yadav propose PhyULSTM, a physics-informed network marrying a U-Net, which reads patterns across scales, with LSTM layers that track sequences over time. Governing physical laws are written into the training loss, curbing overfitting and improving generalization when data are scarce. The model beats earlier seismic predictors such as PhyCNN on the authors' tests. It can even run without explicit physical constraints, extending it to structures whose material behavior is only partly known.
arxiv-2511-21376:
Lukas Pin, Stef Baas, Gianmarco Caruso, David Robertson, and Sofía Villar bring system to a guesswork corner of clinical trial design in 2025. Response-adaptive randomization shifts enrollment toward treatments that look better as results accumulate, benefiting patients. Trials first need a burn-in, an opening phase of plain equal randomization that stabilizes estimates; 88 percent of such trials use one. Picking its length, though, has been improvised, with no guideline.

Pin and his coauthors build the first systematic framework for that choice. Their formula blends total sample size, problem difficulty, and two new metrics, reactivity plus the expected error in final allocation, into one principled rule. Simulations grounded in real trial designs show the formula finds a sweet spot. Type-I error inflation and estimation error stay controlled, while the power and patient-benefit advantages of adaptation survive, replacing rule-of-thumb choices with a defensible calculation.
arxiv-2511-21476:
Filippo Stocco, Michele Garibbo, and Noelia Ferruz survey how to steer protein-generating AI toward rare but valuable designs, in a 2025 review. Generative models have produced working binders, receptors, and new enzymes, but they imitate their training data, so they mostly sample the most probable proteins. The unusual regions of protein space, where novel functions hide, stay underexplored.

Stocco and his coauthors organize the steering toolbox into two camps. One camp changes the model itself, through reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning toward target properties. The other leaves the model frozen and guides sampling instead: conditional generation, retrieval-augmented prompting, Bayesian guidance, and tailored sampling schemes. Their taxonomy maps which knobs suit which constraints. The review closes on an open tension: natural protein fitness is fluid and context-dependent, so no single score defines the design goal.
arxiv-2511-21576:
Ridha Horchani imagines a force of nature that only quantum objects can feel, in a 2025 theoretical proposal. His Quantum Latent Gauge framework adds a hidden gauge interaction, a cousin of electromagnetism, that couples exclusively to quantum coherence. The trick is a coherence current built by coarse-graining the ordinary mass current: it vanishes for classical matter but switches on for superpositions and entangled states.

The theory keeps gauge invariance, causality, and healthy time evolution while staying invisible to every classical fifth-force search. It predicts three distinctive signatures. Interferometers should see phase shifts growing in step with fringe visibility. Decoherence rates should grow with the square of mass in a pattern unlike collapse models. Distant entangled masses should feel selective forces. Horchani works out a benchmark version in detail. Current atom interferometers and levitated nanoparticles can already place the first constraints, opening a new window on the quantum-classical border.
arxiv-2512-00376:
Protein language models learn from amino acid sequences, and their layers may store different kinds of knowledge. Ajit Kumar and Indra Prakash Jha probe those layers for kinase functional prediction in 2025. Most applications use only the final layer's embeddings, possibly missing useful signals.

The authors systematically evaluate embeddings from the ESM-2 model with unsupervised clustering and supervised learning. Kinases are enzymes central to cell signaling and drug design, so predicting their function matters. If intermediate layers carry extra functional information, practitioners can improve predictions simply by reading more of a model they already use. Kinases are heavily studied drug targets, so even small prediction gains have wide impact.
arxiv-2512-00476:
Heavy sterile neutrinos are hypothetical particles that could explain why known neutrinos have mass. Tim Kretz and Ulrich Nierste compute QCD corrections to charged-current decays involving such neutrinos in 2025. Searches profit from precise predictions of inclusive decay rates, which set branching fractions and lifetimes.

Once semi-hadronic decay channels open, reliable rates require the neutrino to be heavy enough for perturbative calculation. The situation mirrors the well-known case of semi-hadronic tau decays. Precise rates sharpen experimental searches, including those using tau decays, by removing theory uncertainty from the list of excuses for a null result. Branching fractions decide which decay channels experimentalists should watch most closely. Inclusive rates sum over many final states, which is what makes them computable.
arxiv-2512-00676:
Kiri Wagstaff, a computer scientist, wrote a 2025 paper on reading handwritten numbers. Most past work asked machines to name one digit at a time. Real life is messier, since numbers usually come as strings of digits written by one person.

Wagstaff looks at cases like ZIP codes, check amounts, and appointment times. In such strings, digits can touch, slant, or change style from one to the next. A system that shines on single digits may fail on these groups. The paper sets out the challenges that a fair, realistic test of number reading must face.
arxiv-2512-01176:
Cole Treyturik and four coauthors revisit two puzzling supernova remnants in a 2025 astronomy paper. The remnants 3C 397 and W49B have long been debated. Did each come from a thermonuclear explosion, a white dwarf blowing up, or a core-collapse explosion of a massive star? Earlier studies gave conflicting answers.

The team presents a systematic, spatially resolved spectroscopic analysis of both remnants using the XMM-Newton telescope. Spectroscopy across each region maps the elements left behind, which differ between explosion types. Settling the engines behind these remnants sharpens our picture of how stars die and seed space with heavy elements.
arxiv-2512-01276:
Guy Blanc and co-authors ask if learning gets easier when data can be sampled. Classic learning theory asks a learner to work for all data spreads. Some of those spreads are too hard to even draw samples from. That demand may be stronger than real tasks need.

A weaker rule asks for success only on spreads that can be sampled. The team shows that this weaker rule can make some tasks much easier. They give cases where the gap is large. The result helps sort which hard tasks are hard due to learning, and which are hard due to odd data spreads.
arxiv-2512-01476:
Peter Lott and co-authors build a frame to rebuild fly-by events of black hole pairs. In such events, two black holes sweep past each other once. They do not merge. The pass sends out a short, single-cycle wave burst. These bursts should occur in dense star clusters and galaxy cores.

Their frame makes few prior claims about the burst shape. That freedom helps it fit odd real events. It can work on both loud and faint bursts. A model-free tool raises the odds of spotting these rare passes in wave data from current detectors.
arxiv-2512-01576:
Nihaal Bhojwani and co-authors model how black holes and galaxies grow together with neural operators. The physics spans a huge range of scales. Gas near the hole acts at tiny scales. Galaxy-wide feedback acts at vast scales. Full simulations of both ends are too costly.

Their neural operator frame learns the coupled dynamics fast. It bridges accretion at the center with feedback across the galaxy. Fast surrogates let teams scan many what-if cases. Those scans test how black hole growth steers star birth over cosmic time. Surrogate speed also lets observers fit live merger data faster, since galaxy feedback priors can be scanned while wave data is still fresh.
arxiv-2512-01676:
Jiangdong Ai and co-authors study feedback vertex sets in directed graphs with bounded degree. A feedback set hits every directed cycle. Removing it leaves the graph acyclic. In oriented graphs, with no opposite arc pairs, the task has set traits.

Degree here sums in-arcs and out-arcs at each vertex. Bounded degree caps how linked each node can be. The team proves bounds for feedback sets under that cap. Such sets help break deadlocks in networks and find orderings in dependency graphs. Bounded degree mirrors real networks, where each router or person links to few peers, so the bounds stay tight for practical cases.
arxiv-2512-01876:
Engineers often must learn how an unknown machine behaves by feeding it test signals and watching the response. A 2025 paper by Amir Shakouri, Henk J. van Waarde, and M. Kanat Camlibel asks how to design those test signals for a linear system whose inner workings are not known in advance.

The data gathered must be good enough either to identify the system or to design a controller that keeps it stable. The authors build in prior knowledge about two key properties, controllability and stabilizability, so the experiment respects what is already known. Their approach aims to collect the right data the first time, instead of relying on trial and error.
arxiv-2512-01976:
Designing proteins from scratch with AI depends on training data, and synthetic datasets often pair sequences with structures they could never actually fold into. Danny Reidenbach and a large team tackle that quality problem in 2025, aiming for fully atomistic designs with far greater structural variety.

Their approach leans on ProteinMPNN, whose proposed sequences are known to be experimentally friendly and able to fold. Combined with structure prediction models, it aligns synthetic structures with sequences that can genuinely realize them. Cleaner training pairs should make generative design models more reliable, widening the range of new proteins they can credibly propose.
arxiv-2512-02076:
Learning from data spread across many owners, each holding several kinds of data, runs into privacy, imbalance, and forgetting problems at once. Haozhe Wu's 2025 paper proposes FDRMFL, a federated feature extraction method for multi-modal regression that is driven by the task itself.

The method combines information maximization, squeezing the most signal from each modality, with contrastive learning to fuse them. It is built for three real-world headaches: limited data that are not identically distributed, the need to merge different data types well, and catastrophic forgetting as learning proceeds. Federated designs like this aim to learn jointly without pooling private raw data.
arxiv-2512-02176:
Kagome metals, whose atoms sit in a woven triangular pattern, can frustrate magnetism into strange quantum states. R. Guehne and nine co-authors study one such compound in 2025, a scandium-manganese kagome metal, hunting for signs that its electrons pair up in a spin-singlet pattern.

The material drew attention as a place where geometric frustration and mobile electrons might cooperate to keep magnetism disordered at the quantum level. The team combines bulk thermodynamic probes, low-noise transport on tiny cut devices, and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements. Converging evidence from several probes is what a claim of emergent pairing in such an exotic metal requires.
arxiv-2512-02576:
Yafei Song, Peng Zhang, and Bang Zhang generate videos of speakers whose hands move naturally with their words. Co-speech gestures make a talking avatar feel alive, but syncing them with speech is hard. Recent methods borrow motion from graphs built out of existing video clips.

Choosing the right path through that graph is the weak point. Older methods match audio features to motion features, or embed both in one shared space. The team's motion based graph retrieval picks clips by motion fit. More natural gesture video could improve virtual presenters, sign aware tools, and remote communication. Hands do much of the talk in a speech, so stiff hands make the whole clip feel false at once.
arxiv-2512-02776:
Fivos Perakis, Takeshi Kawasaki, and Shinji Saito study a particle wandering through an environment that flips between two states. In their Langevin model, friction switches at random between low, liquid like values and high, glassy ones. Two clocks govern the motion: the switching time and the velocity relaxation time.

The ratio of those clocks decides how diffusion behaves. The team finds conditions where switching enhances diffusion beyond either state alone. Flickering environments occur in cells and soft materials, so these results help explain transport where surroundings never sit still. A flicker can speed a trip, a quirk that shows up in gels and in the goo that lines our lungs as well.
arxiv-2512-02876:
Yinke Cheng and a large team build light sources that emit many evenly spaced colors at once, at useful power. Soliton microcombs, made in tiny optical resonators, promise compact sources for next generation communication. Power per comb line, though, has fallen short of what real systems need.

Their integrated Fabry-Pérot microresonator sidesteps the usual dispersion engineering limits. The platform yields bright soliton microcombs with record power per line, the authors report. Stronger comb lines could carry more data channels from a chip sized source, cutting cost and energy in optical networks. More power per line means more lanes per chip, and more lanes per chip is the whole game for cheap fast links in towns.
arxiv-2512-03176:
Reasoning models think for a long time before they answer. Anthony Liang and co-authors propose a change to that pattern in this 2025 work. While a model thinks, users get no hint if it is on track, and no chance to correct it.

Their method, called Plantain, weaves planning and answering together. The model shares parts of its plan as it goes, so users can step in early. Early feedback could save time and stop flawed reasoning sooner. The work speaks to anyone who uses AI tools for complex tasks. Users gain a window into the plan early, rather than a long silence before the reply.
arxiv-2512-03676:
Daria Kryvosheieva and colleagues locate grammar inside large language models and ask whether agreement rules of each kind share hardware. Subject-verb, pronoun, and determiner agreement all police the same sentence marks. Their 2025 study borrows functional localization from brain science to find the units behind sixty-seven syntactic phenomena.

Across seven open-weight models, the units tuned to syntax were reused again and again and truly backed performance. Different rule types drew on shared unit sets, a sign that agreement is a real working category for the models, not a made-up label. The pattern held in Russian and Chinese too. Among fifty-seven languages, languages closer in structure shared more subject-verb units.
arxiv-2512-03876:
Entropy counts how disordered a system is, and for dense matter full of strongly interacting particles the bookkeeping is subtle. David Blaschke, Gerd Röpke, and Gordon Baym revisit a classic tool for that bookkeeping in a 2025 nuclear theory preprint: the Beth-Uhlenbeck formula. They generalise it for dense fermion systems where two-particle correlations, including bound states, cannot be ignored.

Working inside the Phi-derivable framework for thermodynamic potentials, the authors write entropy as an integral over a distribution function times a special spectral density. Near the mass shell, that density takes a squared Lorentzian shape rather than the expected Lorentzian one. The connection between the classic formula and their framework is exact at the two-loop level. Their version also handles bound states dissolving at high density, as Levinson's theorem requires. Applications to nuclear matter and quark matter are discussed.
arxiv-2512-03976:
Large language models speak major languages fluently and low-resource ones poorly, because training data for the latter barely exists. Lifeng Chen, Ryan Lai, and Tianming Liu tackle that gap for Tibetan in a 2025 language technology preprint. Tibetan is morphologically rich and underrepresented online, so a general model starts with weak grounding in how the language works.

Their two-stage recipe first continues pretraining a three-billion-parameter Qwen model on Tibetan text, then fine-tunes it under supervision for tasks and translation. Perplexity on Tibetan fell sharply, and Chinese-to-Tibetan translation quality rose several-fold on standard scores. A layer-by-layer look inside a related model showed adaptation concentrated in embeddings, output heads, and later projection layers. The authors read this as the first stage building a Tibetan semantic space while the second sharpens task behaviour gently. They release the framework openly for other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2512-04976:
João Brito, Atsushi Higuchi, and Luís Crispino study what happens to gravity's energy when a small mass falls straight into a black hole. Simple theory says the share of energy swallowed by the hole grows without limit, which cannot be right. The trouble traces back to treating the falling body as a perfect point, with an infinitely strong field packed tightly around it.

The authors break the falling mass's field into layered wave patterns near the point where it crosses the black hole's edge. Piece by piece, they show the endless energy comes from that trapped field around the particle itself, which pours into the hole along with it. Each layer contributes a steady, matching amount, which clears up the puzzle without new physics. The result sharpens how physicists model small bodies spiraling into black holes.
arxiv-2512-05176:
Brittany Johnson, Erin Reddick, and Angela Smith argue that judging whether language models respect a community's values needs a benchmark built for communities, not nations. General-purpose models tend to reflect majority Western narratives, and recent culturally informed models try to correct that — but the tools to evaluate them lag behind. A national-level benchmark, the authors contend, cannot capture the range of cultural identities inside the United States.

Their proposal, CIVIQ, adapts the process behind KorNAT, a Korean national alignment benchmark, to the community level. It would test how well a model infers and honours the social values and common knowledge of specific communities, giving developers a way to measure cultural alignment where people actually live it. The work lays groundwork for building and evaluating culturally informed models in practice, rather than assuming one national yardstick fits a diverse country.
arxiv-2512-05276:
Yvelin Gansou, Karim Oualkacha, Marzia Cremona, and Lajmi Lakhal-Chaieb introduce a statistical test for whether genes and chemical marks on DNA interact in shaping a trait. The question is whether DNA methylation — marks that regulate genes — modifies the effect of a set of genetic variants on a measurable outcome. Methylation is naturally a curve over genomic position, so the authors treat it functionally, extending functional regression models into a test of the overall interaction.

In extensive simulations, the test holds its false-positive rate at the promised level while beating existing methods on power, especially when several interactions act at once — the realistic case. The authors then apply it to data from obesity patients and controls, showing the procedure at work on a real question. The contribution is a sharper instrument for a subtle effect: not whether genes or marks matter alone, but whether they matter together.
arxiv-2512-05576:
Ting-Ting Xie and Yixin Zhang diagnose why small clinical language-model agents fail at diagnosis despite finding the right evidence. Agents like TxAgent retrieve information competently thanks to supervised fine-tuning, then fail to ground their conclusions in it — a failure the authors name Context Utilization Failure. Their CureAgent framework separates the two skills. Small agents execute tool calls with syntactic precision, while long-context foundation models do the clinical reasoning over what was retrieved.

An ensemble strategy, preserving the diversity of evidence instead of pooling it, beats global pooling. Stress tests add two warnings: stretching the context too long injects noise and degrades accuracy, and enlarging the toolset creates a dimensionality curse that demands hierarchical retrieval. Without end-to-end fine-tuning, the training-free architecture reaches state-of-the-art results on a benchmark — an argument that in medical AI, architecture can substitute for training.
arxiv-2512-05776:
Muhib Omar leads an eleven author team that detects nuclear magnetic resonance signals with a sensor carved from diamond, at almost no magnetic field. Ordinary NMR needs strong magnets. At near zero field, signals shrink to a few cycles per second, but carry sharp chemical fingerprints from nuclear couplings. The diamond sits in a tiny truncated pyramid, with samples approaching within a millimeter.

Samples were boosted with parahydrogen through a reversible exchange trick. The sensor then read the expected coupling pattern of acetonitrile, with signal lines at just a few hertz. Its sensitivity reaches tens of picotesla per root hertz. Because no magnet is needed, the platform could become portable. The authors point to uses in medical diagnostics on tiny samples, sensing through metal walls in industry, and field ready analytical devices. It is a step toward NMR that travels to the sample, not the other way round.
arxiv-2512-05976:
Antonio Varagnolo, Giuseppe Romano, and Raphaël Pestourie teach a neural network just enough physics to design materials that steer heat at the nanoscale. Heat at this scale obeys the Boltzmann transport equation, exact but too slow for design loops. Cheaper solvers err wildly; data driven learners demand thousands of simulations. Their surrogate couples a differentiable Fourier solver with a neural generator that learns corrections.

A learned mixing coefficient slides between the macroscopic picture and the nanoscale one. Uncertainty driven active learning picks the simulations worth running. The payoff: training data needs fall by up to seventy percent against data driven baselines. Errors sit near five percent with only three hundred full simulations, and porous geometries were designed with average errors near four percent. The mixing parameter also tells engineers which regime a design lives in. The pattern travels well beyond heat.
arxiv-2512-06376:
Xinhao Xiang, Abhijeet Rastogi, and Jiawei Zhang ask whether videos of driving made by AI are good enough to train self driving cars. Text to video tools can spin up street scenes from a sentence, cheaply and in any mix. That promise only holds if clip cars move like real ones and obey road rules, which often they do not.

The team maps the common faults: warped images, motion no real car could make, and breaches of traffic sense. They build a bench of driving clips with human quality grades and dense labels for tasks like spotting and tracking cars. Their scorer blends scene meaning, motion cues, lane keeping, and vision model checks into one grade per clip. Raw clips hurt car training; clips filtered by their scorer helped. The study shows made up video can aid real driving work, if it is screened first.
arxiv-2512-06576:
Maxim Grigoriev and Mikhail Markov study what happens at the edge of anti de Sitter space, the curved spacetime that anchors much of modern gravity theory. Fields such as gravity itself live in the bulk of that space, but their observable fingerprints sit on its boundary at infinity. Making that edge precise is tricky, because infinity is not a place until the theory treats it as one.

Their approach folds the function that defines the boundary into the fields of the theory itself, so the boundary becomes an ordinary surface inside spacetime. A new notion, the Q boundary, systematizes that move. The payoff is a boundary calculus: a step by step recipe that writes down the equations the boundary fields obey and how their gauge freedoms act, for higher dimensions. Famous obstruction equations fall out, plus a higher Yang Mills equation in eight dimensions.
arxiv-2512-06976:
Ondřej Ježek and co-authors solve a finishing problem in topology optimization, the engineering method that lets an algorithm carve a part into its lightest strong shape. The raw output is a fuzzy density map, and turning it into clean geometry for manufacturing usually trades off smoothness, exact volume, and fine features. Their method describes the boundary with a signed distance function, which stores at each point its distance to the surface.

A two-stage process first builds that distance description from the density contours, then polishes the shape with radial basis functions. The result looks as though it came from a far finer calculation than the coarse one actually run, saving computing effort. In tests, peak stress dropped compared with standard methods, thanks to smooth transitions. The implicit surface exports directly to common manufacturing formats, skipping the usual rebuilding step that can introduce errors.
arxiv-2512-07076:
Chen-Yang Wang and co-authors argue that the scores used to grade camouflage-finding systems ignore the very thing camouflage is about: context. A hidden animal fools the eye by blending with its surroundings, yet standard metrics compare a predicted map against a binary ground truth as if each pixel stood alone. The authors name two flaws. Predictions carry both labels and probabilities while truth carries labels only, a dimension mismatch. And pixel-by-pixel scores miss dependencies spanning the whole image.

Their replacement, Context-measure, enriches the ground truth with pixel-level contextual affinity, scoring how each point relates to its surroundings. A perception cycle then judges predictions in a way designed to track human judgment more closely. Across experiments scored by four meta-measures, the new metric beat every widely used rival for camouflaged object segmentation.
arxiv-2512-07276:
Mai Tsujimoto and co-authors build a benchmark that asks vision-language models to reason about the three-dimensional world from ordinary aerial photographs. Planning cities, adapting to climate change, and assessing environments all need height-aware spatial reasoning. Yet the professional tools depend on pricey sensors like LiDAR that much of the world cannot deploy. Geo3DVQA instead gives models plain color imagery and asks questions involving elevation, how much sky a point can see, and land cover patterns.

The set holds a large bank of curated question-answer pairs across sixteen task categories, from single-feature reading to multi-feature reasoning and applied analysis. Ten leading models were put through it, and the results expose basic limits in how they infer three-dimensional structure from flat color. Focused instruction tuning on the domain lifted performance in every category, including open-ended questions.
arxiv-2512-07476:
Klaus Jansen, Dirk Nowotka, Lis Pirotton, Corinna Wambsganz, and Max Wiedenhöft wrote this 2025 paper in theoretical computer science. It studies patterns, which are strings mixing fixed letters with variables. Filling each variable with real letters yields the pattern's language.

In the classic setup, two uses of one variable must receive the same filler. Relational patterns loosen that rule in an organized way. Variables can be tied by many other relations, set independently of the pattern's shape. The authors carry three classic questions over to this richer world. The questions ask whether two patterns agree, whether one sits inside another, and whether a word fits. They test the questions across a wide range of chosen relations. Their results give a broad foundation for all three lines of work. Pattern languages matter wherever exact string structure must be reasoned about.
arxiv-2512-07976:
Lazar Milikic, Manthan Patel, and Jonas Frey wrote this 2025 robotics paper on teaching machines to navigate. End-to-end policies that steer robots straight from camera images are hard to train. Simulation skills transfer poorly, and real action labels are scarce.

Their framework, VLD, splits the problem into perception and control. A distance-to-goal predictor is trained first, on internet-scale video alone. Self-supervision lets it judge how far any image sits from a goal. Goals may arrive as pictures or as plain text descriptions. A reinforcement learning policy then learns to minimize that predicted distance. Training happens entirely in simulation with true geometric distances. Noise is injected to mimic the predictor's real-world uncertainty. At deployment, the policy consumes the learned distance signal instead. Semantic knowledge of where to go comes from the video training. Sturdy low-level steering comes from the simulated practice.
arxiv-2512-08076:
Min Seung Ko, Jae Woong Shim, and Hao Zhu, power systems engineers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is the strain that hyperscale artificial intelligence datacenters place on the electric grid. Huge training loads ramp and fluctuate sharply, stressing grid frequency and voltage stability for everyone else on the network.

The authors propose a hybrid energy storage system that pairs a battery with a supercapacitor under coordinated control. A filter splits demand into slow and fast parts, sending slow swings to the battery and fast ones to the supercapacitor. Extra mechanisms handle repeating patterns and keep both devices at healthy charge levels over long, random training cycles. Case studies show the scheme smooths both ramping and fluctuation, steadies system frequency, and keeps storage use sustainable. The work offers grid operators a practical buffer against datacenter load shocks.
arxiv-2512-08276:
Kristoffer Simula, Johannes Hauskrecht, Evelin Martine Corvid Christlmaier, and colleagues, quantum chemists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is computing the wave functions of solids accurately, a task plagued by three errors at once: finite size, incomplete basis sets, and electron correlation. They bring a method called transcorrelation, long used for molecules, into the world of crystals.

The team extends transcorrelated theory to periodic systems and unifies it with embedding, where a fragment of the solid gets a high level solver. Silicon serves as the test case, checked against coupled cluster and quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks for the bulk crystal. They then compute formation energies for two silicon self interstitial defects, a classic hard problem. The transcorrelated approach converged fast with basis size and gave reliable defect energies at modest cost. That eases the basis set bottleneck that has limited wave function methods for real, defected materials.
arxiv-2512-08576:
Hannah Bakker, Gianfranco Guastaroba, Stefan Nickel, and M Grazia Speranza, operations researchers in Germany and Italy, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their problem is a logistics classic: choose which warehouses to open, and assign every customer to exactly one, without overloading any facility. Their method, PaKS, is a two phase heuristic that first reads the geography hidden inside the problem.

Phase one applies pattern recognition to split candidate sites and customers into regions where siting and assignment choices are tightly linked. Phase two runs an enhanced kernel search, a method that solves small chosen sub problems exactly, now guided by those regional links. On over a hundred benchmarks, PaKS beat standard kernel search and the best known heuristic, landing essentially on the best known solutions. On fresh, larger instances it again found the most best solutions.
arxiv-2512-08676:
Dung The Tran extends a classic result in combinatorics on partitions of the natural numbers to curved surfaces with circle symmetry. Raimi theorem says a partition of the numbers has a strong unavoidability property under any finite coloring. Recent work carried a similar idea to the circle group, using measurable partitions and rotations.

Tran shows the phenomenon also holds on spheres, on rotational power surfaces such as cones and paraboloids, and on circular cylinders. Each surface carries a rotation action by the circle and splits as a product, so a partition from the base circle can be lifted to the surface. A general circle bundle theorem unifies the three cases. The proof checks the needed symmetry and measure properties for each family of surfaces.
arxiv-2512-08776:
Ferhat Tas introduces surfaces built from brachistochrone curves, the paths that minimize travel time under gravity. The classic brachistochrone is a cycloid in a constant gravitational field. Tas first builds a Newtonian worldsheet whose rulings are such time minimizing paths between pairs of endpoints.

The construction is then extended to stationary relativistic spacetimes. Arrival time problems there reduce to length problems of Finsler or Jacobi type on a spatial manifold, so relativistic brachistochrones become geodesics of that structure. Worked examples cover flat spacetime, where the curves are straight timelike lines and a simple ruled family is fully geodesic. The curved Schwarzschild case is also treated, with time minimization at fixed energy reduced to a Jacobi metric and a numerical scheme outlined. Basic geometric properties and natural Jacobi fields along the rulings are discussed.
arxiv-2512-08976:
Isha Chaturvedi and coauthors introduce Contrastive Region Masking, a training free diagnostic for how multimodal language models use visual regions during reasoning. Prior tools look only at final answers or at attention maps, which cannot show causal dependence on specific image regions. Their method fills that gap at the level of individual reasoning steps.

The diagnostic masks annotated regions one by one and contrasts the resulting reasoning traces with an unmasked baseline. Applied to a visual argument data set, it reveals distinct failure modes across models. Some models keep their reasoning structure but invent details when key evidence is masked. Others ground tightly to visual cues yet collapse when the input is perturbed. By shifting evaluation from answer correctness to reasoning faithfulness, the method reframes visual benchmarks as diagnostic tools. The authors argue that future evaluation should measure robustness and fidelity of reasoning, not just final performance scores.
arxiv-2512-09676:
Shahroze Shahab, Aditi Chakrabarty, and Sanjoy Datta study how two ingredients reshape the topological phases of one-dimensional p-wave superconductors. The ingredients are Rashba spin-orbit coupling and non-Hermiticity, the gain and loss that appears when a system is open. Kitaev chains are the model of such superconductors and host boundary modes. The two ingredients had been studied separately.

The authors consider two kinds of complex on-site potential: a uniform gain-loss term, and a complex quasiperiodic potential. Rashba coupling's impact proves model-dependent. In the uniform model it leaves the Hermitian topological boundary untouched but alters the landscape once non-Hermiticity is on. In the quasiperiodic model it moves boundaries in both regimes. Combining non-Hermiticity with Rashba coupling drives topological transitions at much lower potential strengths than the Hermitian limit. Expressions for the transitions are checked against numerical spectra and real-space winding numbers.
arxiv-2512-09876:
Frédéric Déglise, Niels Feld, and Fangzhou Jin build a general theory of Milnor-Witt cycle modules over arbitrary base schemes. The new theory works over an excellent base scheme equipped with a dimension function. From any such module the authors build a Rost-Schmid type complex. Its homology gives a Borel-Moore style intersection theory with quadratic coefficients, enjoying the standard package of properties.

The theory enjoys homotopy invariance, localization, pushforwards, pullbacks, and Gysin maps. Using duality data from pinning structures, the authors define a matching cohomological theory and prove the two versions are equivalent. As applications, Chow-Witt groups now extend to schemes over possibly singular or arithmetic bases. They prove Bloch formulas, representability results, and finiteness in low dimension.
arxiv-2512-10076:
Luca Moreno-Louzada, Guilherme Figueira, and Pedro Picchetti scrutinize a popular research design in economics: using commodity prices to study how regions absorb economy wide shocks. Regions differ in their exposure to a commodity, so one global price swing hits them unevenly, mimicking an experiment. Unlike shift share designs that blend many shocks, this design leans on a single one, which strains identification and statistical inference. The authors ground the design in a multi sector labor model.

Those estimands turn out to be weighted averages of region and sector effects, plus contamination terms driven by how prices covary and by general equilibrium responses. The authors give conditions for a clean causal reading, plus simple sensitivity checks when conditions fail. They also show standard errors in this design overreject: results look significant too often. Their corrected estimator, tested in simulations, behaves better. In their Amazon case, the headline effect loses significance.
arxiv-2512-10176:
Phuc V. Trinh leads a team reviewing how classical and quantum communication might share one set of radios. Next generation wireless networks want quantum communication integrated for security against quantum computing attacks. Running it as separate infrastructure is expensive, creates compatibility problems, and demands extra hardware everywhere. The alternative explored here is simultaneous classical and quantum communication: a single transceiver jointly encodes and decodes both kinds of information on the same signal. The authors survey recent progress on such protocols and what they make possible.

A second theme is range beyond optics. Most quantum communication lives in optical bands; the authors argue for pushing into terahertz and even millimeter wave and microwave frequencies, where future wireless systems will operate. That would widen where quantum security can be applied. The paper closes by naming three open challenges that block practical deployment.
arxiv-2512-10476:
Ricardo Peña Román and a large team report the first detailed magnetic imaging of a synthetic antiferromagnet, a layered material built to hold complex three-dimensional spin textures. Reading those textures without disturbing them is essential for learning how they work and how to tailor them. But measuring their stray fields at the nanoscale, in numbers, has stayed hard.

The team used a scanning probe built around nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond, working at room conditions, and ran it in several imaging modes with probes of different orientations. They mapped antiferromagnetic domains whose borders hold narrow ferromagnetic stripes, and separated steady stray fields from the hiss of thermal spin waves at gigahertz rates. The result is a non-invasive way to measure modern magnetic materials with nanometre detail and high sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-10676:
Ali Ghalavand and co-authors probe the anti-Ramsey number, a quantity from a 1975 problem of Erdős and others. Colour the edges of a complete graph with as many colours as possible while avoiding a rainbow copy of a target graph, one using every colour distinctly. The most colours possible without one is the anti-Ramsey number. The authors study which edges of the target are neutral, removable without changing that number.

Their target is a disjoint union of paths, some of length four and some single edges, and they focus on the inner edges of the longer paths. Neutrality was known when the single edges outnumber the paths. This paper finds the values where neutrality survives in the opposite regime, for graph sizes in a set range. And since matching numbers are understood, that completes the anti-Ramsey number in those cases. A conjecture extends the pattern further.
arxiv-2512-10776:
Bruce Elmegreen, Deidre Hunter, and Edvige Corbelli test whether pressure governs star formation in the smallest galaxies. In spiral galaxies, the rate of star formation tracks the midplane pressure, the weight of gas, stars, and dark matter pressing on the gas layer. The authors take twenty-four dwarf irregular galaxies from the LITTLE THINGS survey and ask whether the link survives where pressures are feeble and dark matter rules the gravity.

The correlations held at every resolution. They compare with the outer disc of M33, a similar, slightly richer galaxy in metals, where carbon monoxide can be detected. From that comparison they estimate the molecular share. The star formation rate per molecule comes out constant across the dwarfs. At low pressure and metal content, carbon monoxide traces dense gas, like HCN does in spirals. So the CO-bright regions in dwarfs should be self-gravitating.
arxiv-2512-10876:
Pierre-Alexis Roy and a large team report a surprise from the James Webb Space Telescope: three similar sub-Neptune planets with three different skies. Transits of K2-18b and TOI-270d had shown molecular absorption and little haze, suggesting temperate sub-Neptunes have clear atmospheres and water-rich compositions. Whether that held for the whole class was an open question. And LP 791-18c was the third test, sitting between the other two in size, mass, and temperature.

Its transmission spectrum looks drastically different. Methane is present, as in the others, but haze scattering dominates the spectrum and no carbon dioxide absorption shows. The team infers a deep, metal-enriched atmosphere with little carbon dioxide relative to methane, implying less water in the envelope and a dry birth inside the water ice line. Near-twins in density and temperature, it turns out, can differ wildly in haze and chemistry.
arxiv-2512-10976:
Xin Li proposes a new framework for understanding how the brain turns messy sensory input into fast, coherent thought. Brains run on slow, noisy, costly tissue, yet perception feels quick and unified. Older theories based on vectors and instant error correction struggle to explain that gap between slow learning and fast understanding.

The Homological Brain view uses algebraic topology, the math of shapes and holes, to describe neural computation. A parity principle splits stable content from changing context, and a three step process of search, closure, and condensation turns hard searches into easy navigation over learned structure. Li links this process to sleep, memory consolidation, and fast versus slow thinking, treating the brain as an engine that reduces topological complexity.
arxiv-2512-11076:
Jack Brady, Andrew Dailey, Kristen Schang, and Zo Vic Shong survey how event based cameras could help cities track human movement while protecting privacy. These cameras do not record full colour frames. Instead, they register changes in light, which lets them work in low light and capture fast motion with little redundant data.

The survey traces how urban monitoring grew from manual observation to cameras and sensors, then reviews event camera uses, strengths, and limits. Because the devices record motion patterns rather than detailed images, they can supply useful crowd and traffic information with less intrusion. The authors also propose pairing them with infrared, lidar, or vibration sensors. Such fusion, they argue, could overcome the cameras' weaknesses and improve studies of city dynamics.
arxiv-2601-06676:
Yingchaojie Feng and co-authors present IDRBench in 2026, an interactive deep research benchmark. Deep research agents use language models for multi-step reasoning. They explore the web and generate long-form reports from findings.

Most existing systems operate autonomously, assuming fully specified user intent. They are evaluated only on their final outputs, the authors note. In practice, research goals are often underspecified at the start. Goals also evolve during exploration as users learn more. Sustained interaction is thus essential for robust alignment with users. IDRBench evaluates agents across that interaction, not just final reports. Benchmark designers get a model for testing dialogue-driven research. Agent builders can see where clarification helps or hurts quality.
arxiv-2601-07076:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Ewa Bednarczuk and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Primal-Dual algorithms for abstract convex functions with respect to quadratic functions. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The authors consider the saddle point problem where the objective functions are abstract convex with respect to the class of quadratic functions.

The authors propose primal-dual algorithms using the corresponding abstract proximal operator and investigate the convergence under certain restrictions. We test our algorithms by several numerical examples. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07176:
Guanglin Rang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with local linearization for the nonlinear damped stochastic Klein-Gordon equation. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Abstract: For the 1+1 dimensional nonlinear damped stochastic Klein-Gordon equation driven by space-time white noise. We prove that the second-order increments of the solution can be approximated.

After scaling with the diffusion coefficient, by those of the corresponding linearized stochastic Klein-Gordon equation. This extends the result of Huang et al. [ 18 ] for the stochastic wave equation. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07776:
Roger Casals writes a short note linking two counts from different parts of mathematics. Bruhat numbers come from real Morse theory, which studies smooth functions through their critical points. Cluster variables come from braid varieties, spaces tied to algebraic combinatorics. Casals relates the first to the second. The note appears as a 2026 preprint on wall-crossing coordinates in Cerf theory.

Wall-crossing coordinates track how quantities change as a path crosses a boundary between regimes. Cerf diagrams organize families of functions and their changes. Finding cluster variables inside this story connects Morse theory to a fast-growing algebraic framework. Short bridges like this often open new computation tools on both sides. The note is aimed at geometers and topologists. Its subject classifications span contact geometry, topology, and cluster algebras.
arxiv-2601-07976:
Hongwei Lin and Howard C. Gifford advance task-based assessment of medical images with a model observer that searches like a person. Their 2026 preprint develops an anthropomorphic thresholded visual-search model observer. The model is an ideal observer adapted to thresholded data and inspired by the human visual system. It selectively processes high-salience features. That filtering improves discrimination performance in the search task.

Model observers predict how well imaging systems support real diagnostic tasks. Thresholding mimics how humans ignore low-value detail to focus effort. Filtering out irrelevant variability raises accuracy and computational efficiency together. Such models let designers compare scanners without costly human reader studies. The paper serves medical imaging scientists. It refines a tool used to judge image quality by task value rather than looks.
arxiv-2601-08076:
Mikolaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki reply to a recent proposal in quantum theory. Their 2026 arXiv comment examines a paper by Vigoureux on superposition of states. Vigoureux had suggested swapping the usual linear superposition rule for a Mobius-type composition law.

The proposal drew on three sources for support. They were bounded composition laws in special relativity, transfer-matrix formulas in layered optics, and the inclusion-exclusion rule for classical chance. A comment paper tests whether such analogies can carry a change to a core quantum rule. Readers get a close check on a bold claim, written for physicists who follow debates over quantum foundations.
arxiv-2601-08176: Lavanya Prahallad and co-authors study how prompt design shapes automatic clarity scoring for political answers. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that judging language model responses needs clarity, not just factual correctness. Political question answering makes clarity and evasion especially important to track. Recent datasets supply human labels for clarity and evasion in this setting. The team uses the CLARITY dataset from the SemEval-2026 shared task. Their focus is the underexplored effect of prompt wording on whether automatic judges match human clarity judgments.
arxiv-2601-08376: Masahiro Kawamata and co-authors determine the magnetic structure of EuTi2Al20. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a compound where magnetic europium ions form a diamond network. The team used neutron and resonant X-ray diffraction on powder and single-crystal samples. From these measurements they fixed the propagation vector at (1, 0, 0) in reciprocal lattice units. The structure is collinear, with moments aligned along one axis. Diamond lattice magnets host rich physics, so a firm structure anchors later work on their excitations.
arxiv-2601-08676:
Yilei Zhao and five co-authors work on green and fair scores for firms. Such scores judge how a firm treats the earth, its staff, and its own rules. The facts for these scores lie in many loose text sources. That spread makes expert checks slow and hard to do well.

The team builds an expert level agent for this task. An agent here is a program that can plan steps and use tools. They also build a broad test set for green finance work. The test set lets others check how well such agents do. A reader gets both a new tool and a fair way to grade tools of this kind.
arxiv-2601-08776:
Yanhua Zhao works on a way to make lab images look like the stained slides doctors know best. In most labs, tissue is dyed pink and blue so staff can read it with ease. Light sheet scans give rich views, but they look quite unlike those dyed slides. Staff may find them hard to read at first.

Zhao uses a pair of rival nets called a CycleGAN. One net turns light sheet views into fake dyed views. The next net turns them back, which keeps the first net true to the source. No paired slides are needed to train the pair. A reader in lab work gets a bridge from new scan types to a form the eye knows well.
arxiv-2601-09676:
Rob Behary and eight co-authors study how a steady electric field tilts a quantum transparency effect. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines electromagnetically induced transparency involving highly excited Rydberg states. The team varies the angle between the laser polarization and the external field.

That orientation changes the transparency resonances in ways the paper maps out. Rydberg atoms are prized sensors because their outer electrons reach far and react strongly. Knowing how a stray field's direction shifts the signal matters for precision devices. The results help calibrate sensors that use transparency as their readout.
arxiv-2601-09776:
Khalid Oublal and four co-authors explain black-box forecasts of time series with sparse decoding. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents TimeSAE, built for faithful explanations. As pretrained models spread in time series work, users need to know why a forecast came out as it did.

The stakes are highest where trust matters, such as medicine and finance. Most explanation methods work only inside the training distribution. They falter on new regimes, exactly where explanations are needed most. TimeSAE aims for explanations that stay faithful well beyond the range of the training support.
arxiv-2601-10076:
Matthew Zhang proves sharp rates for how a crowd of grains acts as one. Each grain is pushed by the rest. Over time, the crowd can settle to a fixed spread. That shift is named propagation of chaos. It says the grains act more free as the crowd grows.

Zhang works at the rest state of such a crowd. He uses a ranked chain of facts from past work. He bounds the gap in Rényi terms, a broad gap gauge. The bounds hold when the base spread is well curved and the push is weak. The rates are sharp, which means no slack is left.
arxiv-2601-10176:
Mingyu Zhao, Haoran Bai, Yu Tian, Bing Zhu, and Hengliang Luo guess the long term worth of a user. This worth is named lifetime value. It is a core call in ad work. Most users are worth a small sum. A few whales are worth a vast sum.

That shape makes the guess hard. The mass of small users can swamp the whales in the math. Small users also vary a lot among them. The team built CC-OR-Net to split the task in two. It parts users by kind first. It then makes a worth call for each kind on its own terms.
arxiv-2601-10376:
Mohammad Rowshan and Vlad-Florin Drăgoi build polar codes with both reach and weight in mind. Polar codes rank their bit paths by trust. That rank plan gives codes that can hit the cap of a line. But it can yield poor low weight forms at short lengths.

Low weight words set how oft a code fails at high trust. Past algebra gives each path's part in those words in closed form. The team blend the two guides. Trust ranks one part. Weight counts rule the rest. The aim is a code that is sound on both counts.
arxiv-2601-10576:
Shaohua Yue, Siyu Miao, Shuhao Zeng, Fenghan Lin, and Boya Di study massive MIMO, a core tool planned for 6G wireless networks. Massive MIMO uses many antennas at once. It offers many degrees of freedom, which raise how much data can flow at once. The team asks how many of those degrees a real system can truly reach.

They bring in characteristic mode analysis, a tool from antenna theory, to derive the reachable degrees of freedom. The method looks at the natural modes of the antenna structure itself. That view can guide how antennas are shaped and placed. The paper speaks to engineers who design the next wave of wireless hardware.
arxiv-2601-11276:
R. Ricci studies a new class of special functions in this 2026 preprint. The functions arose in work on hot, magnetized plasma. There they enter the linear susceptibility tensor, a core plasma tool. The class sits close to Bessel, Anger, and Weber functions.

Ricci checks the basic traits of these new functions. They solve a Bessel-type equation with an added term. Set starting values pin down which solution is meant. The added term meets a known condition due to Nielsen. Such checks turn a handy formula into a sound tool. Plasma physics can then use the class with more trust.
arxiv-2601-11376:
Karsten Muller and Michael Taktikos make a deep number theory bound effective. Their 2026 preprint links the ABC conjecture to Roth's theorem. Roth's theorem bounds how well irrationals can be approximated. Bombieri showed in 1994 that ABC would imply Roth's result.

Van Frankenhuysen gave a full proof of that link in 1999. The new work builds on an explicit formula by Bombieri. Van der Poorten shares credit for that formula on coefficients. The formula covers continued-fraction coefficients of algebraic numbers. The team narrows it to cubic roots as the test case. From it they derive a hard bound for a Roth-type constant. The bound holds if an effective form of ABC is true.
arxiv-2601-11476:
Allen Shafter and Kamil Hornoch read basic traits of novae in M31. Their 2026 preprint uses a large sample from Clark and others. Novae are stellar blasts on white dwarfs in the Andromeda galaxy. Peak brightness and fade rate are logged for each nova.

The team fits those logs with Yaron's nova models. From the fits they estimate traits of the whole population. The white dwarf mass spread comes out near Gaussian in form. Its mean sits near 1.16 solar masses in their count. That is heavy, close to the known Chandrasekhar limit. Such census work tests how novae enrich and shape galaxies. It also checks the models used to read stellar blasts.
arxiv-2601-11776:
Kaituo Zhang, Zhimeng Jiang, and Na Zou present a way to clean toxic output from large language models. Large models can fix and grade their own text to some degree. Most clean-up tools so far do not use that skill. They add outer parts, hand marked data, or human help, which is slow and hard to scale.

Their frame leans on the model's own self-checks in place of outer help. A self-led clean-up could stay more smooth as models grow. It could also cut the cost of marked data. The work tests if a model can spot and fix its own toxic text in a sound loop.
arxiv-2601-12076:
Haochen Jiang, Yuzhe Sun, Zhe Dong, Tianzhu Liu, and Yanfeng Gu track objects named in text in remote sensing video. The task joins video segmentation with a text brief for the target. Far views make targets faint, and dynamic scenes often cut off key views.

Their tool, named in the work, controls memory quality as it tracks. Good memory keeps the target's traits clear across frames. Weak memory lets drift and clutter spoil the cut. The work aims for steadier cuts in hard aerial video.  Good tracks help watch coasts, fields, and roads from air.
arxiv-2601-12376:
Ofek Raban, Ethan Fetaya, and Gal Chechik write on watermarking text from language models. A watermark marks text so that readers can tell it came from a model. It also helps link the text back to its source. Most past methods were built for models that write one token at a time, in strict order.

That order based design fits a world that is now changing. A newer class of models, called diffusion language models, does not write in the same strict sequence. Old marks lean on the text sampled so far, so they may not carry over well. The team puts forward LR-DWM, a mark built for this newer class. The goal is a mark that stays fast and still holds up.
arxiv-2601-12476:
Omkar Dhamane and a large team study energy conversion in the solar wind during a solar storm. The storm is an interplanetary coronal mass ejection, a cloud of plasma thrown off by the Sun. Inside the magnetic cloud of such an event, bursts of turbulence are less common than outside. The team found two such bursts in data from the Wind spacecraft.

The data come from June 8 and 9 in the year 2000. The plasma there is weakly collisional, so particles rarely bump into each other. The team characterize the wave types present in the two bursts. Waves are a main route for energy to move in such plasmas. Knowing which waves appear helps explain how energy converts during these storms.
arxiv-2601-12776:
Yonghui Bo and Yushun Wang construct numerical schemes for Hamiltonian partial differential equations. Hamiltonian systems conserve energy, and good schemes should preserve that trait. Their approach uses Lagrange multipliers to build linearly implicit schemes of arbitrary order. Linearly implicit methods are cheap per step, while high order keeps errors small.

A widely used rival approach relies on auxiliary variables. That approach needs the nonlinear part of the energy to be bounded below. The new method drops that requirement, offering broader applicability. Energy preserving schemes run longer without drifting off course. They matter for waves, plasmas, and molecular dynamics alike. The work was supported by Chinese science foundations.
arxiv-2601-12976:
Wenhao Gao and ten co authors jointly analyze galaxy clustering and galaxy galaxy lensing from BOSS galaxies. Clustering maps how galaxies group in space, while lensing measures the mass around them. A joint analysis squeezes more cosmology from the same sky survey. Their method uses simulation based emulation with a halo occupation model.

The emulators are built from a suite of N body simulations with massive neutrinos. Those simulations treat neutrinos as an independent particle species. Emulation replaces slow full simulations with fast learned surrogates inside the fit. Small scale data carry rich signal but are hard to model directly. This approach aims to unlock that signal for cosmology.
arxiv-2601-13076:
Gabriele Parisi wrote a thesis on heavy quarks in the first instants of proton ion crashes. Heavy quarks are the heaviest bits of matter, made fresh in high energy hits. The thesis rests in large part on joint papers with Vincenzo Greco and Marco Ruggieri.

One named paper treats uneven swings of momentum and of spin like motion for heavy quarks. That work sits in the pre balance stage of proton nucleus crashes at the Large Hadron Collider. It appeared in Physical Review D in 2025. Readers get a guide to how heavy quarks move before the hot matter from the crash settles.
arxiv-2601-13176:
Joseph G. Schulze, Natalie R. Hinkel, Wendy R. Panero, and Cayman T. Unterborn warn care in how small far worlds are read. The bulk make up of a small world ties straight to how it was born. Yet no probe can see inside such a world. Its make up must be read from mass and size alone, through a model.

Those models lean on star make up and on laws for how stuff acts at high crush. The team sets models side by side and asks where the laws part ways. They urge care in how much trust a single model read gets. For world birth staff, the piece is a check list for sound claims about rocky worlds.
arxiv-2601-13476:
Jinhao Li and Hao Wang fill gaps in electric vehicle charge data with a retrieval led language model in one joint frame. Charge data feeds demand guesses for the charge grid. Real sets are full of gaps. Old fill tools bend poorly to the rich mix of charge data. Many train one model per station, a form that wastes shared facts.

Their frame imputes gaps in a variational way, a chance based fill with a firm score. A language model fed by pulled kin cases leads the fill. One frame serves all stations at once. For grid teams, a sound fill of charge gaps lifts all down stream guesses.
arxiv-2601-13676:
Fabian Greifeneder and co-authors build a fast brain tissue simulator for virtual neurosurgery in 2026. True-to-life training tools must show how brain tissue bends and shifts. Tool-tissue contact makes complex, nonlinear shapes as the work goes on. Classic solvers can capture that, but they run too slowly for live use.

The team uses autoregressive deep learning, which predicts each next state from the last. That style can run fast once trained, step by step in real time. Trainees could then feel how tissue reacts as they work. Fast, true tissue models could make surgical training safer and richer.
arxiv-2601-14376:
Xiyuan Gao and Amir N. Khan study neutrino masses in this 2026 paper. Neutrinos are the lightest known particles with mass. The authors assume all three known neutrinos are Dirac fermions, particles distinct from their antiparticles. Under that take, the U(1) B-L symmetry can be exact. B-L is baryon number minus lepton number.

The team then relaxes one rule: charge quantization. With that change, the B-L charges of two of the three right-handed neutrinos can be enhanced by arbitrarily large factors. All other fermions keep their canonical charges. Their title calls this enhanced B-L symmetry. The paper maps what such an enhanced symmetry does to neutrino mass models.
arxiv-2601-14776:
Xiaofan Yang and seven co-authors improve multi-modal object detection in this 2026 paper. Recent advances in multi-modal detection have significantly improved detection accuracy in challenging environments, such as low light and overexposure. Integrating RGB images with modalities such as thermal and depth increases data redundancy and system robustness. Significant challenges remain, though.

The hard parts are extracting task-relevant information within and across modalities, and achieving precise cross-modal alignment. Their model, M2I2HA, is based on intra- and inter-modal hypergraph attention. Hypergraphs let one link join many items at once, a natural fit for cross-sensor groups. Rain, glare, and dusk are where weak tools fail, and this one is built for them. When one sense fails, the rest must pick up the slack. Readers get a fusion design for detectors that must work when one sense goes dark.
arxiv-2601-14876:
Antonin Grateau, Alexander Boeschoten, Tanguy Favin-Lévêque, Isael Herrera, and Nicolas Treps test a way to see two light sources that sit very close together. Their 2026 arXiv paper is about beating the blur limit of normal optics. The two sources shine on their own, with no shared phase.

The team sorts the light by its spatial modes, a method called SPADE. They use two such sorters, with one shifted on purpose. In the lab they gauge the gap, the center point, and the brightness split at once. The gaps they find sit well below the classic blur limit.
arxiv-2601-15176:
Alain Lecavelier des Etangs, Paul Strøm, and Darryl Z. Seligman propose names for single comets beyond our solar system. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with exocomets, comets that orbit other stars. The field has entered a new phase in recent years.

At first, scientists just had to prove that a signal truly came from an exocomet. Now single detections are studied in detail to characterize each body. That shift calls for a nomenclature, a shared naming scheme. The authors set one out so that teams can refer to the same object clearly.
arxiv-2601-15576:
Chenyang Xu and Ziquan Zhuang survey open problems in K-stability in a 2026 arXiv paper. K-stability theory concerns Fano varieties, a class of geometric spaces. A central aim in geometry is to find an optimal structure on a manifold. In differential geometry, one such structure is a metric solving the vacuum Einstein equations. The Kähler-Einstein problem asks when such metrics exist. K-stability gives an algebraic test linked to that question.

Rather than solve one problem, the note gathers many open ones. It maps where the theory stands and where it is stuck. Survey notes like this guide a field's next steps. Young researchers can see which questions are ripe. Senior readers get a compact status report on a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2601-15876:
Taofeng Xue and a large team train computer-use agents from synthetic practice in a 2026 arXiv paper. Computer-use agents operate software through its interface. They mark a real leap in multimodal AI. Their growth is bottlenecked by static data scaling, though. Learning by imitating fixed datasets misses causal dynamics. Long computer tasks hinge on causes: one click changes what the next should be. Their system is EvoCUA.

EvoCUA evolves agents through scalable synthetic experience, per the title. Synthetic tasks can be generated in bulk and varied at will. Agents learn by doing, not just by watching. That shift mirrors how people gain computer skill. For software automation, agents that recover and adapt across long tasks are the goal this work pursues.
arxiv-2601-15976:
Gloria Odak and Salvatore Ribisi extend a variant of general relativity in a 2026 arXiv paper. The variant is Weyl-transverse gravity. It is classically equivalent to general relativity, the authors note. Its gauge symmetry is smaller, though. It allows Weyl transformations and transverse diffeomorphisms only. A fixed background volume form is part of the setup. The authors develop its covariant phase space formulation in the presence of boundaries.

Boundaries can be timelike or spacelike in their treatment. Edges matter in phase space methods because charges live there. A formulation that handles general boundaries makes the theory usable for finite regions. Such regions are where physics is actually computed. The work serves relativists comparing alternative formulations of gravity.
arxiv-2601-16376:
Vani Nigam, Achuth Chandrasekhar and Amir Barati Farimani set an agent to design polymers. Their 2026 preprint, named PolyAgent, deals with on call polymer finds. New polymers serve health, build and strength fields. Lab trials for them are slow and eat much time and stock. Past machine tools sped finds but still need much hand work.

An agent built on a large language model can plan find steps. It can call tools, read results and pick next tries on its own. That loop cuts the hand work in each find round. The team tests the agent on real design tasks. The work seeks fast, low cost polymer finds.
arxiv-2601-16476:
The BESIII group hunts a rare glow decay of a strange charmed meson. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Ds meson and a K star end state. The hunt uses clash data from the BESIII probe. Data span a set range of clash heat at its heart. A joint fit hunts the faint sign of the rare decay.

Rare decays test the known model of grains in fine ways. A seen sign would pin a rate the model must match. No sign sets a cap that the model must not cross. Both ends thus sharpen grain maths in the charm field. The work is a probe note from a big group.
arxiv-2601-16576:
W. Geremew, V. S. T. Long, N. M. Nam, and A. Solano-Herrera work on a hard math task. A firm must place sites, like depots or shops, to serve many users. The best count of sites is not known in advance. Their 2026 preprint builds a new model for this task.

The model adds a cost term that curbs needless sites. The team then finds a way to solve it step by step. They prove that best-fit answers do exist. They also study traits of those best answers. Tests on a screen back the math. The work may aid plans for stores, clinics, and charge points.
arxiv-2601-16676:
Andrii Dmytryshyn, Froilán Dopico, and Rakel Hellberg work on a niche task in matrix math. Some tasks use rules that link numbers in a grid over time-like steps. A few of those grids must stay skewed, with a mirror twist. Real data grids are rough and may break that trait. Their 2026 preprint finds the near skewed grid of a set rank.

Their method builds on fresh work on grid forms and splits. It takes a rough grid and trims it to the near fit. The rank cap keeps the fit from mere copy. Such near fits help in tests of speech, signals, and forms. Clean math here feeds tools far past pure math.
arxiv-2601-16776:
Jiaqi Hu, Shu Tian, Xiaopeng Cui, Rebing Wu, Man-Hong Yung, and Yu Shi extend a famed math link in gauge theory. Gauge rules on a grid can map to spin grids in a twin form. That twin form is called Wegner duality. On odd shapes, like rings with holes, the link stayed unclear. Their 2026 preprint clears that fog for all shapes and depths.

Their twin spin grids code shape in far-off wall paths. The work also sets up how quantum sims can use the link. Odd shapes show up in codes that guard quantum data. A clear twin map helps build and test those codes.
arxiv-2601-16876:
Moisés Davi tests guards for the power lines of sea wind farms. Sea farms send power to land through deep cables. New grid gear turns that power for long hauls. Faults in farm cables act in odd ways there. Both cable ends feed fault flow from smart gear. That trait can fool old-style guards.

His 2026 preprint checks how split guards fare on such cables. Split guards compare flow at both ends of a line. The work maps where those guards hold or fail. Sound guards stop faults fast and save costly gear. Sea wind growth makes such checks more key each year.
arxiv-2601-16976:
Estela Sánchez-Carballo, Francisco Melgarejo-Meseguer, and José Luis Rojo-Álvarez grow fake attack data to guard smart gear. Guards that watch net traffic learn from past flows. Attack flows are rare next to plain flows. That skew makes guards blind to rare attacks. Past fixes copy rare flows or grow crude fakes.

Their 2026 preprint grows fakes with a spread-based AI. Such AI can make fakes that look rich and true. It can also run at fair cost on small gear. Rich fakes may teach guards to catch rare IoT attacks. Smart homes and wards need that guard skill.
arxiv-2601-17076:
Jiajun Chen and a team of eight co-authors teach web tools that learn in hard, mixed streams. Web apps join text, shots, and sound from many sources. Class sets grow as new themes show up. Views oft miss from the stream, with gaps in spots. Their 2026 preprint builds a prompt-learn tool for that mix. The tool is named E2PL.
