F. H. Bradley published Ethical Studies in 1876, a set of essays on moral philosophy. Bradley attacks hedonism, the view that pleasure is the good, and Kantian duty done for duty's sake alone. Against both he sets self-realization: the self grows whole by taking its place in a moral community. My station and its duties is his famous phrase for that view.

Morality, he argues, lives in the customs and roles of a real society. Yet the self must also go beyond mere social rules toward an ideal. The book is the great statement of idealist ethics in English. It shaped welfare liberalism through readers like T. H. Green.
britten-art-magic-1876:
Emma Hardinge Britten said a sage's ghost taught her the lore in Art Magic, her dense tract of 1876. The ghost bears the name Cheval Louis de B. Through her hand he maps the schools, rites, and laws of the occult from old Egypt to her own day.

Ranks of spirits, charms, and the risks of rite fill the book. Britten casts it as fact, not tale. Groups in the United States took it as a core text of rite. It is a ground stone of magic in that land. Britten had a flair for the grand claim, and she backs it here with dense lore. Fans must sift her zeal from her facts with care.
britten-ghost-land-1876:
Tales of hunts for truth in far lands fill Ghost Land, Emma Hardinge Britten's book of 1876. It is the mate to her Art Magic of the same year. Britten tracks adepts, bands, and marvels through Europe and past it. She writes as one who claims to have seen much at first hand.

Ghost lore here mixes trek tale with creed. Dark rooms, odd cures, and bands with hid names crowd the pages. Britten kept the teller's name hid at first print. The pair of books maps the hid world she claimed to know. Her claims drew both faith and scorn in her own day. That split still marks the book, which fans read as trek tale and creed at once.
burton-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-1876:
Richard Burton, the boldest traveler of his age, went after the gorilla in 1876. Two Trips to Gorilla Land and the Cataracts of the Congo tells his search in Gabon. Burton had crossed Africa and Arabia; the great ape still drew him on.

He tells of rivers, trade, fevers, and the falls of the Congo, with the gorilla as his grail. His pen is dry, learned, and full of the lore of the coast. The book adds his great name to the gorilla shelf of his century. Few explorers wrote with his mix of grit and wit.
cia-0000009376:
Japan's strategic importance is spelled out in a CIA paper dated April 1948. Japan then sat under American occupation, three years after its defeat in the Second World War. Planners were deciding whether Japan would stay a ward or become an ally.

The paper weighs Japan's ports, industry, and position off the Asian mainland in Cold War terms. An anchored Japan guarded sea lanes and faced the Soviet Union across narrow waters. Judgments like this one fed the policy turn toward rebuilding Japan as a partner. The file shows that turn being reasoned out on paper.
cia-0000009676:
Six American prisoners were held at the Krong R'buk detention camp, a March 1971 item reports, in a Cambodian district the title cuts short. Detention camps in Cambodia's east held men captured as the war spread across the border in 1970. Conditions in such camps were rough and poorly documented.

Naming the camp and its count of Americans gave officials a concrete target for follow-up. Six men at one site could be checked against recent border losses. The report also shows captivity becoming a Cambodian story, not only a Vietnamese one. Its details preserve a camp that few outsiders ever saw.
cia-0000009876:
Four American prisoners were seen on May 15, 1968, walking north near a Laotian village. The title cuts the village name off at Ban Nath, and the report was filed that June. A precise date stands out in files where many sightings float undated. Walking north suggested movement toward central camps or toward Vietnam.

Dated sightings let analysts build timelines no memory could blur. Four men on a road on a known day could be matched against camp movements. The northward direction fit the prison system's known flow. This file preserves the day, the direction, and the number, a small hard point in a soft record.
cia-0000010476:
Britain's position in Egypt is examined in a September 1951 CIA paper. British troops still held the Suez Canal Zone, and Egyptian nationalists demanded they leave. Egypt's government was weeks from scrapping the old treaty that kept them there.

The paper weighs the canal's strategic worth against the rising cost of holding it. Suez guarded the sea road to Asia and Middle East oil routes alike. Within five years, the Suez crisis would humiliate Britain before the world. This file catches the position early, as analysts measured an empire's slowly loosening grip in the autumn of 1951.
cia-0000012276:
Joseph Bulik, a CIA officer on the Soviet side of the house, wrote a memo for the record in July 1960 about a briefing of Mr. Helms. Richard Helms then ran the agency's clandestine side, and briefings to him carried weight. The memo sits in the Penkovsky file, among the earliest papers of the case that would define Helms's watch.

A memo for the record fixes what was said while memory is fresh. This one preserves an officer's account of decisions taken near the top. For readers, it shows the great case being weighed at the level where careers and policy met.
cia-0000012376:
Soviet intelligence had to be told, formally, that the United States cared about Oleg Penkovsky, and an April 1963 plan works out how. Informing the KGB and GRU of American concern was a signal, not a courtesy. Washington hoped open concern might soften the colonel's treatment, or at least mark that his fate was watched from the highest level.

Signaling games like this were planned as carefully as operations themselves. Draft messages to Moscow were weighed word by word for tone and leverage. For readers, the plan preserves the endgame's strange diplomacy, where even grief was expressed by design.
cia-0000014776: A printed protest from Haditu fills a CIA file dated June 5, 1953. The group spoke out against the death sentence passed on the Rosenbergs. Haditu sought freedom for its own land, per the title's plain words. The Rosenbergs died later that same month. Small groups far away still took up their cause in print.
cia-0000015276: Flying saucers are the clipped subject of a CIA file dated August 2, 1952. The name at the head of the title is cut out as deleted. The summer of 1952 was the peak of the first great saucer wave. A file from those weeks belongs to the season when Washington itself reported lights overhead.
cia-0000015376: A flying object was observed near a deleted place, in a CIA file dated September 6, 1955. The source date is marked unknown in the title. With the place cut out, little can be checked or weighed. The file still marks that a sighting claim reached the agency and was kept. The sighting claim is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015476: Non-orbit sightings of unidentified flying objects, from December 10, 1953, into March 1954, fill a CIA record filed in 1954. The odd label non-orbit sets these reports apart from satellite tracking. Winter sightings across three months were bundled for review. Such dated bundles were the bookkeeping of the saucer watch, letting staff count and sort claims season by season.
cia-0000037176:
An American man was sighted hiding in the southern part of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated March 2, 1980 reports. A man in hiding was a stranger claim than a man in a camp. The report raised questions the file itself could not answer at once.

Inside, the sighting is recorded with the odd detail that made it memorable. Was the man a prisoner, a deserter, or someone else entirely? The record leaves the question open. Files like this show the wide range of stories the postwar search had to sort, from solid leads to tales that never found an explanation.
cia-0000042676:
Further reportage on the murder of Jesuit priests fills a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. The title links the coverage to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The killings in San Salvador shocked readers far beyond El Salvador.

Inside, more reporting on the murders is gathered as it appeared. Each new account added names, places, and claims to a fast-growing file. The record shows an atrocity becoming a world story in print. Priests killed at a university drew the eyes of churches, parliaments, and editors onto one small country's war.
cia-0000042876:
El Salvador: Update on Jesuit Killings, 4, is a CIA record dated February 4, 1990. The fourth update came a month after the third in the series. That slower pace marked the case's move into legal channels.

Inside, the investigation's February position is set down in brief. Court steps, rather than fresh accusations, fill updates of this stage. The file shows the probe becoming a court case in form. Its dry entries are the sound of a scandal turning into procedure. Hard cases are usually won or lost in that dry country, far from the headlines that opened them.
cia-0000045276: President Jose Napoleon Duarte spoke in 1985 about his armed forces backing peace talks with El Salvador's rebels. A CIA item dated September 6, 1985, preserves the president's remarks. Army support mattered because the military held real power beside the elected government. The short report catches a president trying to show that his generals stood behind a negotiated end to the civil war.
cia-0000049076: Actions taken by El Salvador's minister of defense against officials accused of wrongdoing are recorded in a CIA item from 1983. Discipline from the top was the rarest commodity in the armed forces, so each move drew close reading. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, beside the many records of discipline refused.
cia-0000049176: A trace reply on Francisco Antonio Moran is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Moran is a common name in these files, attached to officers and suspects alike, which made exact traces matter. The reply gathers what the system held on this one man of the name.
cia-0000049276: Representatives Frank McCloskey, Barbara Boxer, and colleagues sat for a CIA briefing in 1989, and the session is preserved in this item. Members who fought over Central America policy armed themselves in such rooms, fact by fact and map by map. The record sits among the congressional paper in the Truth Commission files.
cia-0000049376: Managing the Salvadoran military is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049376, dated April 1, 1988. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper takes up the handling of El Salvador's armed forces. It remains a short declassified item whose title states its managerial focus, part of the later record on the military question in El Salvador.
cia-0000096476: Views of Prime Minister Jagan on British Guiana elections are recorded in declassified CIA document 0000096476, dated October 5, 1964. The heading names Jagan and the election as its paired subjects. The brief file preserves the premier's outlook as reported, filed the same day as the agency's item on the colony approaching its critical election.
cia-0000102976: USSR: Irkutsk Labor Camp for Juvenile Offenders Detailed is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000102976, dated August 2, 1983. The title promises detail on one camp near Irkutsk that held juvenile offenders. Young prisoners are the stated subject, set apart from adult camp reports nearby. The brief record is a single camp detail item from Soviet Siberia.
cia-0000106276: Communist Activity in the Laos Panhandle is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000106276, dated September 5, 1965. The heading names a region, the southern panhandle of Laos, and an activity, communist activity. No group, town, or incident is named in the title itself. The brief record is a regional activity item from the Vietnam War years in Laos.
cia-0000107976: Japan's Economic Role in the Development of Free Asia is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107976, dated April 3, 1967. The heading places Japan inside a regional story, the development of Free Asia. Free Asia is the title's own label for the region it covers. The brief record is a regional economy item from the spring of 1967.
cia-0000108476: Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism 20 August 1980 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108476, dated July 3, 1980. The title dates its week to August 20, 1980, weeks after the July file date. That gap stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is one weekly issue in the long terrorism series from 1980.
cia-0000111776: Blank and Use of Forced Labor on the Soviet Siberian Gas Pipeline are the two numbered items in declassified CIA document 0000111776, dated March 1, 1985. The catalog marks the first item blank in the title itself. The second item returns to forced labor on the Siberian gas pipeline. The brief record is a two-item cable with one item withheld in its heading.
cia-0000119676:
Dated around February 1969, this CIA item is headed U.S. Marine Deserts: Letter Explains Action. It preserves a letter in which a Marine explained why he deserted, as the report of it reached the agency. The Marine's name does not appear in the heading.

Desertion letters drew attention because they spoke to morale and to opinion about the war. Officials clipped and filed such reports to track how the conflict was playing at home and abroad. The item keeps that explanation in the record. Read with the Sweeney statement filed the same month, it shows the agency gathering the words of men who walked away from the war.
cia-0000124276: A January 1958 CIA item lists Soviet stations for watching artificial earth satellites by eye, with their map coordinates, drawn up for the International Geophysical Year. That year-long science campaign ran through 1957 and 1958 across the world. The item preserves the station list as filed. Visual tracking by volunteers armed with telescopes filled gaps that radar could not, and station lists like this one organized that worldwide amateur watch into data.
cia-0000126876: An August 1968 CIA report surveys how the world's communist parties reacted to the invasion of Czechoslovakia. Parties from Rome to Hanoi had to choose between condemning Moscow and defending it. The paper collects those reactions as they came in during the crisis. The split among parties mattered beyond the bloc, since Western communist parties lost members and standing over their answers to the invasion for a decade.
cia-0000126976: Dated October 1975, this CIA Weekly Summary covers Angola after independence, a companion to the Weekly Review's treatment of the same subject that month. The summary gives the week's condensed picture of the Angola watch for busy senior readers. Companion products served different desks, the summary condensing for general readers what the review argued at length for specialists following the same African war.
cia-0000132276:
A Soviet peace plan for the Gulf is the subject of Situation Report 582 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 1, 1991. Moscow was still working the diplomatic track while the coalition prepared for war over Kuwait.

The report examines the Soviet proposal and the shuttle diplomacy behind it. A Soviet envoy moved between Baghdad and coalition capitals carrying the plan. It looked like the last peaceful exit before fighting began. Readers can see how one final diplomatic option was weighed, day by day, inside the crisis reporting that reached American decision makers at the time.
cia-0000132776:
Regional fear shapes this CIA paper on Cuba and the Caribbean, dated August 4, 1960. Castro's example, analysts worried, was spreading encouragement to movements across the islands and coasts nearby. Washington watched Cuba's neighbors almost as closely as Cuba itself.

The Caribbean framing returns here after appearing in the spring papers, now with exile training under way. The briefing treats one revolution as a possible spark for others, the core Cold War fear in the hemisphere. Its declassified text, held through the CIA Reading Room mirror, preserves that worry in the language of the time.
cia-0000134276: Strain across the Caribbean that would not lift fills a CIA paper dated November 3, 1959. Ten months into the revolution, the neighborhood had yet to calm down. Cuba was the source of the strain, and the whole island chain felt it. The short paper surveys the tensions island by island as analysts mapped them that fall.
cia-0000135676: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 November 1960, from the declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade of Cuban exiles was training that fall for the landing it would make in April 1961. The catalog record for this item is minimal, with no subject or author stated. Among the hundreds of Spanish texts in this release, this one is identified by its date alone. It is held in its original language through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000136276: A cable dated 1 May 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on the need for consolidation phase policy plans, planning for the day after the victory. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136676: A document in Spanish dated 4 February 1961, held in the CIA's declassified 2506 Brigade files. The brigade, made up of Cuban exiles, was in the last phase of preparation for its April landing. The catalog record carries no subject for this item. It is kept in the original Spanish, one of many dated February records in the brigade's archive, and described here on that basis alone.
cia-0000136776: A Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade, dated only to 1961 in the catalog record. That year covers the brigade's final training, its April landing in Cuba, and the operation's aftermath; the record does not place this item within the year. No subject is stated for it. The text is in Spanish, preserved as released through the CIA Reading Room, part of the exile force's declassified archive.
cia-0000138976: Russian behavior in Harbin mirrors Mukden, this March 1946 report relates from a hotel manager who left Mukden in October 1945 and stayed in Harbin until March 1946. Russian forces acted as badly in Harbin as in Mukden, he states: looting, raping, and shooting at night were very common. Economically Harbin is comparatively comfortable since food is available, the excerpt adds before breaking off. The sub-source is considered fairly reliable. It is occupation reporting from Soviet-held Manchuria, months after Japan's surrender.
cia-0000139476: Father Lawrence Jenco's second debriefing leads this task force report. It covers 9-15 August 1986. Jenco was a released hostage. David Jacobsen would likely be the next one freed, he said. The captors believe Thomas Sutherland is a CIA case officer. They see Terry Anderson as a rebellious captive. A captor known as Hajj spoke in early June. All Americans would soon be released, he said. Jenco added detail on his south Beirut site. He could not identify its exact location.
cia-03020476: January 5, 1956: the bulletin opened the year's intelligence. The daily summary went to senior readers. The Cold War's new-year brief. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. This declassified paper is filed. It is filed.
cia-06485476: COMMUNIST COMMENTS ON THE DEATH OF MARTIN LUTHER KING/REFERENCE TO "BLACK POWE, a CIA document. The communist reaction. This file preserves that declassified paper. It waits for future eyes. Its place in history is secure.
cia-06568476: WARSAW PACT MILITARY PERCEPTIONS OF NATO NUCLEAR INITIATION, a CIA assessment. The Soviet view. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
cia-06929976: BIWEEKLY DEVELOPMENTS IN IRAQ, a CIA publication. The Iraq roundup. This file preserves that declassified summary. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
coley-clavis-astrologiae-1676:
Henry Coley was a London astrologer and mathematician who succeeded William Lilly as the art's leading English teacher. His Clavis Astrologiae Elimata, published in 1676, is his complete textbook of astrology. The Latin title promises a key, filed smooth for the student's hand.

Coley teaches the casting of charts, the judgment of questions, and the reading of nativities in plain, ordered lessons. He trims Lilly's vast practice into rules a beginner can actually carry into a consultation. The Clavis served English astrologers as their standard manual into the next century. His almanacs kept his name before the public year after year.
europmc-pmc10344776:
Prjibelski and colleagues built IsoQuant in 2023, a tool for long-read RNA data. RNA carries gene messages out of DNA, and one gene can make many message forms. Long reads can span a full message, but errors make the forms hard to rebuild. IsoQuant maps the reads to a genome and traces the joins between gene parts.

The tool works with or without a known gene list. Prjibelski found that it cut false finds fivefold when a gene list was used. In free mode, with no list, false finds fell by a factor of 2.5. It links splice joins, the cut points in a message, into a graph. Paths through that graph give the full message forms and their counts.
europmc-pmc10435576:
Agu and co-authors reviewed in 2023 a computer method that helps find what food compounds do in the body. The method is molecular docking. It predicts how well a small compound grips a target protein. Food-derived compounds with health effects are called nutraceuticals.

Docking can reveal which proteins a nutraceutical may act on. Agu covers the main software tools and the basic steps of a docking run. Scores from the method can mislead, so lab proof must follow, the authors warn. Case work spans sickle cell disease, cancer, heart disease, gut and womb health, and brain decline. New paths found this way may seed fresh drugs.
europmc-pmc1088276:
Okada and colleagues filmed immune cells meeting inside living lymph nodes in this 2005 study. B cells make antibodies, the proteins that tag germs, and they need help from T cells to do it well. How the two cell types find each other was unclear. The team used a laser microscope that can image deep in intact tissue.

After B cells met their target germ part, they moved toward the T cell zone, the authors found. A signal receptor called CCR7 guided that drift. Paired B and T cells stayed joined for ten minutes to over an hour and kept moving as a pair. Pairs with the wrong target broke up in under ten minutes. The work gives early proof of directed immune cell movement inside the body.
europmc-pmc1189076:
Hannah, Heyer, and Hincha charted cold response genes in a small plant in 2005. The plant, Arabidopsis thaliana, can gain freezing tolerance after chilly days. That gain is called cold acclimation. Hundreds of genes shift activity while it happens.

Earlier work tracked only a few genes at a time. Here, genome-wide chips followed 14 days of cold exposure. Data from two chip types and past studies were merged. The result is a database covering more than 22,000 genes. Hannah gives plant science a shared map of cold response over time. The team also tracked which pathways matter most at each stage of the cold response.
europmc-pmc12230676:
Blin and many co-authors released version 8 of antiSMASH in 2025. Microbes make small active compounds that shape soil and microbe life. Many such compounds become drugs or farm chemicals. Their recipes hide in gene clusters inside microbe genomes.

Since 2011, antiSMASH has been the lead tool for finding those clusters. Version 8 detects 101 cluster types, up from 81. Support grew for terpene compounds and for tailoring enzymes. Big builder enzymes also get sharper analysis. Blin keeps the tool current as genome data floods in. It appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2025. The tool scans genomes from both bacteria and fungi for these clusters.
europmc-pmc1420676:
Some cancer cells switch off genes that would curb growth, without changing the DNA code. Pruitt and co-authors probed one such switch in 2006, a protein called SIRT1 that trims chemical tags from gene packaging. They found SIRT1 sitting on the start sites of silenced tumor suppressor genes in breast and colon cancer cells.

Blocking SIRT1 woke those genes back up. The genes spoke again even though a dense methyl tag layer, long blamed for the silence, stayed in place. Pruitt also saw shifts in cancer cell traits after the block. The work points to a fresh drug target for turning curbed genes back on.
europmc-pmc1525176:
Older women in Spain use health care more than older men. Redondo-Sendino and co-authors asked why, in a 2006 survey of 3,030 people aged 60 and over. Women saw doctors more often, got more home visits, and took three or more drugs more often. Hospital stays and flu shots showed no gap.

Much of the gap shrank once illness was taken into account. Women carried more chronic diseases and worse quality of life, classed as need factors. Schooling, marital status, and social ties also explained part of the gap. Redondo-Sendino concludes the higher use largely reflects greater health need, not waste.
europmc-pmc1877876:
Mosher, Ostrander and colleagues found in 2007 a gene fault that makes whippets both bulkier and faster. Double muscling, seen in cattle and sheep, comes from faults in the myostatin gene, which normally limits muscle growth. In whippets the extreme form is nicknamed the bully whippet.

Bully dogs carry two copies of a two-letter deletion in the gene's third section, which stops the protein early at amino acid 313. Dogs with one copy were on average more muscular than normal dogs. They were also significantly faster in competitive racing events, a measured link between this fault and athletic performance. It is the first time a myostatin mutation has been tied quantitatively to racing success. Two copies overshoot into the bully form, while one copy hits a racing sweet spot.
europmc-pmc1899176:
Lee, Jayaraman and Wood demonstrated in 2007 that indole, a chemical E. coli bacteria pour out in rich food, acts as a signal between species that shapes biofilms. Biofilms are surface communities of bacteria, and indole was known to control several genes and drug pumps. Its effect on biofilm building had not been well studied.

Gene activity scans, microscopy, and mutant strains showed indole is a non-toxic signal that represses swimming, switches on the sensor protein SdiA, and boosts acid resistance. A mutant lacking SdiA formed 50 times more biofilm, tying the sensor directly to the effect. Indole flattened biofilm shape from scattered towers to even colonies. In mixed films, partner bacteria engineered to destroy indole let E. coli grow 12-fold more, confirming the signal crosses species lines.
europmc-pmc1968876:
Levine delivered the 1993 Walter Hubert Lecture, published in 1994, on p53, the gene most often broken in human cancer. The p53 gene is mutated in about 60 percent of human tumors. Its protein normally restrains cell division by switching on other genes.

Raising p53 levels either halts cells in the G1 resting phase or triggers apoptosis, their orderly death. DNA damage raises both the amount and the activity of p53, which likely protects the body from mutation buildup. After radiation, some cell types arrest while others, such as thymus cells, die. Cells lacking p53 lose that checkpoint and pile up damage-driven mutations on the road to cancer. Losing p53 also speeds tumor growth and alters responses to DNA-damaging treatment. Radiation therapy, Levine argues, should account for a tumor's tissue origin and p53 status.
europmc-pmc1974776:
Thibault, Gant and Landfield expanded in 2007 the calcium hypothesis, which blames faulty calcium control for brain aging and Alzheimer's disease. Two decades of work had tied faulty calcium control inside neurons to aging and dementia. In rodent and rabbit memory circuits, aging raises calcium-driven aftereffects, calcium currents, and L-type calcium channel activity, and several changes track memory loss.

One version of the hypothesis blames those surface channels for most other calcium changes. The authors shift focus to the cell's internal calcium store and its release channels, the ryanodine receptors. Those channels amplify incoming calcium by releasing stored calcium in response, and they work in series with the surface channels in heart and some brain cells. Evidence links altered store release to cell toxicity, aging, and Alzheimer's models. Minding the store, their title urges, is essential to the full picture.
europmc-pmc2073776:
THOMLINSON and GRAY studied the structure of human lung cancers in 1955 and its meaning for radiotherapy. These squamous tumours grow in solid cords of cells fed by surrounding tissue, not by vessels between cells. Large cords have dead centres ringed by living tumour cells. The authors reasoned that oxygen must fall from the cord edge toward its centre. Cells starved of oxygen resist radiation damage far more than well-oxygenated cells.

Simple calculations showed the oxygen drop could be large and significant. At the centre of a cord just 150 micrometres in radius, complete oxygen absence was expected, using average tumour oxygen use. The team then measured many tissue sections quantitatively. Most tumours studied were poorly differentiated squamous cancers, a pattern in about 40 percent of bronchial cancers examined.
europmc-pmc2125376: A medical paper on spontaneous and experimental leukemia of the fowl. The chicken leukemia. This article preserves that oncology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2126276: A medical paper on a pleomorphic bacillus from pneumonic calf lungs simulating actinomyces. The shape-shifting germ. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128576: A medical paper on the soluble specific substance of pneumococcus, second paper. The germ's signature again. This article preserves that bacteriology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2131476: Putting pneumococcus beneath the rabbit's skin produced its own peculiar illness, and this paper pushed those intradermal experiments further. The team tested new variations of the skin infection. The under-the-skin disease, explored. The article preserves that bacteriology research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2131776: Two bug germs looked just alike, so this paper drew the line between them. The team found the marks that set them apart. The twin germs, told apart. The article keeps that germ study. Kept for study.
europmc-pmc2247476:
Drummond and Rambaut presented BEAST in 2007, a software package for Bayesian evolutionary analysis of DNA sequences. Evolutionary questions are statistical, and Bayesian methods combine prior knowledge with data through sampling. BEAST implements many stochastic models of sequence evolution, plus tree-based models for data within and between species. Its features include relaxed molecular clocks, population history analysis and handling of sequences sampled at different times.

Version 1.4.6 comprises 81,000 lines of Java code in 779 classes and 81 packages. The design is object-oriented and modular, making it a platform for developing new models. It offers a wide range of prior distribution options. The source is freely available under an open licence. The authors describe BEAST as a powerful, flexible framework for analysing molecular sequence variation and testing evolutionary hypotheses.
europmc-pmc2265676:
Fierro and co-workers evaluated methods in 2008 for reconstructing time profiles from complex two-colour microarray designs. Two-colour arrays compare two samples per slide, and alternative designs beat the standard reference design in theory. Their measurements, however, give ratios that must be mathematically converted into the true expression profile. The team compared how far different linear models agree in reconstructing ratios and time profiles from one complex design.

Estimated ratios correlated highly on average, and all methods predicted the same profile for most genes. Agreement was best for genes with large expression swings across time points. Methods sharing underlying principles gave the most similar results. Models including a dye effect proved more robust against array failure, compensating for dye-related inconsistencies. Normalisation choice mattered less, and its impact did not depend on the method.
europmc-pmc2360676:
Gray-Schopfer and co-authors examined how moles avoid becoming melanoma in 2006. Melanoma is a deadly skin cancer, and moles are its common starting point. Cells can enter senescence, a permanent stop to division, and the authors asked whether this stop acts as a barrier in real tissue.

In lab-grown human pigment cells, switching off a protein called p16 was required, alongside telomerase, for cells to divide forever. Staining of real moles showed wide p16 presence and signs of senescence, without rises in two other markers, p53 and p21. Early melanomas had less p16, while advanced melanomas lacked both p16 and p21 in most areas. A faulty growth gene, BRAF, found in about 80% of moles, switched p16 on. The authors concluded senescence blocks melanoma, which explains why p16 loss promotes it.
europmc-pmc2365976:
Forche and co-authors mapped a shortcut life cycle in a yeast-like fungus in 2008. Candida albicans is a fungus that lives on humans and can cause thrush and worse infections. It mates to form cells with double the usual DNA, but no true meiosis, the division that halves DNA in sex, had ever been seen in it.

Instead, doubled cells shed whole chromosomes at random until they return near the normal count. Using DNA arrays, the team showed the offspring carry shuffled mixes of the eight chromosomes. Many also swapped segments between matching chromosomes, including multiple small patch events. Removing a gene called SPO11, normally a meiosis gene in other fungi, stopped that swapping. Offspring colonies looked visibly different from parents, proving the cycle creates real variety without meiosis.
europmc-pmc2408576:
Riker and colleagues profiled gene activity in skin tumors and spread melanoma in 2008. Melanoma is a skin cancer that turns deadly when it spreads, or metastasises, to other organs. The team compared 42 primary skin tumors with 40 metastatic melanoma samples using gene chips that measure thousands of genes at once.

Primary tumors, including thin melanomas, ran high in skin-identity genes such as keratins and the gene LOR. Metastases instead ran high in a different set, including MAGE genes, the survival gene BCL2A1, and a matrix-cutting enzyme, MMP14. The switch between the two patterns happened as melanomas grew thicker, but each gene flipped at its own thickness. That makes the switch zone a window where spread begins. The authors listed candidate driver and brake genes that changed across it, checked by targeted tests.
europmc-pmc2430176:
Rehak and Rehak reviewed a blocked retinal vein condition in 2008. In branch retinal vein occlusion, a vein in the retina, the eye's light-sensing layer, is squeezed where an artery crosses it. Wall damage and abnormal blood factors complete the block, cutting blood drainage from part of the retina.

The outlook is often fair: 50% to 60% of eyes end with vision of 20/40 or better even without treatment. Vision at first presentation is the strongest clue to the final result. The main treatment problem is macular edema, swelling at the centre of vision. A grid pattern of laser burns is the established fix for a defined patient group. Injections of steroids or of new vessel-growth blockers showed promise, and surgery to free the vein helped some eyes that laser could not treat.
europmc-pmc2447176:
Driemeyer, Boyke, Gaser, Büchel, and May revisited how fast learning reshapes the adult brain in 2008. An earlier study from the same group found that three months of juggling practice grew gray matter in a motion-sensing brain area. Gray matter is the brain tissue packed with cell bodies. The open question was the time scale.

They rescanned 20 healthy adults learning the three-ball cascade, using a 3 Tesla scanner to track whole-brain structure. The growth in the occipito-temporal cortex, at the back underside of the brain, was already detectable after just seven days of training. Neither raw performance level nor sheer exercise amount explained the change. The authors concluded that the qualitative step of learning something new, not continued drill, is what drives structural change. The effect had earlier proved temporary once practice stops.
europmc-pmc2561076:
Caulfield and a large team of collaborators tested in 2008 whether a gene found in genome scans, SLC2A9, actually moves uric acid in the body. Uric acid levels track with gout, blood pressure, and diabetes, and scans had tied variants of this gene to higher levels. The gene makes a transporter protein in the kidney, where uric acid is handled, but its cargo was unproven.

Expressed in frog eggs, both forms of the protein carried uric acid fast, at rates 45 to 60 times faster than its known cargo, glucose. A gout drug blocked the transport, and human kidney cells given the gene took up at least twice as much uric acid. In men, gene variants matched reduced uric acid clearance in urine. However, meta-analyses found no link to blood pressure.
europmc-pmc2600276:
Zilberberg, Shorr, and Kollef documented in 2008 the rapid rise of Clostridium difficile disease in American hospitals. This gut infection, usually triggered when antibiotics clear normal gut bacteria, kills more Americans than all other intestinal infections combined. Using national hospital data from 2000 to 2005, the team asked whether more patients were being hospitalised and whether each case had grown deadlier.

Adult hospitalisations for the disease doubled over the period. The rate climbed from 5.5 cases per 10,000 people in 2000 to 11.2 cases five years later. The age-adjusted case-fatality rate climbed from 1.2 percent in 2000 to 2.2 percent in 2004, so the average case became more lethal as well as more common. The authors link the trend to hypervirulent strains and resistance to widely used antibiotics, and frame the infection as a growing public health hazard.
europmc-pmc2690576:
Bradley and colleagues argued in 2009 that health care improves fastest by studying its own stars, an approach called positive deviance. Decades of quality campaigns had left poor care stubbornly common, and under one percent of medical research money targeted delivery itself. The approach starts from a bet: somewhere, an organization already performs exceptionally with the same resources as everyone else.

The method runs in four steps. Find the consistently top performers. Study them closely, with interviews and observation, to form guesses about the practices behind their success. Test those guesses statistically across a broad sample. Then spread what survives, working with the very people expected to adopt it. The authors illustrate with hospital care for heart attacks, where speed of treatment varies hugely. The approach suits problems where the knowledge exists but sits trapped in a few bright spots.
europmc-pmc2729376:
Ji and co-authors showed in 2009 that restoring microRNA miR-34 shrinks the tumor-initiating cell pool in pancreatic cancer. MiR-34 is a small RNA switched on by the tumor guard p53. Pancreatic cancer cells that had lost p53 also lost miR-34, which normally lowers Bcl-2 and Notch proteins that help cells survive and self-renew. A small stem-like cell group drives new tumor growth in this cancer.

Restoring miR-34 in two human pancreatic cancer lines lowered Bcl-2 and Notch, slowed growth and invasion, and made cells more sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation. The stem-like cell group, rich in Notch and Bcl-2 and lacking miR-34, fell by nearly nine tenths. Sphere growth in dishes and tumor formation in animals also dropped sharply.
europmc-pmc2761376:
de Jager and co-authors set out in 2009 the prerequisites for measuring cytokines in clinical trials. Cytokines are immune signal proteins. Multiplex immunoassays read many cytokines from one sample. Such measures can track whether antibody drugs hit their immune targets in patients. Trivial handling steps, they warn, can badly distort the low natural levels.

Spiking known cytokine amounts into blood samples, they found recoveries mostly within eighty to one hundred twenty percent. Most cytokines stayed stable for up to two years frozen, but several fell sharply by four years. Only two of fifteen cytokines survived repeated freeze-thaw cycles well. They also demonstrate an internal control, and stress tube choice and storage rules for trials.
europmc-pmc2785876:
Kretschmer and co-authors traced in 2009 how fungicide use drives multidrug resistance in Botrytis cinerea. This grey mould fungus rots fruits, vegetables, and ornamentals worldwide. Yearly monitoring in French and German vineyards found three distinct resistance types rising fast. All resistant strains pumped fungicides out of their cells faster and overproduced the pump genes.

One type carried activating mutations in Mrr1, a switch gene for one pump. The second type owed its resistance to a rearranged control region before another pump gene, reshaped by inserted jumping-gene DNA. The same rearranged version appeared in both countries, suggesting migration from France to Germany. Crossing experiments showed that combining both changes yields a third, broader resistance. In field trials, fungicide sprays selected the combined strain over sensitive ones. Growers then lose spray tools they still need badly each year.
europmc-pmc2841576:
Carlsen and a large team built a worldwide antioxidant food table in 2010, measuring over thirty-one hundred foods, drinks, spices, herbs, and supplements. Antioxidants are plant chemicals that neutralize damaging free radicals, and plant-rich diets are tied to lower chronic disease. Samples were gathered from many countries and tested with one standard assay so the values could be compared fairly.

Scores ranged over several thousand-fold between foods. Spices, herbs, and supplements packed the most antioxidants, some exceptionally high, while berries, fruits, nuts, chocolate, and vegetables led the everyday foods. Plant foods delivered far more antioxidants than animal foods. The authors say such a full table is essential for diet studies to register foods correctly.
europmc-pmc2848976:
Halaban and colleagues reported a troubling paradox in 2010 for PLX4032, a drug built to block the mutant BRAF kinase that drives many melanomas. In tumor cells carrying the V600E or V600K mutation, the drug shut down the ERK growth pathway as designed. In cells with normal BRAF, however, it did the opposite.

Working through a partner kinase called RAF1, the drug switched ERK on persistently in normal-BRAF cells. Those cells changed gene activity widely, stuck less to surfaces, moved more, and in some cases multiplied faster. The authors warn the drug may hand an advantage to normal-BRAF tumor cells in patients, so treatment should target only mutation carriers, with monitoring for new growths.
europmc-pmc2871176:
Marre and the LEAD-1 SU study group tested in 2009 whether adding liraglutide, a once-daily copy of a gut hormone, beats other add-ons for type 2 diabetes. Over one thousand adults whose sugar stayed high on a standard pill, glimepiride, joined the twenty-six-week trial at sites in twenty-one countries. Extra arms added a rival drug, rosiglitazone, or a placebo for comparison.

The two higher liraglutide doses cut the long-term sugar marker far more than placebo or the rival drug did, with gains visible within two weeks. Patients on liraglutide also lost weight, while those on the rival drug gained, a double advantage for a disease tied to weight. Nausea was the main added side effect, and it faded with time on the drug.
europmc-pmc2887476:
Okagaki and colleagues showed in 2010 that the yeast Cryptococcus neoformans grows giant cells during infection, and that the size change reshapes the disease. Normal cells span a few micrometers, while the giants can reach ten times that width. Enlarged cells were found in infected tissue and studied for how they interact with host defenses.

Giant cells were swallowed far less by immune cells, tying size directly to survival in the host. They also resisted chemical attack by oxygen and nitrogen stress better than normal cells, though they crossed into the central nervous system less readily. Each giant carried many copies of the genome in a single nucleus and still budded off daughters. Living alongside the opposite mating type boosted enlargement, and mutant strains missing a pheromone sensor enlarged less.
europmc-pmc2924276:
Croset and colleagues demonstrated in 2010 that the smell and taste receptors of insects descend from an ancient family far older than insects themselves. The receptors, called ionotropic receptors, are variants of channels best known for carrying signals between brain cells. A cousin family, the odorant receptors, exists only in insects and was assumed to be the original animal smell system.

Surveying genomes and gene activity across the protostome branch of animals, arthropods, worms, and mollusks included, the team found ionotropic receptors switched on in smell organs throughout. A conserved core set, the antennal receptors, likely formed the first smell system of the protostome ancestor. Insects later bolted on their private odorant family, while the ancient system still handles acids, amines, and taste.
europmc-pmc2928176:
Kim and colleagues fed in 2010 silver nanoparticles to rats for thirteen weeks to set safe limits for a material now common in antibacterial consumer goods. The study followed international test guidelines, with groups receiving daily oral doses from low to high or a plain vehicle. The particles averaged fifty-six nanometers across, the size class used in sprays, fabrics, and medical products.

Males on the higher doses gained weight more slowly from the fourth week, though they ate and drank normally. Blood chemistry, tissue examination, and silver measurements in organs showed dose-dependent changes, with silver accumulating chiefly in liver and kidneys. The authors derive the dose levels that produce no observable harm, numbers regulators need as nano-silver spreads through homes and clinics.
europmc-pmc2944076:
Anenberg and co-authors estimated the worldwide death toll from human-made air pollution in a 2010 modelling study. Ground-level ozone and fine particles have risen since pre-industrial times and are tied to heart and lung deaths.

Using a global atmosphere model to contrast past and present air, they paired pollution levels with risk figures from health studies. Their estimates linked man-made ozone to hundreds of thousands of yearly respiratory deaths, and fine particles to several million heart, lung, and cancer deaths. Adding assumed safe thresholds cut the totals by roughly a third, showing how sensitive such counts are.
europmc-pmc3012676:
Du and co-authors compared two ways of summarising DNA methylation readings from a popular array platform in a 2010 study. The Beta value reads as a simple fraction methylated, while the M value stretches the same data on a log scale, and users lacked guidance on choosing.

They show the two are linked by a standard mathematical transform, but the Beta value's scatter balloons at the near-full and near-empty extremes. In a mixing experiment with known answers, the M value found truly differing sites far more reliably at both extremes. A minimum gap threshold helped the M value further. Intuition favours Beta; statistics favours M.
europmc-pmc3022776:
Buchon and coauthors studied in 2010 how the gut of the fruit fly rebuilds itself after a bacterial infection. Eating a mild pathogen had earlier been shown to trigger a sharp rise in stem cell division in the fly gut. The team measured gut cells and shapes in detail to see how new cells form, mature, and replace damaged ones.

One growth signal pathway, centered on the epidermal growth factor receptor, proved central at every step. It drove stem cells to divide, guided new gut cells to take proper shape, and helped push damaged cells out to die. A second pathway worked alongside it to boost division. Flies lacking the receptor could not keep the gut sealed and died easily from infection. The work shows gut repair is one coordinated program, not separate fixes.
europmc-pmc3053476:
Heeb and coauthors reviewed in 2011 the double life of quinolones, a family of ring shaped compounds found across nature. Relatives of quinine, the fever tree drug, these compounds show effects from allergy relief to killing cancer cells and microbes, and they inspired a major class of synthetic antibiotics. One notorious bacterium makes several quinolones of its own, not mainly as weapons but as signals.

In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these signals report how crowded the population is and switch on attack genes accordingly. The review covers the family's naming, chemistry, and making, plus side roles such as grabbing iron and blocking energy systems in rival cells. It also traces how the signals plug into the bacterium's wider control network. Understanding the signal system could suggest ways to disarm this hospital pathogen without classic antibiotics.
europmc-pmc3084176:
Russell and colleagues documented in 2011 how a decade of rising bed net use in rural Tanzania quietly rewired malaria mosquito behavior. Nets and indoor spraying work because local malaria mosquitoes bite people indoors late at night. The team compared hourly biting patterns from before nets arrived with two later milestones of community net coverage, during which malaria transmission had fallen dramatically.

By the final survey, one mosquito group bit less at night and had shifted toward a sibling species that bites earlier and more outdoors. The other group bit indoors only half as often as before. Overall, the share of human mosquito contact happening indoors fell sharply for both. The remaining transmission now happens where nets and sprays cannot reach. The authors call for new tools aimed at outdoor biting mosquitoes, as adults or as larvae, to finish the job.
europmc-pmc3176276:
Tiago dos Santos and colleagues probed how plastic nanoparticles enter human cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Particles sized like natural cell cargo are candidates for delivering drugs and genes, but their entry route decides where they end up inside. The team fed two particle sizes to three human cell lines while blocking known entry pathways one at a time.

Entry always needed cell energy, never passive drift. Beyond that, routes diverged sharply by cell type. Two lines leaned heavily on the cell skeleton's actin mesh, while lung cells suffered most from blocked microtubule tracks and from blocking one entry portal. A third blocker hit only the brain tumour line. The same particle, in short, sneaks in by different doors in different cells, a warning for delivery design.
europmc-pmc3180276:
Andrew Gaudet, Phillip Popovich, and Matt Ramer reviewed inflammation after peripheral nerve injury in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Unlike spinal cord axons, peripheral fibres can regrow, and that success depends on a well-run inflammatory cleanup in the severed stump. The review opens with history, then walks through the response stage by stage.

Damage signals open the blood-nerve barrier and wake support cells, which shed their insulation, multiply, eat debris, and call in blood-borne scavengers. Those cells finish the clearance within days and leave once re-insulation begins. The spinal cord runs the same programme badly, with lingering toxic inflammation and scarring. Comparing the two, the authors argue, points to ways of coaching the cord to behave more like the periphery.
europmc-pmc3261976:
Nicole Janssen and colleagues evaluated black carbon as an extra indicator for air quality policy in this 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Standards regulate particles by total mass, yet combustion particles are thought to be the most harmful fraction, and traffic measures barely move the total mass figure. The team systematically reviewed studies that measured both black carbon and particle mass.

Per unit of mass, black carbon showed larger health effects than the standard particle measures, and in studies modeling both at once, its effect held up more robustly. A worked example of traffic reduction suggested the gain in life expectancy looks four to nine times bigger when counted in black carbon than in fine particle mass. The authors recommend black carbon as a valuable additional indicator where combustion dominates.
europmc-pmc3297576:
Eizirik led a team that cataloged which genes are active in the human pancreatic islets, reporting in 2012. These cell clusters house the insulin making beta cells that the immune system destroys in type 1 diabetes. Using RNA sequencing, the team listed the genes switched on in healthy islets and in islets exposed to two inflammatory signals.

Nearly thirty thousand gene transcripts showed up in the islets, roughly doubling what was known before. Inflammatory signals changed about a fifth of them, including many alarm chemicals that call in immune cells. Many genes known to raise diabetes risk were active in the islets themselves. The signals also reshuffled how genes are spliced together, suggesting the islets talk back during immune attack.
europmc-pmc3335876:
Neal, Ahmad, Gordon-Weeks, and Ton showed that maize roots use a defense chemical to recruit helpful bacteria, in a 2012 study. Maize releases compounds called benzoxazinoids from its roots, known for fighting pests above ground and microbes below. The team asked what these chemicals do to Pseudomonas putida, a soil bacterium that colonizes maize roots and benefits the plant.

One compound, DIMBOA, proved to be the main form in root secretions. The bacterium tolerates it by breaking it down, and exposure switched on its genes for chemical sensing and movement. In swim tests the bacteria actively moved toward the compound. In soil, wild type maize roots, which make the chemical, drew far more of the bacteria than roots of a mutant that cannot. The authors cast the chemical as a recruitment signal protecting young, vulnerable maize.
europmc-pmc3338676:
Delhaes and colleagues mapped the full community of microbes living in the airways of cystic fibrosis patients, in a 2012 study. Cystic fibrosis thickens airway mucus, trapping bacteria and fungi that drive lung decline. Standard cultures catch only part of that community, so the team used high throughput gene reading on sputum from four adult patients, alongside normal cultures.

Sequencing revealed complex fungal communities, with most kinds missed entirely by culture, alongside the expected bacterial diversity. Patients with worse lung function and poorer clinical scores harbored noticeably poorer communities, with fewer kinds of both fungi and bacteria. Certain pairings recurred, such as a yeast appearing alongside the notorious Pseudomonas bacterium. The authors argue the whole community should be treated as one disease entity, and that fungi deserve a real place in care decisions.
europmc-pmc3445676:
Elwyn and a large team offered a practical model in 2012 for shared decision making between doctors and patients. The approach, where patients help choose their care, was well described in principle but rarely translated into routine steps a clinician can remember. Their answer is a three-step conversation built on relationship first.

Step one is choice talk, signaling that options exist. Step two is option talk, laying out the alternatives, often with patient decision aids. Step three is decision talk, drawing out what matters most to this patient and settling the choice together. The model treats decisions as the fruit of informed preferences, carefully explored, and doubles as a guide for training the skill.
europmc-pmc3447976:
Friedman and Alm exposed a statistical trap in 2012 lurking in microbial survey data, then built a tool to escape it. Surveys report each species as a share of the whole, not a headcount, and correlation on shares is notoriously unreliable, a warning going back to Pearson. Using simulated data and Human Microbiome Project samples, they showed how badly the standard approach misbehaves.

Many apparent links between species were artifacts, and some true links appeared with the wrong sign. Diverse communities softened the distortion; sparse ones suffered most. Their method, SparCC, estimates true correlations from share data anyway. Judged against its network, the standard approach invented roughly three false links per true one in gut data and missed most real ones.
