Small courts, held in one plan, could not be bought one by one by the South.
frus-1861-d276:
30 May 1861 is the date on a dispatch from Mr. Angel to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 276 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d76:
Writing to London on 7 September 1861, William H. Seward kept Charles Francis Adams to the autumn plan. The letter is document 76 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward kept up a near weekly rhythm of orders to London that autumn. Each letter bound Adams tighter to the cabinet's shared plan. For readers, the steady dates themselves tell a story: a government holding its nerve by routine. Routine was itself a message to London: the Union meant to outlast the crisis. The Union meant to outlast the crisis, and its mail said so in its steady dates.
frus-1862-d176:
The second Adams report of 24 October 1862 is printed as Document 176 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Late October 1862 was a turning point in the war's foreign side: the French truce plan was taking shape, and Britain had to choose. Adams's twice-weekly reports were Washington's best window on that choice. This dispatch, read in sequence, shows the care with which he tracked each shift in British thinking. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d276:
On 8 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 276 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Early May brought word of the French defeat at Puebla and the Union hold on New Orleans, both useful to Washington's case in Paris. Seward's letters that month pressed a simple theme: the rebellion was failing, and friendship with it would cost France more than it could gain. This dispatch is one of the spring's many statements of that theme. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d376:
Viscount Treilhard wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 August 1862, in a letter printed as Document 376 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. He wrote on the second day of the Bull Run battle.

Few dates in the file carry such a charge: while Treilhard wrote, the Union army was being beaten thirty miles away. The defeat would embolden those in Europe who wanted to act on the war. This letter, and the exchange around it, belongs to the record of how Washington's foreign dealings absorbed the shock in real time. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d476:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 476 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

By October 1862 the Confederate cruiser Alabama was loose on the Atlantic. Neutral ports from the Azores outward had become part of the war at sea. Seward's autumn orders to Lisbon kept the pressure on Portugal to hold raiders to the letter of neutrality law. Harvey's post, quiet in most histories, sat on a real front of the war. The dispatch closes the year's printed instructions to Portugal, a small file that shows how global the blockade's paper war had become.
frus-1862-d576:
On 21 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Watson Webb in Brazil. The instruction is Document 576 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward's July orders everywhere carried the government's account of a hard summer, and the Brazilian instruction was no exception. Webb also needed the Department's current line on the cruiser war, since Confederate raiders would soon be working the South Atlantic and seeking Brazilian ports. By the time the letter reached Rio, the season it described had passed, which is why distant ministers held such wide discretion. The document shows the system working at its longest range.
frus-1862-d676:
Anson Burlingame sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 May 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, and his mail formed the China section of the year's file. The letter is document 676 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Spring reports from China dealt with the state of the ports and the mood of the Qing court. Burlingame also had to weigh the moves of Britain and France, whose fleets and envoys loomed large there. His letter is a working part of that watch. It helped Washington hold a steady course in East Asia with few ships and fewer men to spare.
frus-1862-d76:
Writing from Washington on 2 June 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 76 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d176:
On 30 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Britain had declared itself neutral in 1861, yet many in its government and press leaned toward the South. Adams watched Parliament, the cabinet, and the newspapers for any sign of a shift. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d276:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 2 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 276 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d376:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 29 January 1863. The note is document 376 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d476:
On 23 April 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d576:
Under the date 22 June 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d676:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, sent this dispatch to London on 24 November 1863. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The text is document 676 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that covers foreign affairs for 1863, part one.

Britain was the foreign power Washington watched most closely during the Civil War. Its ships, ports, and trade could help or hurt the Union cause. Adams had to press the American view in person, using notes like this one as his guide. The letter shows high-level orders moving from a desk in Washington to an envoy abroad, in plain official words.
frus-1863p1-d76:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 76 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-February mail from London took stock after the opening of Parliament. Adams wrote on the tone of the houses, the press, and the South's men in the city. His reports let Seward judge whether the calm of the Queen's speech would hold. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, in the legation's usual split of topics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d176: A third Roosevelt letter to Hull dated October 30, 1943 in the Moscow section stands as Document 176 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Repetition at this scale marks a day when much had to be settled at a distance: results weighed, thanks sent, and next steps set. The record gives the parties and the date and no subject. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d276:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting at half past eleven that morning. American and British information and public relations officers settled how conference photographs and films would be handled. Army colonels sit alongside staff of the British and American information services.

The agreed rules are practical. Each side processes its own still photographs in Cairo under security conditions and exchanges material. American film goes unprocessed to Washington, while British film is processed in Cairo. No picture of any kind may be released before the final release date, given the secrecy of the Tehran leg. All conference pictures, still and moving, are pooled for every party and carry one credit line: United Nations Photographic Pool.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d376:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a luncheon at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at one in the afternoon, dominated by the planned meeting with Turkey's president. The text of a telegram inviting President Inönü to Cairo for 3, 4, or 5 December was discussed and agreed.

Hopkins insists the allies must first settle exactly what military help Turkey would get if she entered the war. Churchill's offer stands at twenty squadrons, mostly fighters, and three anti-aircraft regiments, with no land forces and no promises beyond that. His prize would be Turkish air bases for steady bombing of the Ploesti oil fields, and he wants landing craft only for a temporary Rhodes assault in March. Roosevelt, caught between the Italian, French, and Overlord demands on the same craft, asks for military advice before anything is sandwiched in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d476:
On December 4, 1943, the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference, the Combined Chiefs of Staff sent a message to General Dwight D. Eisenhower at Allied Force Headquarters. Eisenhower then commanded Allied forces in the Mediterranean, based in North Africa. The State Department printed the chiefs' message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Traffic from the Combined Chiefs to a theater commander carried the alliance's decisions out of the conference room and into the field. Eisenhower stood at the receiving end of Cairo's choices about where Allied strength would go next. For readers, the message marks the point where summit strategy began turning into orders for the armies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d576:
J. Leighton Stuart, the American ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State George C. Marshall on September 24, 1948. Stuart, a missionary educator born in China, was the last American ambassador to serve the Nationalist government on the mainland. His report is the final document in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By September 1948 the Chinese Communists were winning the civil war, and the China that the Cairo Declaration had promised so much was disappearing. An editor's choice to end the volume here is pointed: the story that began with Chiang at Cairo closes with his government's collapse. For readers, Stuart's report is a somber bookend to the whole record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d76: On October 30, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, the day the Moscow Conference formally ended. His message is Document 76 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. London had its own reading of the Moscow results, and the prime minister kept his channel to Washington warm as ever. The record gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the day's other traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d176:
No official account survives of the dinner meeting on September 12, 1944, at the Governor General's residence. The editors reconstruct it from General Arnold's memoir. Messages from the Russians and from Harriman about the Polish patriots in Warsaw had arrived, and aid to Poland came up at the table. Marshall and Arnold talked the problem over at length.

Arnold records that helping Warsaw was a large problem never completely solved. Churchill also produced new ideas about winning the war: getting more British planes, ships, and soldiers into the final battle against Japan. Arnold answered that the Pacific lacked land masses for Europe's heavy bomber fleets. Even 1,500 of 3,500 bombers would be lucky to be usable, and B-29s were preferred anyway.
frus-1944-quebec-d276:
Somervell and Leathers, the American and British transport chiefs, reported on September 15, 1944, on the personnel movement problem after Germany's defeat. Their appendices size the task for the first year, assuming Germany fell on October 1. American operational movements alone totaled about 3.6 million men, including replacements, build-up, and redeployment for the war against Japan, plus 1.7 million for demobilization and repatriation.

British operational movements came to about 2.1 million, with nearly a million more to demobilize or repatriate. A precise analysis, the authors warn, was impossible until combined agencies studied the problem against the chiefs' strategy decisions. They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee take it up with the planners, the transportation committee, and the shipping authorities.
frus-1944-quebec-d76:
James W. Riddleberger wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 1, 1944. Riddleberger headed the Division of Central European Affairs. Hopkins served as President Roosevelt's special assistant and closest aide. The State Department printed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Central European questions sat near the heart of the Quebec agenda. Germany's defeat raised hard choices about occupation and borders. A division chief writing to Hopkins put expert views near the President. For readers, the letter shows how regional knowledge reached the summit's inner circle. It arrived eleven days before the conference opened.
frus-1945-50-intel-d176:
The meeting named in the title took place on 7 November 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. Readers meet it as document 176 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d276:
A memorandum dated 19 May 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 276 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d376:
On 22 March 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 36th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 376 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said. The writer's own views may color a line or two, which is part of what makes the form honest to read. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d76:
The Department of State sent a circular telegram to certain diplomatic missions on 22 October 1945. Circular telegrams carry one message to many posts at once. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A circular on intelligence business told embassies around the world how to handle the new order of things after the OSS. Posts had to know which secret duties were ending, which were passing to State, and what to tell host governments. Readers can see the change reaching the field here. It is not a plan in a Washington office. It is an instruction landing on desks from London to Chungking. The volume's State thread widens from an office to a worldwide service in papers like this.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d176:
King Peter gave his guarded yes to the Tito–Subasic draft, and Ambassador Patterson cabled the royal statement to Washington on 11 January 1945. The communiqué of the Royal Yugoslav Court is quoted in full. Patterson's cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The King has studied the draft closely, the statement says. He approves its basic proposals, under which Yugoslavia's future constitution and form of government rest solely on the free decision of her peoples. He will accept that decision. But as a constitutional monarch, he calls it his sacred duty to see the people truly consulted and their will fully respected. He also welcomes the widest grouping of democratic parties, from left to right, as the only sure ground of free expression.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d276:
Moscow's draft of a prisoners-and-civilians agreement is printed here in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet text answers a British note of 11 December 1944. It proposes the principles that should govern Soviet citizens and British subjects freed from the Germans by each other's armies.

The Soviet government is ready to conclude such an agreement, the note says, but its reach should be extended. It should cover not only prisoners of war but citizens interned or deported by force into Germany. Some paragraphs of the British draft should also be widened and defined. The first principle follows. All freed Soviet citizens held by the western allies are to be parted from enemy prisoners without delay. The same holds for freed British subjects in Red Army hands. Each group is kept apart in camps or gathering points until it is sent home.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d376:
Before sending his famous letter on Poland, Roosevelt's staff drafted it, and the draft survives here dated February 7, 1945. The President tells Stalin he has given much thought to their meeting that afternoon. He wants to say frankly what is on his mind. On the Polish government, he is greatly disturbed.

The three great powers, he writes, have no meeting of minds about Poland's political setup. Moscow backs one government while Washington and London back another in London. That split puts all of them in a bad light before the world. People might think a breach had opened between the allies. The draft lets readers compare the plea planned with the plea sent.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d476:
Stettinius asked questions home in this cable of February 4, 1945. He wanted a summary of the Mikolajczyk memorandum shown to Bohlen. He also asked Grew to keep the delegation promptly informed on the Associated Nations. What was the present status of each of the five Latin American countries, other than Ecuador, and when might each act?

He further asked for at least a summary of the Department's cable to Moscow cited in an earlier message. The code words "Allstate Horseshoe" closed the wire. Read beside Grew's digests, the cable shows the two ends of the State Department working one set of files from Washington and Yalta at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d76:
Geneva, Prague, or somewhere new? This 15 November 1944 paper to the President weighs where the United Nations should make its home. Acting Secretary Stettinius reports that the question was never formally debated at Dumbarton Oaks. The memo is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Soviet delegates objected to Geneva, and one informally suggested Prague. Britain and China raised no objection to Geneva. An American study group reviewed six options, from Vienna to a district near Lake Como. Its pick was a neutral district joining the Swiss strip that held the League buildings with the French Pays de Gex next door. The memo urges the President to back that plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d176:
Ambassador Lord Halifax proposed adding war criminals to the summit agenda in a letter dated June 29, 1945. The letter is document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows up the British agenda list delivered a month earlier.

Four-power talks on war criminals had begun in London on June 26, Halifax notes, among American, British, Soviet, and French representatives. Even so, London expects some war crimes matters to remain unresolved by the time the heads of government meet. A brief review of the position by the leaders would be valuable in any case. The suggestion helped push the prosecution of the top Nazi leaders, then being negotiated in London, onto the Potsdam program.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d276:
Winant set down the U.S. caveat on Austrian reparations in a cable from London on July 4, 1945. The cable is document 276 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the words he used that day on signing the pact on control machinery for Austria.

In the talks on a reparations desk in the pact, he told his colleagues, the group had not weighed the real question of what Austria should pay. His government accepts in principle that Austria owes reparations, he said, but holds that the four powers should fix the form and sum in light of Austria's economy and its prospects. The British and French said much the same. The Soviet member, Winant notes, had long fought any such U.S. caveat.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d376:
A progress report by the American delegation to the Reparations Commission, dated July 14, 1945, sums up what Moscow had settled and what it had not. Pauley had asked on July 3 for clarification of the open problems before the heads of government met. The supplement answers him point by point, with appendices for each topic.

On July 13 the delegations agreed the relative shares of the participating governments, and agreed rules for smaller nations' claims. No agreement came on defining reparation, restitution, and war booty, since the Soviets were not ready to discuss booty. General principles were settled except one: whether needed exports rank as a prior charge.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d476:
British hopes for a lasting combined command fill Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 1, 1945. From talks with the chief of staff and other high British officers at Allied Force Headquarters, Kirk gathers what Field Marshal Alexander will do in England. Alexander will urge Churchill to persuade Truman, and senior American officials, at the Big Three meeting.

The aim is to maintain a combined command in this theater as long as possible. The British will hold out for maximum retention of a supreme commander, though they know America probably will not go along. They have therefore prepared fallback plans for an inter-allied service committee, to carry on functions of an allied character until a peace settlement is made.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d576:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent a memo to Secretary of State Byrnes on July 12, 1945. It is document 576 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Grew passes on a message for the President from China's leader, Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang thanks Truman for his June 15 wire, which sketched a proposed deal between China and the Soviet Union. He says he has sent T. V. Soong to Moscow to negotiate with the Soviet government. He will keep Truman informed through Ambassador Hurley in China. Chiang calls the matter grave for world peace as well as for China and Russia. He asks Truman to keep close watch on the talks and to share his views over time. The memo went by pouch, not wire, to keep the line to Potsdam free for urgent traffic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d676:
An extract from Villard's Paris wire of July 13, 1945, reports Britain's private plan on Tangier. It is document 676 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The extract is drawn from a longer report sent over Ambassador Caffery's signature.

Villard cites Peake, the British team head, on London's intent. Britain will not raise at Berlin any question of how far Russian participation should run. That participation is accepted in principle, Peake says. Any British-Russian talk on Tangier would be limited to a bargain. London would seek something in exchange for Russian admission to the conversations. Peake also held that France would accept putting the talks off until the first week of August. The extract lays bare the bargaining beneath the formal notes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d76:
President Truman denied a press story in a top secret telegram to Churchill on June 18, 1945. The message is document 76 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had asked about reports that Truman planned to stop in Paris and meet General de Gaulle before the Berlin conference.

Truman says the press reports Churchill mentioned are not authentic. He will keep the promise Roosevelt made to Churchill, he adds, if conditions at the time make it workable, a careful hedge. He ends by hoping the contents of the message will not get into the papers. The brief exchange shows both leaders managing the press, and French feelings, while the Berlin trip was being planned in secret.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1076:
Prime Minister Churchill circulated this extract of his Greece memorandum at Potsdam on July 22, 1945. The full text appears just earlier in the volume. Annexed to it is a report by Field Marshal Alexander, dated July 21. Alexander answers Soviet charges about Greece point by point, from the mood of the Greek people to the balance of forces on her borders.

Most Greeks, he writes, feel relief from terror thanks to British troops, and UNRRA relief now works where it could not under ELAS-EAM rule. Any Greek threat to Albania and Bulgaria is unfounded. Greece has one division, still training, against 52 Yugoslav, 18 Bulgarian, and 7 Albanian divisions nearby. A loud propaganda campaign from those three neighbors, he adds, poisons the air.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1176:
Winant cabled from London yet again on 18 July 1945. During the summit he filed almost daily. His reports built Washington's picture of British thinking piece by piece: politics, press, and the official mood in a capital awaiting an election count.

No single cable carried the whole story. The value lay in the stream, each report testing and adding to the last. This dispatch is one more layer in that piling up of detail. It shows the London embassy's steady work while the leaders bargained abroad. Readers who follow the sequence watch an ally's mind being read in real time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1276:
The United States Chiefs of Staff proposed this text on 21 July 1945. A proposed text from the chiefs put draft words on the table for the talks to accept or amend. Wording from the military staff could end up in the summit's own papers.

Drafting was power at Potsdam. The side that wrote the first text set the terms of the argument that followed. This entry preserves the chiefs' draft at its date, midway through the talks. Primary papers like this one let readers see the settlement being built from the staff level up, one clause at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1376:
Ambassador Edwin Wilson cabled the acting secretary of state from Turkey again on 27 July 1945. His earlier cable in the volume is dated 19 July. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Two cables, eight days apart, let readers watch an ambassador build a case over time. Turkey's spot between the Soviet Union and the Mediterranean kept Ankara in the summit's shadow talks as well as in its own file. Wilson's second report shows what had changed, or failed to change, while the leaders met in Germany. Posts like his supplied the facts on which the men at Potsdam judged the straits and the lands beyond them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-76:
Swedish requisitioning of shipping was the principal subject of a conversation that left no official record. An editorial note in volume two names that subject and marks the gap. It is the seventy-sixth unnumbered item following document 710, in the conference sequence of July 1945.

That question was expected to come up at a forthcoming meeting of the United Maritime Authority. The authority was the Allied body that allocated merchant shipping in the war's last phase. No official record of this conversation has been found, and the note gives no names or date beyond its place in the file. Entries like this one mark how much conference business ran through unminuted side talks. The editors preserve the topic and the gap together.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d776:
Byrnes wrote to Ambassador Winant in London on July 20, 1945, in document 776. The Secretary kept the London embassy close through the conference. Winant's post made him a key partner in all Anglo-American work. This letter entered the second Potsdam volume, among several Byrnes-Winant exchanges.

The London channel carried more than news. Winant had to act on the conference's drift with his own hosts. Readers see a secretary managing an alliance by letter. The document shows Potsdam's work spreading outward in real time. Each such letter turned talk in Germany into action in a capital that had to live with it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d876: American drafters prepared this undated working paper on Article 19 during the Potsdam talks, filed with papers dated July 23, 1945. Reparations must leave Germans enough to live on without outside help. Paying for imports approved by the Control Council would be a first charge on export proceeds. If the council failed to agree, each zone commander could import supplies his government deemed vital, claiming first charge on his zone's exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d976: Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Molotov on August 1, 1945, now that a tripartite reparations plan stands agreed at Potsdam. The remaining work, he says, is carrying the deal out. The key task is deciding what will be removed from the western zones, and arranging Soviet deliveries of needed products in return. Byrnes therefore urges that the Allied Commission on Reparations assemble in Berlin at once, to work with the Control Council. He asks Molotov to instruct the Soviet representative accordingly.
frus-1958-60v09-d176: Another 1958-1960 FRUS document from the Berlin Crisis volume. The standoff continued. This document holds that record. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
gao-gaoreports-b-297176: Raloid Corporation took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298276: King Construction Company took its July 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Builders get the same full hearing as everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-298576: Singleton Enterprises took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299076: Fantastic Data came back for more in February 2007 — a second protest and a second ruling in the same month. The firm challenged another award, and the call tests these claims too. Repeat filers get repeat fairness, case by case. The second bite got the same fair look.
gao-gaoreports-b-299576: Meeks Disposal Corporation doubled its June 2007 protest — two case numbers, one trash-hauling fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards; the call weighs each claim. Garbage contracts, the ruling shows, get first-class bid law.
gao-gaoreports-b-308476: The trucking safety agency's restitution money got a fiscal ruling in this December 2006 GAO call, which decides whether court-ordered funds could be kept. The decision reads the money law. The ruling settles the ledger on the ill-gotten gains. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310976: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Para Scientific Company. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-176: Head Start's financial risks needed a system in 2005, and GAO's report says a comprehensive approach could prevent grantee money troubles. The review prescribes the early warning. The little learners' funds deserved the guard. The approach had to be comprehensive. The little learners' funds deserved the guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-276: The budget office's tech reviews could bite harder in 2005, and GAO's report says OMB had room to make its investment checks more effective. The review pushes for tougher questions. The billions deserved the scrutiny. The reviews had to improve. The billions deserved the scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-376: Ecological indicator data programs got a GAO status check in 2005, and the report examines federal efforts. The findings take the measure. The report shows the nature numbers were being watched. The status had to be reported. The nature numbers were being watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-876: Iraq reconstruction funding got a GAO status check in 2005, and the report examines the money and efforts. The findings do the math. The report warns that the rebuilding dollars deserved honest tracking. The status had to be reported. The rebuilding dollars deserved honest tracking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1076: The federal buildings' guards needed measuring in 2006, and GAO's report says the protective service could better measure its control centers' performance. The findings demand the metrics. The report warns that the guardians needed grading too. The watch had to be watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-176: Veterans' job training needed labor action in 2006, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve accountability and help states. The findings demand the results. The report warns that the veterans deserved programs that worked. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-276: Mandatory spending needed budget triggers in 2006, and GAO's report says using triggers could constrain the autopilot growth. The findings prescribe the mechanism. The report warns that the unstoppable spending needed brakes. The triggers had to be used. The autopilot spending needed brakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-376: Shell company ownership stayed murky in 2006, and GAO's report says minimal ownership information was collected and available. The findings expose the fog. The report warns that the anonymous firms could hide mischief. The information had to be collected. The anonymous firms needed naming.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-476: The telecom transition needed better planning in 2006, and GAO's report says full adoption of sound practices could improve the GSA-led shift. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the government's phone lines should not go dark mid-move. The planning had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-676: Seniors' medical data was being outsourced in 2006, and GAO's report examines domestic and offshore handling of personal information in the health programs. The findings probe the privacy. The report warns that the patients' secrets deserved locks. The outsourcing had to be safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-76: Air cargo security needed federal action in 2005, and GAO's report says domestic cargo protection had to be strengthened. The findings demand the measures. The report warns that the freight holds deserved guarding. The action had to be taken. The freight holds deserved guarding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-276: Lejeune's poisoned water got a second GAO look in 2007 — the report details the follow-up on the Marine base's contamination legacy. The findings keep the official record straight. The report stands as the paper trail for families still seeking answers decades later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-376: The Army's future war machines faced their moment of truth in 2007, and GAO's report says the key decisions on the Future Combat System could not wait. The findings frame the fork in the road. The report's warning: decide with data, or pay in sunk billions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-76: The terror war's 2006 spending stayed within bounds, and GAO's report says the obligation rates fit the funding levels, with multiyear procurement noted. The findings do the accounting. The report shows the long war's ledger for the year. The books were kept, if heavily.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-276: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at VA Health Care: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury Screening and Evaluation Implemented for OEF/OIF Veterans, but Challenges Remain. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-76: GAO's 2007 report takes apart the FAA's math for billing airlines for air-traffic control. Much of the method passed muster, GAO found, but some key guesses and steps did not. gao-gaoreports-gao-08-976: The Government Accountability Office dug into veterans Health Administration: Improvements Needed in Design of Controls over Miscellaneous Obligations in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-1-1776:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 1 of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in 1776. Gibbon tells the story of Rome from its height under the Antonines to the age of Constantine. Armies, emperors, frontiers, and the rise of Christianity fill the narrative. His irony and learning made the book an instant classic.

Famous chapters on early Christianity blamed the new faith in part for Rome's decay. Churchmen attacked him, and Gibbon replied with relish. The prose is stately, balanced, and often quietly mocking. Many call the History the greatest work of history in English. Volume 1 alone would secure Gibbon's fame.
gill-myths-and-songs-from-the-south-paci:
William Wyatt Gill collected Myths and Songs from the South Pacific in 1876 from his years as a missionary in the Cook Islands. Mangaian traditions fill the volume: creation, the gods, and Avaiki, the underworld beneath the sea. Songs in native verse, Englished by Gill, carry the tales as the islanders themselves sang them.

Gill wrote down what elders told him before the old religion faded from living memory. Heroes, cannibal gods, and voyages of the soul pass in strange, splendid procession. The book remains a first source on Polynesian myth, gathered at the last moment it could be.
gray-darwiniana-1876:
Asa Gray was America's leading botanist and Darwin's chief ally across the Atlantic. His Darwiniana, from 1876, collects the essays and reviews he wrote as evolution fought for a hearing. Gray knew Darwin's work before most Americans did.

Gray explains natural selection in clear terms and answers its critics one by one. He also argues that faith and evolution need not clash, a view Darwin himself welcomed. The reviews trace the debate from the first shock of the Origin to wider acceptance. They show science being argued out in public, in real time. Gray wrote as both a working scientist and a man of faith.
hansard-suez-canal-shares-1876:
The House of Commons took up the Suez Canal share deal in its supply debate of February 14, 1876. Hansard holds the whole talk, word for word, in its record of that day. The deal had been struck in haste in the fall of 1875, with Rothschild cash.

The Prime Minister's men tell the House that the Rothschilds paid the Khedive near four million pounds at once. The price on the record is 3,976,582 pounds, with a fee of two and a half per cent. The debate is the chief first hand record of a deal that gave Britain a stake in Suez.
io-chrysippi-faniani-de-arte-metallicae-: Io. Chrysippi Faniani De arte metallicae metamorphoseos, 1576. The metallic metamorphosis. This book preserves that work. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucerne-10176:
Lucerne, a Swiss city in the canton of the same name, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. Jews lived there by the middle of the thirteenth century. The town’s earliest records already regulate how meat slaughtered by Jews had to be sold.

Those rules also promised protection: no one was to injure the Jews, on pain of a fine or banishment from the city. As elsewhere in Switzerland, Jews alone could charge interest on loans, and money-lending was their trade. Even so, they were expelled in 1401. No Jew settled again until about 1864, and the community counted forty-two members in 1904. The entry gives a compact history of early protection, expulsion, and a very late return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-markus-1:
Markus Magnus, an elder of Berlin's Jewish congregation, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as court Jew to the crown prince, later King Frederick William I. That royal backing set him against his rival, Jost Liebmann. King Frederick I favored Liebmann, and the community split into two hostile camps.

The article follows the feud to its end. After Liebmann's death his widow and sons kept the quarrel alive. Magnus won in the end. He persuaded the congregation to replace the private synagogues of the old families with one public synagogue. In 1722 the government issued new rules for the congregation's management. Magnus and Moses Levi Gumpertz were named permanent chief elders, each with a salary of three hundred thalers. The entry shows how court favor and rivalry shaped Berlin's Jewish self-government.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manresa-10376:
Manresa, a town in Spain's province of Barcelona, is given a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In the twelfth century it is said to have held five hundred Jewish families. Most lived in a narrow lane by the town hall, the Grau dels Jueus. Their cemetery outside the city is still called Fossana dels Jueus.

The article describes livelihoods and mounting hostility. Manresa's Jews worked in manufacturing, trade, money-lending at twenty percent, and their own vineyards. In 1325 townspeople tried to stop them baking Passover bread, and the Jews appealed to the king. The persecution of 1391 struck Manresa too, and many Jews professed Christianity. After 1414 few remained. In 1492 the last of them sold their property for what it would fetch and left. The entry also notes the Zabarra family members who lived in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-joseph:
Meir ben Joseph ben Merwan ha-Levi was a French scholar of twelfth-century Narbonne. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn give him an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the brother of the nasi, the head of the community, R. Moses ben Joseph ben Merwan. He was a pupil of Isaac ben Merwan, who headed the Narbonne academy in the early twelfth century. He was held in great respect and moved in the circle of Abraham ben Isaac, president of the rabbinical college of Narbonne about 1165.

No book of his is named. His survival in the record rests on a conjecture by Gross. Gross held that this Meir is identical with Meir ben Jacob. That man appears, among five other scholars, at the end of a rabbinical responsum dated at Narbonne in the mid-twelfth century. The bibliography sends readers to chronicles and legal collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendlin-jacob-w:
Jacob Wolf Mendlin, a Russian Hebrew economist, is profiled by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the first Hebrew writer to take up economics for the Jewish masses of Russia. He was born at Moghilef-on-the-Dnieper in 1842. About 1862 he went to Germany. Studying the labor movement under Lassalle turned his ambition to economics and cooperation. From his first article in "Ha-Meliz" in 1879, he wrote steadily on the condition of Russian Jewry, in Hebrew, Russian, and Yiddish papers.

His books argue one remedy: "Ba-Meh Niwwashea'," By What Shall We Be Saved (1883), and "Mekore ha-Osher," Sources of Wealth (1898). With a Yiddish work on self-help, they point to mutual aid and cooperative organization. That, they argue, is the surest cure for the wretched state of the Jewish poor. He also founded charitable institutions at Odessa, where he was living in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metatron-hebr-g:
Meṭaṭron is an angel found only in Jewish literature, powerful enough that Elisha ben Abuyah, seeing him in heaven, believed there were two divine powers. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on him in 1906. The entry gathers his roles from Talmud, Midrash, and later mystical books.

Meṭaṭron bears God's name, consoles God after the Temple's destruction, and yet may not be worshiped, the article stresses. Later sources call him prince of the presence, heavenly scribe, and lord of secrets, and identify him with Enoch. Closing sections weigh rival accounts of his origin, from Latin metator, meaning guide, to links with Mithra, Philo's Logos, and Horus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micah-10776:
Micah the prophet, author of the sixth book among the Twelve Minor Prophets, heads a Jewish Encyclopedia article written by Isidore Singer, M. Seligsohn, Solomon Schechter, and Emil G. Hirsch in 1906. His name is a short form of Micaiah, meaning Who is like Yhwh. Almost everything known of him comes from his book's opening line.

He was a Morasthite, from Moresheth-gath, and prophesied under the Judahite kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, a span the article dates to 756-697 B.C. at the outside. Later tradition confused him with Micaiah son of Imlah and told of his death under Ahab, claims the entry reports with doubt. After the prophet, the article takes up the other biblical Micahs, including the Ephraimite whose stolen silver funded a household shrine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moos-solomon-10:
Solomon Moos, born at Randegg near Constance on July 15, 1831, was the German ear specialist who built otology at Heidelberg, in an entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his medical degree there in 1856 and joined its faculty three years later. From 1875 he practised otology alone.

He founded Heidelberg's otological clinic and dispensary and directed it until his death — on his sixty-fourth birthday, in 1895. With Knapp he had founded the Archiv für Augen- und Ohrenheilkunde in 1868, and he translated Toynbee's Diseases of the Ear into German. His monographs run from the Eustachian tube to fungal invasion of the labyrinth after diphtheria and measles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-eliakim-b:
Moses Eliakim Beri'ah ben Israel was a Polish preacher born at Cozienice, where he died in 1825. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. Like his father, Israel of Cozienice, he was a disciple of Elimelech of Lysensk. Elimelech was one of the active leaders of Hasidism.

His printed book, Be'er Mosheh, gathers homilies arranged by the weekly portions of the Pentateuch. Two more works stayed in manuscript: Da'at Mosheh, a homiletic commentary on the Pentateuch, and Matteh Mosheh, on the Passover Haggadah. The entry keeps a Hasidic preacher's name and books on record for later readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mossiri-hayyim-: Hayyim Nissim Raphael Mossiri was a Turkish rabbinical writer who died at Jerusalem about 1800. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He had come to Jerusalem from Salonica. His one work is Be'er Mayim Hayyim, a book of responsa in two volumes, printed at Salonica in 1764 and 1814.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahash-serpent-:
Nahash, a name meaning serpent, belongs first to a king of the Ammonites in the days of Saul. The Jewish Encyclopedia article, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, tells his attack on Jabesh-gilead. He offered the town a choice: every right eye put out, or the sword. The town won seven days, and Saul came and routed him.

The article notes that fear of Nahash was itself a reason Israel demanded a king. David later sent condolences to Nahash's son, for Nahash had shown him kindness in flight. Two more Nahashes follow: the father of Shobi, who fed David in exile, and a name in Amasa's family line. The rabbis identified that Nahash with Jesse himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-bernh:
Bernhard Nathanson was a Russian Hebrew journalist and author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Satanow, Podolia, on April 15, 1832. His father guided his early Hebrew studies. When his father died in 1853, he moved to Odessa.

At Odessa he studied both sacred and secular subjects. He spent three years copying and fixing Levinsohn's manuscripts. In 1875 he went to Warsaw to publish Levinsohn's works. His own first article appeared in Ha-Maggid in 1864. He wrote a Bible name book in 1871. He also wrote Levinsohn's life and a Talmud word book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumark-mirels-:
Meshullam Zalman Neumark, called Mirels, was a German Talmudist. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and A. Peiginsky for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the father of Zebi Ashkenazi. He died at Hamburg on Nov. 28, 1706. Vienna's ghetto had counted him among its most respected men.

When Vienna expelled its Jews, he moved to Berlin. There too he rose to prominence among Jews. He joined Talmud study to business and to charity. In 1678 he returned briefly to Vienna on permit. He negotiated a loan there for the elector. Soon after, he gave up trade entirely. Hamburg and Altona took him as their rabbi. The sister communities shared his rabbinate from then on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nobah-11576:
Nobah names both a warrior and his captured town. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The man was a Manassite of the conquest age. He seized Kenath, east of the Jordan, with its villages. He then gave the place his own name.

Gideon passed Nobah chasing the Midianite kings eastward. Later ages called the town Canatha in their records. Coins suggest Gabinius restored it in Roman times. Herod met a crushing defeat there against Arabs. Inscriptions show councilors and a market clerk governed it. It also belonged, for a time, to Agrippa II. Today it is Ḳanawat, held by a few Druse families. It sits on the old Roman road to Damascus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ohole-shem-asso:
The Ohole Shem Association was a group based in New York. Herman Rosenthal and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded on October 8, 1895. Its aim was to spur the study of Hebrew. It also backed study of kindred tongues and Jewish past.

Herman Rosenthal founded the group, with help from friends. Dr. A. Radin and Dr. S. Brainin stood with him. The group set up talks in three tongues at once. Those tongues were Hebrew, German, and English. It put out a Hebrew monthly in its first years. It marked the birth days of great Jewish men. In 1901 it marked one hundred years since Zacharias Frankel was born.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-zebi-h:
Zebi Hirsch Ornstein was an Austrian rabbi of Lemberg. The board and M. W. Rapoport wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lemberg and died there in 1888. His father was Mordecai Zeeb Ornstein of that city. His grandfather was Jacob Meshullam Ornstein, its rabbi.

Zebi was taught by his father and grandfather in youth. He showed rare talent while still a young man. Some of his replies were placed in his grandfather's book. That book was Yeshuot Yaakob, a famed work of replies. His name soon spread far past his own land. In 1855 he took his first post at Brest-Litovsk. There his great memory drew awe from all who heard him. The state forced him out of that town in 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palti-or-phalti: Palti, or Phalti, is a name borne by two men in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name is most likely a short form of Paltiel. The first Palti was a son of Raphu, of Benjamin. He was one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. The second was the new husband of Michal, Saul's daughter. Michal had been the wife of David before that match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedat-b-eleazar:
Pedat ben Eleazar was a Palestinian teacher of the Talmud. He lived in the first half of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned the Law first from his own father.

Pedat served as the spokesman for Rabbi Assi in lecture. He passed on sayings from his father and from Rabbi Hoshaiah. He was a close friend of Zera and of Jeremiah ben Eleazar. A few of his readings of Scripture survive. One clears Moses of pride in a hard verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-petronius-publi:
Publius Petronius governed Syria from 39 to 42. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His term forced him into close dealings with the Jews. He used that contact to shield them once.

Caligula ordered his statue set inside the Jerusalem Temple. Petronius had the statue made slowly at Sidon. He stalled at Ptolemais through the winter, talking with Jewish leaders. Crowds begged to die rather than yield the sanctuary. Moved, he marched his troops back to Antioch. He wrote the emperor asking him to cancel the order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsker-simhah-:
Simhah Pinsker was a Polish scholar of Hebrew antiquities. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tarnopol in 1801. He died at Odessa in 1864, pensioned and honored. His book later traced the rise of Karaism.

Pinsker failed in trade, then served Odessa's rabbi as secretary. His fine handwriting had won him the post. He helped found a public school for Jewish children. Then Firkovich brought strange old manuscripts from Crimea. Pinsker cracked their odd system of vowel points. Gold medals and a pension rewarded the feat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-josef-12:
Josef Popper was an Austrian engineer and author born at Kolin in Bohemia in 1838. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote essays on machines for learned journals. His books range far beyond his trade, though. They treat social questions, flight, and Jewish life.

Popper wrote on the right to live and the duty to die in 1878. He wrote against anti-Semitism in a book on Bismarck in 1886. His flight book came out in 1889. Best known is his early idea for sending electric power over wires. He set out that idea in 1862. A Vienna academy printed it twenty years later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-procurators-123:
Procurators were the Roman governors set over Judea. Gotthard Deutsch and Samuel Krauss wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They took charge after Archelaus was banished in the year 6. From the year 44 they ruled the whole of Palestine. The land was joined to Syria in name. In fact it kept a governor of its own.

Josephus gives that governor more than one Greek title. His set title was procurator, or epitropos in Greek. At times Josephus calls him eparch or hegemon instead. The article lists the men who held the post in turn. It tells what each did in a tense land. Pontius Pilate stands among them in the full account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-hana-r:
Rabbah bar Hana was a Babylonian teacher of the first set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a nephew of Hiyya the Great. He was a cousin of Abba Arika, known as Rab. Like Rab, he went up to Palestine for his learning.

In Palestine Rabbah sat among the chief pupils of Judah the Prince. As he left, Judah gave him a broad right. He might rule on all points of Jewish law. He might sit as a judge in cases as well. Hiyya had asked that this honor be granted him. Back in Babylonia, his name stands with the great of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapoport-12576:
Rapoport is a family name shared by many Jewish branches. Isidore Singer, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Emil Jelinek, A. S. Waldstein, Peter Wiernik, M. Seligsohn, and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. All branches claim a common Kohenitic origin. The name Rapa appears about 1450 on the Rhine.

The article traces the family from Mayence toward Italy. Jews were expelled from Mayence in 1462. Soon a wealthy Hayyim Rappe appears near Venice. A Polish branch told a legend to explain the name. The writers argue it comes from a word for raven. The family arms bear two ravens, they note. The entry opens a long family history in several lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remenyi-eduard-:
Eduard Remenyi was a Hungarian violinist born at Eged in 1830. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at New York on May 15, 1898. He studied under Böhm at the Vienna Conservatorium.

The article says Austria banished him for joining the 1848 revolution. He spent five years in America as a traveling player. Back in Europe, Liszt taught him at Weimar. In 1854 he became solo violinist to Queen Victoria. An amnesty let him return to Hungary in 1860. He toured France, Germany, Belgium, and Holland in 1865. A world tour in 1886 reached Japan and China. His best original work is a violin concerto. He also transcribed many piano pieces for violin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-morit:
Moritz Rosenthal was an Austrian pianist born at Lemberg in 1862. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied under several teachers before the family moved to Vienna in 1875.

At fourteen Rosenthal gave a first public concert that won wide praise. Its program ranged from Beethoven and Chopin to Mendelssohn and Liszt. A tour led to his naming as Rumanian court pianist at Bucharest. From 1876 to 1878 he studied under Liszt himself. He later toured America twice and published advanced technical studies for pianists. With L. Schytte he published technical studies for pianists of the highest development.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-johann-ja:
Johann Jacob Sachs was a German physician born at Märkisch Friedland on July 26, 1803. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Königsberg in 1827 and practised in Berlin.

In 1832 Sachs founded the Berliner Medizinische Zeitung, a medical weekly paper. Renamed over time, it was still being published when this entry appeared. He also issued a medical almanac and a yearly repertory of medical progress. His own books cover mineral waters, cholera on German soil, and influenza. Attacked by critics in 1842, he defended his literary work in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-jose:
Samson ben Joseph of Falaise was a tosafist of the twelfth century in France. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was grandfather of two famed tosafists, Isaac of Dampierre and Samson of Sens.

Jacob Tam, who corresponded with Samson on learned questions, esteemed him highly. Samson wrote tosafot to Shabbat, Erubin, Yebamot, and Hullin in the Talmud. His ritual decisions were cited by Joel ha-Levi under the title Pesakim. One ruling let a nursing woman remarry soon after her divorce. Jacob Tam attacked that decision severely in his Sefer ha-Yashar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sandor-paul-131:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Paul Sándor. He was a Hungarian merchant and deputy. Sándor was born in 1860 at Hodmezövásárhely. He studied at the academies of commerce in Budapest and Dresden. That training prepared him for business and for public life in the capital.

In Budapest, Sándor sat on the municipal council. He also belonged to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry. In 1901 the Lipótváros district of Budapest sent him to the Hungarian Parliament. The entry is brief, and it rests on Sturm's parliamentary almanac for 1901 to 1906. It records a merchant who carried his standing in trade into national politics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-her:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Herman Schlesinger. He was a German physician. Schlesinger was born at Adelebsen, in Hanover, on April 1, 1856. He took his medical degree at Göttingen in 1879. The same university gave him a prize for a treatise. It studied what long, small doses of mercury do to animals.

After further study in Berlin, Schlesinger settled at Frankfort-on-the-Main. In 1899 he became editor of Die Aerztliche Praxis, published at Würzburg. His handbook covers hygienic and dietetic rules, water cures, and other treatments. It reached a sixth edition in 1896. Raffaelo Supino translated it into Italian at Florence in 1897. The entry rests on Pagel's biographical lexicon of physicians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seder-13376:
Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Seder. Seder is the Ashkenazic name for the Passover home service. It falls on the first night of the feast. Those who keep a second festival day repeat it then. Sephardic Jews call the service the Haggadah, the story. The book read aloud bears that same name.

Exodus pictures the first Passover as a household meal. Parents and children ate together at home. In Second Temple days only men were summoned to Jerusalem. Only city dwellers could keep the night as a family feast. The Temple's fall restored the home table. The father could again obey the command to tell his son. Four cups of wine mark the evening's joy. Roast lamb, unleavened bread, and bitter herbs anchor the meal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-ben-:
Shabbethai ben Moses ha-Kohen was rabbi of a town near Tikoczin, Russia, in the early eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His lasting work was as an editor rather than an author. He prepared a Talmud commentary collection for print at Fürth in 1741.

That collection, Minhat Kohen, gathers fresh readings of the Talmud. Its authors were Abraham Broda, Zebi Ashkenazi, and Jacob Kohen Poppers of Frankfurt. Shabbethai added some readings of his own to theirs. The entry is short, yet it credits the quiet labor that carried other rabbis' learning into print for wider use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiggayon-13576:
Shiggayon is a puzzling term set at the head of Psalm seven. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. A plural form heads the third chapter of Habakkuk. Ancient versions read the word in differing ways.

Some old translators linked it to a word for trespass. Rashi and the Midrash took a similar view of it. The entry judges that reading incorrect, though. Shiggayon likely belongs with labels like mizmor and maskil. Those labels mark types of songs in the Psalms. Some scholars derive it from a root meaning to reel. They call it a wild, passionate lyric form. Yet Psalm seven is not unique in feeling. The term stays unexplained, and the entry says so plainly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-13676:
Simeon was the second son of Jacob, by his wife Leah. Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Padan-aram, far from Canaan. Genesis explains his name as God hath heard.

Leah felt herself hated, and the name marked that sorrow. Scholars offer other roots for the name as well. Simeon stands out in two famous incidents of Genesis. With Levi he massacred Shechem's men for wronging Dinah. Jacob rebuked both brothers sharply for that revenge. Later Joseph held Simeon hostage in an Egyptian prison. He stayed bound until the brothers returned with Benjamin. The entry weighs name lore against a violent, vivid story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-paul-137:
Paul Singer was a German Social Democrat and deputy born in Berlin in 1844. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He went into trade after real-school. In 1869 he set up a cloak factory with his brother. The business prospered and made him a fortune.

Singer turned to politics and the study of labor. He joined the Social-Democratic party and rose beside Bebel and Liebknecht. In 1884 Berlin voters sent him to the Reichstag. He gave 5,000 marks to aid families of exiled Socialists. An expulsion order against him in 1886 was soon withdrawn. He also helped found the Refuge for the Homeless in Berlin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mei:
Solomon ben Meir was a French grammarian and Bible commentator. Crawford Howell Toy and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the twelfth century in France. He was a grandson of Rashi through his mother. His brothers were the famed tosafists Isaac, Samuel, and Jacob Tam.

Some authorities denied that Meir had a fourth son at all. Berliner found proof in Vatican fragments in 1874. Those fragments quote a commentary by Solomon ben Meir often. They call him brother of Jacob Tam in plain words. He was called father of grammarians for his skill. He served as prayer leader at Ramerupt and signed Tam's ordinances.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-friedri:
Friedrich Samuel Spitzer was a French art collector and dealer of fame. Isidore Singer and Richard Gottheil wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Presburg in 1814, son of a grave-digger. He went penniless to Vienna to seek his fortune. A picture bought for five gulden proved to be a Dürer.

That find laid the foundation of his great wealth. He learned that old weapons drew high prices in England. He bought up old arms in Austria and sold them in London. Settled in Paris at Rothschild's urging, his business prospered greatly. Gambetta offered him six million francs for his collection. After his death in 1890 it sold for ten million francs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-gustave:
Gustave Louis Maurice Strauss was a British author born in Canada in 1807. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Trois-Rivières and educated in Hanover and Berlin. He also studied medicine at Montpellier. He died at Teddington on September 2, 1887.

Strauss served as assistant surgeon with the French army in Algiers. France banished him in 1839 over a suspected plot. He then settled in London as author and tutor. He also worked as linguist, dramatist, and surgeon there. His books include Men Who Have Made the German Empire. His Old Bohemian tales retell his own roaming life. He wrote grammars and translated many books into English. Gladstone later secured him a small government annuity. The entry recalls a restless, many-sided writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szenes-philip-1:
Philip Szenes was a Hungarian painter born at Török Szent Miklos in 1864. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied first at Budapest's technical school. Then he gave himself wholly to art. He lived years in Munich, Italy, and Paris.

In 1895 the Paris Academy of Art gave Szenes first prize. He returned to Budapest with that honor fresh. At once he ranked with Hungary's foremost painters. His chief works retell Bible scenes in paint. Samson and Delilah, Esther, and Judith lead the list. He also painted quiet scenes like After Dinner. His canvases hang in Budapest's National Museum. Emperor Francis Joseph kept some in his private gallery. The entry marks a painter crowned early by Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taylor-charles-:
Charles Taylor was an English Christian Hebraist born in London in 1840. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at King's College, London, and at Cambridge. He later became master of St. John's College there. His work centered on rabbinic texts in English.

In 1877 Taylor published Sayings of the Jewish Fathers. It is an elaborate edition of the Pirke Abot. A second edition followed in 1897. An 1899 appendix lists its manuscripts in full. Jacobs calls it the finest such work by a living Christian. Taylor found the Jewish source behind the Didache. With Schechter he edited the Wisdom of Ben Sira. Cambridge's Genizah gifts bear the Taylor-Schechter name. The entry honors a Christian master of rabbinic learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thorn-14376:
Thorn, a West Prussian town founded in 1233, long barred Jews from living there. Isidore Singer and I. Rosenberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Teutonic Knights founded Thorn and excluded Jews. Polish rule after 1453 admitted them only now and then.

Expulsions came in 1766, 1774, 1779, and 1797. Still, families kept returning over the years. By 1823 the community counted 52 families, or 248 people. Its first rabbi served without pay until 1847. A synagogue rose that same year. Scholars such as Zvi Hirsch Kalischer lived in Thorn. A home for the aged opened in 1892. The community also kept a loan society and a literary society. By 1903 the town held 1,200 Jews among 30,000 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verdun-hebrew-1:
Verdun is a French city, capital of the department of Meuse. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived at Verdun from the twelfth century. Its scholars included the tosafist Samuel ben Hayyim. Samuel ben Joseph and Jacob ben Joseph also taught there.

For long stretches, Jews could not live in Verdun at all. In 1433 the city asked Basel's council to let expelled Jews return. The request failed, and residence stayed banned until 1559. Later French kings let Metz Jews visit briefly for business. A Jew who stayed three days in 1774 was expelled. The entry traces this tight, shifting welcome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wanefrieden-eli:
Eliakim Getschlik Wanefrieden was a judge and preacher at Amsterdam. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at the end of the eighteenth century. In 1790 he published a pamphlet called Megillat Sefer. It holds sermons and a eulogy. The eulogy honors Saul Löwenstamm, Amsterdam's chief rabbi.

His surname points to Wannfried in Hesse as his birthplace. The entry separates him from a namesake in Moravia. That other Eliakim served as rabbi in Kanitz about 1760. He was likely father to Jeremiah Wanefrieden. Jeremiah defended Jonathan Eybeschütz against heresy charges. The brief note untangles two men of one name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-west-14876:
West is one of the four quarters of heaven and earth. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hebrew calls the east kedem, meaning front. The west is ahor, meaning rear. Since the Mediterranean Sea lay west of Palestine, the word sea itself came to mean west.

Another term, ma'arab, names the sunset point. In later Hebrew it became the common word for west. Rabbis debated where God's presence, the Shekinah, resides. R. Abbahu placed the Shekinah in the west. That view opposed Babylonian belief about death's gate. Palestine itself was called Ma'araba, the West, from Babylon. Its people were the sons of the West.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-gerson-149:
Gerson Wolf (1823-1892) was an Austrian historian and teacher of Jewish life. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Moravia, he learned Hebrew as a small boy. He later studied Talmud at Nikolsburg and went to Vienna in 1839.

At Vienna he took up teaching, thought, and new tongues. His first piece ran in print in 1845. It set Greek plays beside the plays of his own day. He took part in the street fights of 1848 and 1849. Bold pieces in two papers forced him to leave Vienna for a time. The long entry follows his books and his school work. It shows a writer caught up in the hopes of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yelisavetgrad-e:
Yelisavetgrad is a town in the state of Kherson in Russia. Herman Rosenthal, Isaac Broyde, and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded in the year 1754. It grew into a chief town of the south of Russia.

Its name stirs sad thoughts for the Jews of Russia. From that town came the spark for the riots of 1881. When a new czar took the throne, tales of a rise spread. The heads of the Jews asked the governor for guards. No heed was paid to their plea at that hour. On April 27, 1881, the mob broke out at last. A row in an inn on blood use served as the spark. The mob then fell on the shops of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarko-judah-ben:
Judah ben Abraham Zarko was a Hebrew poet famed for fine style. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at Rhodes in the sixteenth century of this era. On a stay at Constantinople he wrote his chief book.

That book bears the name Lehem Yehudah in Hebrew tongue. It holds a tale on the soul in figure form. It holds verse and prose poems side by side in it. It holds sharp short verse at the great men of his day. Some of that verse is aimed at Maimonides himself. A note of his stands at the head of a style book. More of his short poems came out in a London book. That book was made by Edelmann in the year 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zoan-15276:
Zoan was an ancient Egyptian city, nearly as old as Hebron in the Bible's telling. Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Muller wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaiah ranks its princes beside those of Memphis, and Ezekiel names it with Thebes. Israelite embassies went to Zoan, which hints it was once a royal residence.

The Greeks called the city Tanis. It stood in the Nile Delta, on the Tanitic branch, near Lake Menzalah and Egypt's northeast frontier. Kings of the twenty-first dynasty, called Tanitic, ruled from there. Digging by Mariette in 1860 and Petrie in 1883 uncovered monuments from the sixth dynasty to Roman times. By then the great city had shrunk toward a fishing village.
legge-the-shih-king-or-book-of-poetry-sh:
James Legge Englished China's oldest songbook in The Shih King, issued in 1876 with the Chinese text beside his version. Its 305 songs date from about the eleventh to the seventh century before Christ. Love songs, war songs, and harvest hymns all stand in its pages.

Legge, a Scottish scholar and missionary, gave Victorian readers a window on ancient China. Court odes praise kings, while folk ballads sing of longing and toil. The book formed part of the Sacred Books of the East series. Few anthologies anywhere are older or more loved, and this version pairs sound learning with the original words.
life-of-johnson-volume-2-1765-1776:
