Jin-Hyang Park and three colleagues show how to measure muscle fibers on ordinary archived slides with a browser based tool, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fiber cross sectional area is the standard yardstick for muscle wasting and regrowth, but the usual workflow needs frozen tissue and fluorescent stains, so old paraffin blocks in hospital archives go unused. Their pipeline runs an artificial intelligence segmentation program through a public web interface, then tidies regions and measures fibers in free image software.

Validated in mouse muscle, the method's area distributions from routine pink stained paraffin sections matched those from a comparison stain and from frozen sections. In a nerve injury model it correctly registered the shrinkage of fibers cut off from their nerve. The payoff is access: decades of stored slides become measurable, and small laboratories without specialist kit can join neuromuscular research on equal terms.
plos-pone-0358576: Zuo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diet, sleep, and lung cancer in southwest China. They compared patients with lung cancer against people without it, in a case-control design. The focus was on polyunsaturated fats in food and on sleep patterns. Links found in such studies can shape diet and sleep advice, though they need care before being read as causes.
plos-pone-0358776: Shimagaki and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on outlook after liver cancer surgery. They tested a blood-based index, built from C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte counts, measured before surgery. The question was whether that index predicts how patients fare after part of the liver is removed. A cheap score from routine blood tests could help surgeons judge risk before operating.
plos-pone-0359776:
Joshua Vo and six colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a scoping review of how medical students and residents around the world are taught telemedicine. Telemedicine, care delivered by video or phone, became a core skill during recent years, yet training in it varies wildly between schools.

A scoping review will map what is taught, where, and how it is evaluated, across countries. Medical schools building telemedicine teaching need that world map before writing their own courses. Educators and accreditation bodies are the audience for a review designed to show the gaps in training.
plos-pone-0359976:
Lei Zhu and colleagues built in 2026 a mosquito recognition system that runs on a mobile device. Identifying mosquito species matters because only some kinds spread diseases such as dengue and malaria, and control efforts differ by species. Their system uses a convolutional neural network, the image recognizing form of deep learning, trained to judge mosquitoes by two kinds of shape evidence at once, which the authors call dual morphology.

Putting the trained model on a phone moves identification out of the laboratory and into the field, where health workers and citizens actually encounter the insects. Fast, accurate identification can sharpen surveillance maps and help target spraying and breeding site removal. The study joins a growing set of phone based tools for tracking disease carrying insects.
plos-pone-0360076:
Andrew Tusubira and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how people living with HIV manage their own care when they also live with high blood pressure or diabetes. Their systematic review gathers studies from low and middle income countries, where clinics are stretched and patients carry much of the daily work of staying well. Self-care covers taking medicines faithfully, watching diet and symptoms, and knowing when to seek help.

Having three long term conditions at once multiplies that work, and health systems built around single diseases can leave such patients unsupported. By mapping what self-care looks like and what helps or hinders it, the review gives program designers a view from the patient's side of the clinic door.
plos-pone-0360376:
Jhon Zabaleta-Santisteban and a large team of collaborators mapped in 2026 where cacao could grow well in the Amazonas region of Peru. Their approach is an ensemble of predictive models, combined through a platform called BIOMOD2, that weighs many data sources at once. The maps fold in territorial management and plant health alongside climate and soil, so the result speaks to farming decisions rather than to climate alone.

Cacao is a valuable export crop and an alternative livelihood in regions pressed by deforestation. Knowing which land suits it, and which land should be left alone, helps planners steer planting toward success and away from forest clearing. The study gives regional authorities a planning tool grounded in the region's own conditions.
plos-pone-0360476:
Amine Ben Safta and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 on the pressure used during a common gallbladder operation. In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, surgeons inflate the abdomen with gas, a pneumoperitoneum, to see and work, and the operation is usually done at standard pressure. Some surgeons argued that a lower pressure, eight millimeters of mercury, would leave patients in less pain afterward.

Patients were assigned by chance to the low pressure or the standard approach, and their pain was scored on a visual analog scale after surgery. The trial's headline result is plainly stated: the lower pressure did not significantly reduce those pain scores. A clear negative answer is useful, since it tells surgical teams that this particular adjustment is not where pain relief will be found.
pmc-13237576:
Mehrabian and colleagues report a hard case of Hailey-Hailey disease eased by an unexpected drug. The patient, a man of sixty-five, had endured three years of burning, itching, and splitting skin in the groin area. Creams, steroids, antifungals, and repeated antibiotics had all given little relief before a biopsy confirmed the inherited blistering disease.

Treatment with naltrexone, a drug better known for blocking opioids, brought success where standard care failed. Why it helps this skin disease is still debated, but case reports build the record doctors consult when usual options run out. For a painful, embarrassing condition, one well-documented success can open a new path.
pmc-13237976:
Brusco and colleagues cost out a new infection-tracking programme for Australian aged care homes. The programme, NISPAC, gives homes a standard, streamlined way to log infections and antibiotic use. Outbreaks in aged care can turn deadly fast, yet until now nobody knew what rolling the system out would cost.

The team tracked implementation costs prospectively, as the work happened, from the aged care sector's own viewpoint. Three coordinating bodies share the running of the programme, and their costs count too. A clear price tag lets funders judge the programme fairly, and lets other regions copy it with eyes open about staff time and money.
pmc-13240876:
Wu's team at Jining exposed autism-model brain organoids to two gut fatty acids and read the gene readout. Short-chain fatty acids are thought to stir inflammation and metabolic trouble in autism. Organoids received sodium acetate, sodium butyrate, or no treatment for seven days. Three repeats per group went through RNA reads.

The two pushed gene activity opposite ways. Acetate mainly shifted genes tied to gene-switch control, enzyme work, and membrane leakiness. Butyrate instead switched on immune processes, with the TGF-beta pathway standing out in the scan. The split suggests each fatty acid nudges the growing autistic brain through its own route.
pmc-13241376:
Feng's team at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan reviewed how rewired metabolism drives fibrosis across the body's organs. Scar-forming cells switch their glucose, amino acid, and fat handling in Warburg-like fashion. The review walks through core pathways before turning organ by organ. Heart, lung, liver, kidney, skin, and peritoneum each get a section.

Tags on metabolic enzymes, including the newly recognized lactylation, recur as control knobs. Some enzymes push fibrosis through side jobs unrelated to their chemistry. The authors close with therapies already aiming at glycolysis and lipid pathways. Targeting metabolism, they argue, could sit beside current anti-scar care.
pmc-13243876:
Alberte Aspaas Lundquist and colleagues add two patients to the tiny known group with disease caused by faulty MRPS34, a mitochondrial protein. Their report appeared in JIMD Reports in 2026. The gene builds part of the mitochondria's own protein factory, and damaging variants on both copies cause a Leigh syndrome spectrum disorder. One new patient died in infancy carrying two severe variants. The other, with two copies of a gentler splice variant, survived into mid-childhood.

The team then reviewed all eleven reported individuals to hunt for patterns. Developmental delay appeared in every case, and lactic acid buildup and brainstem lesions in nearly all. Carrying two copies of the milder variant tracked with longer survival, the clearest genotype-phenotype link so far. The disorder strikes many systems beyond the brain. With so few cases worldwide, the authors argue each new report materially sharpens counseling for families.
pmc-13244076:
Zhicheng Lai and colleagues ran a randomized phase two trial of two liver-directed combinations for advanced liver cancer. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. Seventy-two patients with advanced tumors received chemotherapy infused into the liver's artery, paired either with the immunotherapy toripalimab or with the targeted drug sorafenib. The main measure was how many patients remained progression-free at six months.

The two arms finished close on that measure, at just under two-thirds of patients each. Survival leaned toward the immunotherapy pairing, with a median of 20.9 months against 16.4 months for sorafenib, and time without progression also ran longer. Serious side effects were fewer with toripalimab: a third of its group had severe events against well over two-fifths on sorafenib. The trial was not designed to crown a winner between the arms. The authors call the immunotherapy combination favorable and ready for a phase three test.
pmc-13245076:
Harry Magunia and colleagues surveyed how the world performs right-heart ultrasound, and found a specialty speaking many dialects. Their RVNet survey appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Guidelines have tried to standardize right heart checks, yet practice anecdotes suggested wide variation. The anonymous sixty-eight-question survey drew 588 replies from many countries in late 2024 and early 2025.

Most were certified and experienced, yet their methods diverged at nearly every step. Views captured, timing of measures, image orientation, and what gets reported all varied, in both exam types. The authors organize the chaos with a six-part framework covering views, phase, orientation, interface, timing, and scaling. They propose it as a simple shared checklist, V-POINTS, to make measurements comparable between labs. The message: the right heart deserves the discipline the left received years ago.
pmc-13246876:
Norman, Conduit, and Laycock asked what mental abilities make some people better at spotting changes in a scene, in this 2026 Psychonomic Bulletin and Review study. Missing changes, called change blindness, matters for drivers and radiologists alike. Two hundred sixty participants took a naturalistic flicker task, where two versions of a scene alternate until the change is found, plus nine cognitive tests.

The strongest links to spotting accuracy were top-down visual search control, visuospatial ability and memory, and basic visual inspection speed. Factor analysis grouped the test battery into flexibility, visuospatial working memory, and attention-speed factors, and the visuospatial memory factor was the main predictor of change detection. The authors conclude that holding a scene in spatial memory is central to noticing what changed.
pmc-13246976:
Yang, Huang, and Wei systematically reviewed how football boot design affects injury risk, in this 2026 Sports Medicine - Open article. Boots are the player's interface with the ground, and their studs and soles shape the forces reaching knees and ankles. The team searched two decades of literature and kept thirty-two studies, checking each one's quality with a standard scale.

Several patterns stood out. Screw-in and bladed studs grip so hard in rotation that the foot can lock, raising the risk of ligament tears, ankle sprains, and stress fractures. Sole stiffness showed a U-shaped risk curve, with both very stiff and very soft plates creating problems. Mismatches between boot, foot shape, and surface added further risk. The authors call for standardized boot testing.
pmc-13248376:
Farlie and an international group of colleagues argue for a better way to dose balance training, in this 2026 comment. Falls threaten older adults, and balance exercise helps, yet prescriptions rarely state how hard the exercise should feel. The authors say that missing measure, balance intensity, holds back both research and clinical advice.

They call for one standard yardstick of balance intensity and practical ways to sample it during training. With a shared measure, studies could pin down the level that best prevents falls and protects independence. The piece is a position statement, meant to steer future trials and guidelines rather than report new data.
pmc-13248876:
Khatatbeh and colleagues surveyed adolescents in Jordan in 2026 about online gaming habits and how they view its health effects. They used the Health Belief Model, a frame that links behavior to felt risk and prompts to act. Four hundred three students aged 10 to 17 answered an online form covering daily play time, game types, and views on body and mind.

Students played about three hours a day on average. More than a quarter saw no harm to physical or mental health, a sign of low felt risk. Over a third had never been counseled on gaming harms, with parents the main source when guidance came. Older age and longer daily play tracked with poorer self-rated physical and mental health, and beliefs about mental harm also shaped ratings. The authors urge awareness efforts aimed at adolescents, parents, teachers, and school health staff.
pmc-13248976:
Liu and co-authors studied rehearsal training for heart attack teams, in a 2026 report from a Chinese chest pain center. For the deadliest heart attacks, minutes spent reopening the blocked artery shape survival. The center introduced simulation-based team training, then compared two hundred sixty patients treated before and after the program began.

After training, the median time from hospital door to balloon treatment fell from ninety-two to sixty-eight minutes. Arrival-to-treatment times improved as well, and the authors link the drills to smoother teamwork under pressure. Because the study looked backward at one center, they ask for prospective multicenter trials before declaring the training a proven cause.
pmc-13250176:
Prestedge, El-Murr, and Williamson interview Australian health workers about testing done right beside the patient. Their 2026 BMJ Open study concerns point-of-care testing, where results come during the visit instead of from a distant laboratory. Eighteen participants took part, drawn from hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, emergency care, and pathology services.

Three themes ran through the interviews: care centered on communities, connected records, and sound quality control. Workers praised programs that improved fairness of access, but they named weak funding and poor information systems as major barriers. Clearer training guidance for staff outside laboratories was seen as a practical fix. The authors call for funding that covers testing, quality checks, and staff training together.
pmc-13250876:
Wang and co-authors measure how well heart and vessel nurses lead teams in China and what drives it. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine survey covers four hundred eleven such nurses at three large hospitals, surveyed in early 2025. Nurses rated their own leading, their workplace, and their confidence in their own abilities.

Scores ran above average, strongest for urging others on and setting an example, weakest for questioning the status quo. Job title, department, training in leading, workplace quality, and self-belief each lifted the scores. Workplace and self-belief linked most strongly with the ratings. The authors advise focused training, healthier work settings, and self-belief building to grow nurse leaders in practice.
pmc-13251076:
Haiyan Pan and co-authors are the subject of this 2026 retraction notice from the journal Cancer Cell International. It withdraws their earlier paper, published in 2020, which claimed a long non-coding RNA drives stomach cancer cell growth and spread through a partner RNA chain.

After publication, concerns were raised about the Western blot and flow cytometry data in three of the paper's figures. The authors could not provide the raw data when asked to back it up. The editors state they have lost confidence in the results and conclusions. The notice adds that none of the authors replied to letters about the retraction.
pmc-13252976:
Meijun Jiang, Shaoyun Zhang, and Cong Xiao review electrical stimulation around flap surgery in this 2026 article. Skin flaps moved to cover wounds from cancer or injury can partly or wholly die, and no drug has reliably prevented that loss.

Drawing on more than 120 studies, the review sorts benefits by timing. Stimulation before surgery encourages new blood vessel growth into the flap. After surgery, it helps fight infection, drain swelling, and speed wound healing, while also guiding cells to move and multiply. Because one drug usually hits only one part of the failure process, the authors argue that a physical method touching many steps at once holds real promise.
pmc-13256176:
Jessica Appleton and colleagues report a 2026 study of SleepWellBaby, a phone app that gives parents a seven-day program on infant sleep. The program can be repeated and mixes facts with interactive features on helping babies sleep in a responsive way. Parents of infants under six months joined online and filled in surveys at the start, after seven days, and after thirty days.

Seven hundred parents started the study, with 339 still responding at seven days and 220 at thirty days. Most said the app was easy to use and that they trusted its content, though most had stopped using it by one month. Parents who used it more, or found it most helpful, showed the greatest drop in fatigue. Some also said it kept them on their phones too long.
pmc-13257876:
Xiaoqi Zhang and colleagues study a welding problem that arises when stainless steel meets ordinary carbon steel. Rail vehicle bodies join these metals with resistance spot welding, but mismatched properties shift the weld nugget off center. Their 2026 analysis inserts a thin nickel layer between the sheets.

Computer models tracked force and heat fields through the welding process with the nickel layer in place. Physical welds then confirmed what the models predicted. The nickel insert curbed nugget drift and evened out the metal's internal structure. Hardness varied more smoothly across the joint, and the finished spot welds came out stronger.
pmc-13257976:
Elizabeth A Cook leads a 2026 animal study of two drugs that block chemokine receptors, proteins that guide immune cells, during treatment for hemorrhagic shock. Hemorrhagic shock is a life-threatening state after heavy blood loss. In rats, the team compared the drugs BX471 and INCB3284, given alone or together, against a control fluid. They measured how much fluid was needed to restore blood pressure over six hours.

With control treatment, fluid needs rose sharply and averaged 108 units per kilogram of body weight. With BX471 the average was 31, with INCB3284 it was 51, and with both drugs it was 36.5. Death rates differed between groups but not significantly, and survival time in a second test did not change. Both drugs also shifted markers of body-wide inflammation, which the authors link to their fluid-saving effect.
pmc-13259576: CMAJ's June 2026 obituaries column records the deaths of Canadian physicians in short, uniform notices. Each entry names the doctor, home city, medical school and graduation year, and specialty, from family medicine and surgery to neurosurgery and radiology. Ages at death stretch from the thirties to past one hundred, and every notice links to a fuller published obituary. The column serves as the journal's running roll of the profession's losses.
pmc-13260976:
Neil Ming leads a 2026 case report of subcutaneous emphysema, air trapped under the skin, following postoperative nausea after dental extraction. An 18-year-old female had four wisdom teeth removed in a routine procedure without air-driven instruments, which are the usual source of such air. After multiple episodes of retching and vomiting she developed progressive facial swelling and was transferred to a tertiary care center for evaluation and treatment.

Imaging showed widespread air tracking through the chewing muscle and under-jaw spaces, with no abscess present. She was managed conservatively with intravenous antibiotics, sinus precautions, and supportive care, and the swelling gradually resolved. The authors warn that this complication can spread toward the chest and threaten the airway. They argue that vomiting may force air into unhealed extraction sites, so early recognition matters even without an air source.
pmc-13261976:
Jarosław Kopko and colleagues report a hard-won birth in a woman with Swyer syndrome. In this rare condition, a person with XY chromosomes develops as female but without working ovaries. Donor egg IVF can still work when the uterus is intact, as this 2026 case shows.

The twenty-nine-year-old patient, whose ovaries had been removed earlier, conceived after a frozen embryo transfer. That first pregnancy lodged dangerously in the uterine wall and was dissolved with methotrexate. Six months later a second transfer grew normally, ending in a healthy boy delivered by cesarean at thirty-nine weeks. Early ultrasound for every IVF pregnancy is their firm lesson.
pmc-13262176:
Wenjie Sun and colleagues sew a medicated patch that cooks tumors with light while leaking chemotherapy on cue. Inoperable abdominal tumors need options gentler than surgery and systemic drugs. Their 2026 electrospun patch embeds copper sulfide and polydopamine, which heat under near-infrared light.

Acidic tumor surroundings and light-triggered warmth both unlock the drug stored inside. In animals, the combined patch killed far more tumor cells than heat-only or drug-only versions. Every treated mouse survived the ninety-day watch, with little body-wide toxicity. The authors pitch the implant as a surgical alternative for selected patients.
pmc-13262276:
Franziska Ulrich and colleagues take a famous diabetes drug duel out of the trial clinic and into British general practice. Once-weekly semaglutide beat dulaglutide in a controlled trial, but strict trial entry rules left real-world patients untested. Their 2026 cohort follows over six thousand new users in UK primary care records.

After one year, semaglutide users lost more weight and trimmed blood sugar further than dulaglutide users. The edge survived in the large majority who would never have qualified for the original trial. Trial-eligible patients, though, improved most on either drug. Safety events were tracked while treatment continued, completing the real-world picture.
pmc-13262676:
Tian-Tian Liu and colleagues find obese children need less sedative per kilogram than lean peers, a counterintuitive dosing result. Remimazolam, a new ultra-short benzodiazepine, is spreading into pediatric procedure rooms with thin data on obesity. Their 2026 trial enrolls sixty children, half obese, alongside a fixed pain-drug partner.

A staircase design adjusted each dose by the last child's response until the midpoint dose emerged. In obese children that midpoint sat roughly a quarter lower than in normal-weight children. Dosing strictly by the scale would therefore overshoot in heavier patients. The authors urge weight-band care when sedating obese children for procedures.
pmc-13263276:
Sota Ihara and Akihiro Okamoto propose a new bacterial species from an electricity-linked growth culture in a 2026 journal article. The rod-shaped bacterium was isolated from filtered liquid of an electrochemical enrichment culture, a setup that grows microbes able to move electrons to solid surfaces. They named it Cellulomonas electrica and compared it with its closest relatives by genes and chemistry.

Whole-genome similarity values fell well below the thresholds that define a species, while broader measures kept it inside the Cellulomonas genus. Its main cell fat and its chief quinone, a molecule used in energy handling, set it apart from relatives. It grew best at around 30 degrees and mildly acidic conditions. The strain is deposited in two public culture collections.
pmc-13263376:
Yichen Li and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on an electronic skin inspired by the pitcher plant Nepenthes, whose rim channels liquid in one direction. Their Janus e-skin moves sweat away from the body actively while staying breathable and waterproof. It aims to keep skin dry during long wear.

The material stretches to more than six times its length and senses in several modes, including touch-free signals and Morse code taps. It records brain, muscle, heart, and eye signals cleanly. Paired with machine learning, muscle signals from the skin steered a four-legged robot, and the system recognized letters with over ninety-five percent accuracy.
pmc-13264276:
Nidhal Ben Abdlekrim led a 2026 study of match demands in elite under-19 female basketball players from North Africa. Most past profiles came from men or adults, so youth data were thin. The team compared guards, forwards, and centers, and national against world-level play.

Thirty Tunisian players were tracked through eight playoff games with video, heart-rate bands, and blood tests. World-level players did more hard efforts and spent more time at near-max heart rate. Guards did the most hard side-to-side moves, while centers did more still, hard work and had higher blood lactate, a fatigue marker. Hard effort fell from the first to the last quarter in both groups, less so for world-level players.
pmc-13266276:
Ruth-Ann Yaa Frimpong and colleagues published a 2026 food study on plant-based mayonnaise made by swapping egg yolk for protein from sprouted moringa seeds. Egg yolk stabilizes the sauce's oil droplets, so a plant swap must match its texture. They extracted the seed protein three ways: with ultrasound, with enzymes, or with both together.

Swaps from five to fifty percent were tested. Texture improved over the all-egg control up to a twenty percent swap, then declined. At twenty percent, the combined-extraction version matched a commercial benchmark in firmness, consistency, and stickiness. Several mixes also gave finer oil droplets than the control. Yellowness faded as swap levels rose, and acidity stayed in the low-acid food range. The authors back sprouted moringa protein as a working partial egg replacer.
pmc-13267276:
Marie Oosterlynck and a large team report a 2026 study of tiny particles that may spread tau damage in the brain. In Alzheimer's disease, the tau protein clumps and seems to pass from cell to cell. Small sacs released by brain cells, called extracellular vesicles, carry tau seeds, but which tau forms drive the spread was unknown.

The team took these sacs from frozen brain tissue of patients with three tau diseases and from healthy controls. Protein profiling showed that each disease left a distinct tau pattern in the sacs. Alzheimer's sacs were rich in tau pieces from one key region. A short piece named PHF6 did most of the seeding work. The authors name PHF6 as a possible drug target.
pmc-13267976:
Cristina Kontogiannis, Sami Asif, and Amit Kharod present a 2026 case report on a rare artery squeeze after major weight loss. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome occurs when the gut's third section is pinched between two large vessels. Their patient was a 28-year-old woman with lasting nausea and vomiting after losing 110 pounds. She also had a heart-rhythm condition and slow stomach emptying, which muddied the picture.

Standard scope and ultrasound checks found nothing. A CT scan showed the tight vessel angle and short gap that mark the syndrome. Surgeons used a robot to join the pinched gut section to the next part of the small bowel, bypassing the squeeze. Her symptoms resolved. The authors present the robotic route as a workable fix for this rare problem.
pmc-13268076:
T D Barry and a large team report a 2026 evaluation of Wales' national TB cohort review program. Cohort review is a structured team audit of every TB case, checking care quality and public health data. Wales started its national program in 2012. The team analyzed all notified TB cases from 2012 to 2022 in this low-incidence country.

Of 1,175 cases, 985, about 83 percent, were presented at cohort review. Many care outcomes reached near their targets. Support to finish treatment was aimed more and more at patients with social complexity and higher spread risk. The completeness of surveillance data improved substantially. Weak spots persisted in finding and assessing contacts of cases. The authors offer the program as an efficient model for other low-incidence countries nearing TB elimination.
pmc-13268176:
The editors of PLOS One published a 2026 editorial note on a greenhouse tomato study. The original paper tested a micro-fog system that cools and humidifies greenhouse air, improving tomato growth in summer. After publication, concerns arose about where some of the data came from. The first author admitted that a figure's environmental data came from a different institution and was included by mistake.

The note prints a corrected figure and fixes several results sentences, including midday temperature and humidity readings for the fogged and control sections. The greenhouse's reported dimensions were also wrong and are corrected. Raw data behind the figures and tables, missing from the original submission, are now supplied. The editors state they cannot verify the data's origin because the institutions involved gave conflicting advice.
pmc-13269876: An author correction from 2026, for a paper led by Zicong Huang on a protein that organizes sperm maturation, fixes swapped labels in one table and one sentence. In Table 2, the column headings for two patient groups, labeled NOA and OA, had been exchanged. The correction also reverses the group counts in the results text, which now reads 30 OA samples and 25 NOA samples. Both changes were made in the online and PDF versions.
pmc-13270876:
Yangyang Zhang is lead author of a 2026 review article on the HOXA gene cluster and bone disorders. Bone stays healthy through a balance of building and breakdown, and losing that balance drives diseases such as osteoporosis, where bones thin. HOXA genes help direct early body patterning and cell fate.

The review gathers recent work on how HOXA family members act in bone disease, finding wide, uneven roles across the family. It groups their effects into three shared patterns: setting regional pattern in the skeleton, adjusting signalling pathways, and joining gene-control networks with non-coding RNAs. The authors argue these roles offer possible targets for new bone treatments.
pmc-13271476:
Rui Sun and Zhihao Chen report a 2026 journal article designing a syllabus for Architectural Art English, an English for Academic Purposes course for undergraduate architecture students. The design draws on needs analysis, asking what students must do in English, and genre analysis, studying the text types architects actually read and write.

A university-wide questionnaire gathered 650 students and faculty. It found a sharp gap between students' aims, such as joining international projects, studying abroad, and following foreign lectures, and their current weak listening skills and subject vocabulary. The proposed syllabus teaches seven genres, from textbooks and research papers to design statements and presentation scripts, through themed units using real cases and task-based projects.
pmc-13272276:
Arve Opheim is lead author of a 2026 study protocol, a published plan, for PEER-HOMEcare, a feasibility study of enriched-environment rehab at home after stroke. Recovery happens mostly at home as hospital pressure rises. Animal research shows that stimulating surroundings prompt frequent exploratory use of a weakened arm. Such use drives learning and brain rewiring. But human home translation is limited.

The single-group study will enrol 45 stroke survivors within six months of their stroke across Norway, Sweden, and Latvia. Homes will be modified in meaningful, progressive ways to encourage arm use in daily tasks, and wearable sensors will track exploratory behaviour. Main outcomes are feasibility and acceptability, from surveys, logs, and interviews, with arm function and daily living as secondary measures.
pmc-13272576:
Wenqiao Chang leads a 2026 review of spatial multi-omics, a set of methods that map many kinds of molecules inside intact tumor tissue. Older methods lose where in the tissue each signal came from. The review covers methods that map gene activity, small chemicals, and proteins in place, and how to combine them.

Used together, these tools have shown niches at the edge where tumors invade, shifts in the immune setting over time, and signals cells pass as cancer spreads. The authors say the approach can help sort patients, plan treatment, and tackle drug resistance. They also set out current limits and next steps for the field.
pmc-13272676:
Ludwig Svensson leads a 2026 randomised trial asking whether extra iron for breastfed babies affects behavior at age three. Breastfed infants can run low on iron, which the brain needs, but benefits in healthy infants are unclear. The trial ran in Warsaw, Poland, and Umea, Sweden.

Healthy full-term babies got a low daily iron dose or a placebo from 4 to 9 months of age. Of 221 babies randomised, 133 were assessed at age three with a child behavior checklist. The iron group scored lower for outward behavior problems, 45.6 against 48.6, and for aggressive behavior. The authors urge caution until other studies repeat the finding.
pmc-13272776:
Seleem Ahmad leads a 2026 study of concrete that replaces some stone or sand with recycled plastic particles. The plastic came from polyethylene waste reshaped into pellets. Seven mixes were made at replacement levels of 2.5, 7.5, and 15 percent by weight, for coarse and fine material separately, and cured for 7 and 28 days.

A 2.5 percent replacement of fine material gave the highest compressive strength, about 26.22 megapascals, and the best splitting strength. At 15 percent, strength fell, but replacing coarse material cut density most, by 3.66 percent, aiding light concrete. The authors suggest non-structural uses such as paths and paving blocks, if workability is managed.
pmc-13276376:
Sayyed Ali Siyadati and co-authors report a 2026 engineering article on how fast cooling harms asphalt in freeze-thaw weather. Cracking in cold regions is a leading cause of road damage. Many factors are well studied, but the speed of temperature drop during each freeze cycle had been largely overlooked.

The team made half-disc samples, dry and water-soaked, and put them through seven freeze-thaw cycles. Cooling rates ranged from very slow to a shock freeze, at three low temperatures. Faster cooling cut fracture toughness, fracture energy, and a cracking resistance index. Slow cooling cost the samples about a sixth of their toughness; shock freezing cost nearly half their fracture energy. The authors blame stress that cannot relax in time, steep temperature gradients, and expanding trapped water. Peak load rose as temperature fell to a point, then dropped.
pmc-13276676:
Junru Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how climate change may rewrite the genetics of a Chinese flowering dogwood tree. Cornus kousa subspecies chinensis adapts well but spreads slowly, making it a good test case for woody plant responses to a warming world. Its rich internal variation is at stake.

The team gathered leaf samples from three hundred forty-eight trees across twenty-five populations in China. Today's populations hold abundant genetic diversity. Models of future climates for 2060 to 2080, under two emission paths, forecast a sharp squeeze. Over ninety percent of populations would collapse into one shared genetic cluster, homogenizing variation. Sixty-seven DNA markers tied to climate stood out, and almost all linked to average yearly temperature. The authors say temperature is the main selective force, and they offer guidance for conserving the tree's genetic resources.
pmc-13351476:
Rogerson and colleagues speak with shift workers who make food in United Kingdom plants. The study asks what helps or blocks healthy eating at work. Eleven workers took part in online talks. Most were men with long shift records. Eight themes came out. Workers knew what healthy food was. What they ate still bent toward what was fast and close at hand. Breaks were short and not safe to use in full.

Plant rules on hygiene and safety shut off some food choices. Night shifts made fresh food hard to find. The team says plants must first fix access and breaks. Only then can coaching on food choices help staff.
pmc-13394776:
Feldman and co-authors assess, in 2026, whether the seizure drug cenobamate can be restarted at full dose after a short break without triggering hypersensitivity reactions such as rash. Slow dose escalation is normally required when starting the drug, leaving restart rules unclear. They exploited a natural experiment: epilepsy patients whose medicines were paused during intracranial EEG monitoring at a tertiary center, then restarted before discharge.

Thirty-two patients, median age 29 years, had cenobamate withheld for a median of seven days and restarted at a median of 200 milligrams per day. A quarter resumed at 300 milligrams or more, and 44 percent had a prior history of rash from some cause. Even so, no hypersensitivity reactions or rashes attributable to the drug appeared during hospitalization or two weeks of follow-up. The authors suggest previously tolerant patients may skip retitration after brief interruptions, easing management of missed doses.
pmc-13395276:
Vendhan and Mysore survey, in 2026, how Indian dermatologists use narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for vitiligo, the skin condition that destroys pigment in patches. The light treatment is standard care, but real-world dosing, upkeep schedules, and pre-treatment dose testing vary widely. Their survey, checked by three senior dermatologists with over 15 years of phototherapy experience each, drew 80 replies from doctors in practice.

The response rate was only 5 percent, itself a finding about survey fatigue among clinicians. Among respondents, 65 percent had more than ten years of experience with the treatment. Just over half, 52.5 percent, used whole-body phototherapy units exclusively, while the rest combined whole-body cabinets with targeted devices for limited areas. The authors use the snapshot to argue for more standardized practice, since inconsistent dosing strategies and upkeep plans can change outcomes for vitiligo patients receiving the same nominal therapy.
pmc-13396176:
Wang and team report, in 2026, evidence that microwaves can push electrons in a semiconductor into superballistic flow, a regime where a viscous electron fluid conducts better than free flight allows. Working with point contacts carved from ultrahigh-mobility two-dimensional electron gas, they used photoconductivity, the change in conduction under microwaves. That let them probe how edge magnetoplasmons, waves running along the sample edge, stir the electron fluid.

Weak microwaves at low magnetic fields produced photoconductivity matching superballistic flow, while strong fields flipped the signal negative as phonon scattering took over. The key evidence was geometric: photoconductance scaled with the square of the point contact width, the fingerprint of viscous flow. Edge waves that reinforced each other sharply enhanced the signal, while waves that cancelled were strongly suppressed. pmc-13650976: A 2026 paper on Intergenerational educational mobility and intri advanced medical knowledge. The results guide practice. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
pmc-2247476:
Drummond and Rambaut present BEAST, software for Bayesian evolutionary analysis by sampling trees. Studying how sequences change is a statistical task at its core. Use of probability models for family trees, alignments, and population genetics was growing when they wrote.

BEAST is described as a fast and flexible package that samples many possible trees and weighs each by likelihood. That approach yields not just one tree but a sense of how sure each branch is. BEAST became a central tool for dating species splits and tracing the spread of viruses through time.
pmc-3012676:
Du, Zhang, Huang, and co-authors compare two ways of expressing DNA methylation levels from microarray data. Measuring methylation across CpG sites is crucial for understanding how genes are switched without changing the DNA code. Illumina's Infinium assay offers cheap, high-throughput profiling for that purpose.

Results can be reported as Beta values or as M values, and the choice affects statistics. The authors test both methods side by side to show where each behaves well. Their guidance helps researchers pick a scale that supports valid comparisons in studies of cancer and development.
pmc-3445676:
Elwyn, Frosch, Thomson, and co-authors present a practical model for shared decision making in clinical practice. The principles of sharing decisions between doctor and patient were well documented by 2012. Guidance on how to actually do it during routine care was lacking, though.

The authors translate earlier theory into a practical three-step model that clinicians can easily remember. The steps move from introducing choice, through describing options, to reaching a decision together. Their model gave clinicians a teachable routine for respecting patient preferences without lengthening visits unworkably.  Training programmes for doctors now teach the three steps as core communication skill.
pmc-3447976:
Friedman and Alm present methods for building correlation networks from genomic survey data. High-throughput methods such as 16S rRNA gene profiling promise to reveal the inner workings of natural microbial communities, from ocean water to the human gut. A key step is finding which microbes vary together.

Raw correlations mislead because community data are proportions, not absolute counts. Their method, SparCC, was designed to handle that trap. Better networks help ecologists guess which microbes cooperate or compete, shaping hypotheses that lab work can then test directly.  Ocean surveys used network maps to predict which microbes thrive together seasonally.
pmc-5340976:
Smith, Heger, and Sudbery made UMI-tools in 2017 for more exact gene counting. In many sequencing tests, each starting molecule gets a random tag, called a UMI, before copies are made. Copies that share a tag came from one molecule; copies with new tags were new molecules.

The catch is that the tags themselves pick up read errors, so true groups can split or merge. UMI-tools models those tag errors and groups the reads the right way. That fix makes counts of gene activity far more true to the sample. As tagged tests spread through labs, tools like this became part of the basic kit.
pmc-6366976:
Ake Lu, Austin Quach, James Wilson, and coauthors built the GrimAge aging marker in 2019. It was unclear whether blood protein levels could be guessed from DNA methylation marks. It was also unclear whether such guesses could forecast lifespan.

The team built methylation-based estimates for several plasma proteins tied to health and smoking history. Combined into GrimAge, the score strongly predicted time to death and to major diseases. It beat earlier methylation clocks on those outcomes in their tests. Researchers now use it to gauge biological aging in large cohort studies.
pmc-7857476: A 2026 contribution, Pelvic belts and pregnancy-related pelvic girdle, pushed the boundary, the novel approach. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-9825576:
Brian Alcock and colleagues presented the 2023 update of CARD, a database that collects what is known about how bacteria resist antibiotics. CARD pairs a set of standard terms for resistance with checked gene sequences and the gene changes known to cause resistance. Together they let a lab read a bacterium's genome and say which drugs it can likely withstand.

The update adds more curated records, support for machine learning, and better tools to predict a sample's resistome, the full set of resistance genes it carries. Health teams use CARD when they sequence bacteria from hospitals and towns. Knowing resistance genes with care is key to picking the right drug and to spotting dangerous strains early.
polano-talmud-selections-1876:
Polano's Talmud: Selections, published in 1876, offered English readers early and easy access to rabbinic literature. The Talmud itself is a vast record of Jewish law and debate in Hebrew and Aramaic. Polano chose and translated passages for a general audience.

The selections range over prayer, charity, family duty, court rulings, and tales of the rabbis at work. Readers could meet the Talmud's mix of strict law and warm story without facing its full bulk. The book served as an influential introduction for English readers curious about Jewish tradition. Victorian readers met a living tradition here, not a dead code.
price-observations-civil-liberty-1776:
Price's Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty appeared in 1776 and made him famous in a night. The dissenting minister wrote as Britain moved toward war with its American colonies. His pamphlet defended the American cause on principle, and it sold by the thousand in the year of independence.

Price defines liberty as self-government, for nations as for persons, and argues that Britain's claim to tax and bind the colonies was a form of slavery. He extends the argument to Ireland and India, which widened both the book's reach and its enemies. The government of the day considered prosecuting its author. The tract carried deep thought to the barricades across the sea, and it stands as the English voice of the American Revolution at its birth.
proudhon-what-is-property-tucker-1876:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's What is Property? in 1876. Proudhon, a French printer and self-taught thinker, had issued the memoir in 1840 and shocked France. His answer to his own question became famous at once: property is robbery.

Proudhon distinguished property, the right to use and abuse and charge rent, from simple possession of what one works. He attacked rent, interest, and profit taken without labor. Judges and economists denounced the book, and Proudhon answered them in later memoirs. The work is widely read as the founding text of anarchism, the first time a writer claimed that label with pride.
shi-king-book-of-poetry-legge-1876:
James Legge published his complete translation of the She King, the Book of Poetry, in 1876. It forms volume three of his Chinese Classics, in a revised edition with the Chinese text, prolegomena, and notes. The Shih Ching holds 305 songs and hymns, gathered in China more than two thousand years ago.

Court odes, temple hymns, and folk songs of love, harvest, and war stand side by side. Tradition credits Confucius with choosing and ordering the collection. Legge's prose renderings favor exact sense, while his notes carry the learning of Chinese commentators. The songs remain China's oldest poetry anthology and a school text for ages. English readers meet them whole in Legge.
smith-chaldean-account-genesis-1876:
George Smith, a bank note engraver turned Assyriologist at the British Museum, wrote this book in 1876. He had taught himself to read the clay tablets of Babylon from the museum's vast store. Four years past, he had read out a flood tale from the tablets to a stunned London crowd.

The book sets the Babylonian tales of the making of the world and man by the side of Genesis. A flood tale far older than the Bible stands in its pages in clay writ form. The find shook the firm faith of Victorian Britain in the lone truth of its own text.
spina-quaestio-de-strigibus-latin-1576:
Bartolomeo Spina, a Dominican who served as master of the sacred palace at Rome, wrote his Quaestio de strigibus early in the sixteenth century. This edition of 1576 kept his answer in print. Spina writes against Ponzinibio, the skeptical jurist who had called the sabbath an illusion.

Point for point, Spina defends the sabbath's reality with scholastic logic and old texts. The witches fly in body, he insists, and their assemblies truly meet. His book is the Counter-Reformation's learned reply to early doubt. Orthodoxy strikes back here with full armor. Reading Spina against Ponzinibio shows the sixteenth-century debate at its sharpest, lawyer against theologian over the same frightened women.
taine-ancient-regime-durand-1876:
Hippolyte Taine's The Ancient Regime appears in John Durand's translation of 1876. The book opens Taine's Origins of Contemporary France, his study of the Revolution's causes. Taine applies his method of race, milieu, and moment to old France. Taxes, privilege, and a rigid central state crush the peasantry and starve reform.

He paints the court, the tax farmer, and the village in hard detail. The old regime, in his account, made revolution near certain. Taine wrote after the Paris Commune, and fear of crowds colors his work. Historians debate his science, yet respect his research. The volume is a classic of analytical history in the French style.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume twenty-six of Casanova's memoirs: the story draws toward its end. An extraordinary life, plainly told. The final chapters approach. Twenty-sixth volume: the end approaches, an extraordinary life, plainly told, an extraordinary life plainly told.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Another volume of Hakluyt's great collection — more voyages, more discoveries, more Elizabethan daring on the high seas. The English nation's sea story continues in all its glory. Essential for all lovers of exploration and adventure. No library of English adventure is complete without Hakluyt.
the-valley-of-fear-pg3776: Conan Doyle's The Valley of Fear is the last long Sherlock Holmes novel. A coded message leads from an English manor to the Pennsylvania coal wars. Holmes unravels a deadly secret society. Mystery at its most masterful.
tob-0076:
Edmund T. Whittaker wrote the classic history of how physicists explained light and electricity before Einstein. His subject runs from Descartes, who filled space with spinning whirlpools of fine matter, to the aether theories of the Victorian age. Maxwell's equations and the discovery of the electron close the long story.

Whittaker was a working mathematician who lived through the upheaval he describes, and it shows in his grasp of detail. Generations of students have treated the book as the standard history of field theory. It also reminds readers that the aether, now discarded, once organized the best science of its century.
tob-0176:
G. Horner's translation presents Pistis Sophia, a Gnostic text preserved in Coptic, in which the risen Jesus teaches his disciples over an extended period after the resurrection. Mary Magdalene stands foremost among the questioners. At its center, Pistis Sophia, Faith-Wisdom personified, has fallen into chaos and repents her way upward through thirteen aeons, singing psalms of repentance in each.

Hostile archons, hymns, and detailed maps of higher and lower realms fill the dialogues. The Christianity shown here is stranger and richer than the creeds that won, built on secret knowledge and cosmic drama. Scholars prize the text as a major surviving witness to late Gnostic teaching.
tob-13329-15476:
Books eight to twelve form volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, the epic's dark second half. The great battle grinds to its end as champion after champion dies. A shameful night raid kills the last sleeping warriors of the beaten side.

Aftermath fills the rest: grief on the field, funeral fires, and the slow, unwilling work of rule. Yudhishthira must be coaxed to govern the kingdom he has won at such cost. Long discourses on duty replace the clash of arms. Ganguli's translation turns elegiac with the poem itself. Seldom has a war story spent so much strength on sorrow.
tob-4146-15476:
Books eight through twelve fill volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, and the war burns toward its end. Great champions fall one by one. A night attack slaughters sleeping warriors, an act the epic itself treats as shameful. Victory, when it comes, tastes of ash.

Widows mourn on the field, funerals follow, and Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, takes the throne with a heavy heart. Long talks on duty and grief slow the pace on purpose. The epic turns from deeds of war to their cost. Ganguli's steady translation lets the sorrow build, page after page, without relief.
tob-4176:
Teresa of Avila, the Spanish nun and reformer, described the soul as a crystal castle in The Interior Castle, her mature masterpiece of 1577. Benedict Zimmerman translated her guide for English readers. Seven sets of mansions lead inward, room by room, toward the King who waits at the center.

Each mansion marks a stage of prayer, from stumbling effort to quiet union. Teresa writes from her own trials, with humor about distractions and dry spells that still disarms readers. Nuns under her rule received the book first; the world claimed it next. Many judges call it the greatest guide to the life of prayer ever written.
tob-4276:
William Hickling Prescott wrote his History of the Conquest of Mexico in the 1840s, and it became the most widely read history of its time. Volume one of four sets the scene before Hernan Cortes lands. It describes the Aztec empire at its height, ruled by Montezuma from Tenochtitlan, a great lake city of temples, markets, and canals.

Prescott explains Aztec government, religion, warfare, and daily life in detail drawn from Spanish and native sources. He writes history in the manner of a novel, with vivid scenes and strong characters. Readers get both a rich portrait of a lost civilization and the background they need for the clash that follows in later volumes.
tob-9052-15476:
Grief rules volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, as the war of Kurukshetra ends. The field lies covered with the dead of both houses. Widows and mothers search the corpses, and the victors find their crown brings no joy.

Funeral rites, laments, and hard reckonings take the place of battles. The epic turns, by design, from action to mourning and reflection on what violence costs. Yudhishthira rules a kingdom of ashes and doubts his own part in winning it. Ganguli carries the slow, somber books with patience. Readers feel the full weight the Sanskrit poem places on victory.
tob-9776: A. J. Maas wrote this Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Hexaemeron, the six days of creation described in the first chapter of Genesis. It sums up how early Church writers and later theologians read those six days, whether as plain days, ages, or figures of speech. Maas writes as a scholar for general readers who need a clear map of a long debate. Short and factual, the piece works as a starting point on how Christians have understood the creation story.
tumulus-hermetis-apertus-in-quo-ad-solem: Tumulus Hermetis apertus, 1676. The opened Hermes mound. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
twain-tom-sawyer-1876:
Mark Twain published The Adventures of Tom Sawyer in 1876, complete in the first edition text. The beloved Mississippi boyhood novel drew on Twain's own youth in Hannibal, Missouri, on the river. Its sunny mischief made Twain famous on both sides of the Atlantic at once.

Tom, raised by Aunt Polly, dodges school and chores for swimming, pirates, and treasure hunts. He whitewashes a fence by making the chore look like rare sport to his friends. At night he sees Injun Joe murder Dr. Robinson in the town graveyard in secret. Lost in a cave with Becky Thatcher, Tom finds both terror and buried gold there. The book's glow of boyhood hides sharp satire of village piety and pride.
un-ga-res-376:
Korea's division hardened into war, and Resolution 376, adopted by the General Assembly on 7 October 1950, restates the UN aim. Past votes of 1947, 1948, and 1949 had set the goal: a free, united Korea. The UN Commission on Korea had now reported. The goals, the text admits, had not been met. Worse, an armed attack from North Korea had tried to wipe out the Republic of Korea by force.

The Assembly recalls its 1948 ruling on the south. A lawful state, the Government of the Republic of Korea, held real rule over the part of Korea the UN team could reach. That state rested on votes the team had watched. The text holds to the goal of one Korea, free of outside force.
un-ga-res-a-69-76:
The world's sole forum for arms talks gets a review in Resolution A/69/76, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Conference on Disarmament, based in Geneva, holds the prime role in hard talks on arms cuts. The Assembly had the conference's own report before it. Word from the Secretary-General, and speeches by foreign chiefs, had each voiced both support for the body and worry at its stall.

Real talks on firm points are needed, the text holds, and the state of the world should give them fresh push. Yet worry runs deep: for all the hard work of its member states, the conference had long failed to agree a plan of work. That deadlock, unbroken for years, hangs over the whole text.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 376 (V), adopted on 7 October 1950, addressed Korea in the first months of the Korean War. The Assembly noted that an armed attack from North Korea sought to wipe out the Government of the Republic of Korea by force. United Nations forces were fighting under Security Council calls. They were to repel the attack and restore peace.

The text urged steps for calm across Korea. It urged elections under United Nations watch. It urged one united, free, and democratic government. United Nations forces were to stay only as long as needed. It created the United Nations Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea, a seven-state body. It ordered plans for relief and rebuilding once the fighting ended.

Resolution 69/76 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, takes up the report of the Conference on Disarmament. It records that the Conference again failed in 2014 to begin substantive work or agree on a programme of work. That extended a deadlock of well over a decade. It notes the re-established informal working group. It notes consultations among its successive presidents meant to find a way forward.
un-sc-res-1376:
Congo's peace process gained its third MONUC phase on 9 November 2001. The Lusaka parties' political committee met the Council in joint session that day. The ceasefire generally held, though fighting went on in the east. Some foreign forces had left, including the whole Namibian contingent. The Secretary-General's report of 16 October set out the next deployment plan.

The Council welcomed the ceasefire's broad respect and called on the parties to stop backing armed groups in the east. It demanded again that Kisangani be demilitarized rapidly and without conditions, noting the RCD-Goma pledge on the city. The Council backed the inter-Congolese dialogue as a key part of the peace process. It approved phase III of MONUC's deployment, on the concept in the Secretary-General's report, with weight on the east and within the set ceiling. Grave concern was voiced at rights abuses and the country's humanitarian state.
un-sc-res-1476: Adopted in 2003, Resolution 1476 adds one more entry to the Security Council's long numbered run. The copy here is transcribed from the official record on English Wikisource. Like its neighbors in the sequence, it states the Council's grounds first and then records the decision in numbered operative paragraphs for governments to carry out and report on.
un-sc-res-1576:
Haiti's mission gained six months and a push on aid money in 2004. On 29 November 2004 the Security Council extended MINUSTAH until 1 June 2005. The transitional government was preparing free elections for 2005. The Council praised the Secretary-General's special representative and his support for dialogue. Political reconciliation and rebuilding were called essential and urgent. The mission's mandate stayed as set that April.

Transitional leaders had to widen the political process. Haitians who rejected violence should be brought into the transition. The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's latest recommendations. It urged donors and banks to release pledged funds fast. That money had been promised at a Washington conference in July.
un-sc-res-1676: Resolution 1676 is a formal Security Council text held here through a Wikisource copy of the official record. Its shape is the standard one, and the standard is the story: the same architecture carries ceasefire orders, mission mandates, and court referrals alike. The entry lets readers see that architecture at work in one complete act.
un-sc-res-176:
Security Council Resolution 176, adopted on October 4, 1962, recommended Algeria for membership in the United Nations. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a war of eight years that shook both lands and killed vast numbers of people. A seat at the UN marked the new state's arrival on the world stage in formal terms.

The General Assembly admitted Algeria four days after the council acted. Few admissions carried such weight: France had long claimed Algeria was part of France itself, not a colony. The short resolution thus sealed a verdict that the war had already rendered, and Algeria soon became a leading voice for other peoples still under colonial rule.
un-sc-res-1776:
Afghanistan stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 1776 on Afghanistan on 19 September 2007. The vote passed with fourteen in favor and one abstention. Attacks by the Taliban and other armed groups had grown sharper. Roadside bombs, suicide blasts, and seizures of hostages struck civilians and soldiers alike.

The text extends the mandate of the International Security Assistance Force for twelve months beyond 13 October 2007. States in the force may take all needed steps to carry out that mandate. Members are urged to send more troops, gear, and funds. The Council also presses for faster training of Afghan soldiers and police, so Afghans can guard their own country in time.
un-sc-res-1876: Resolution 1876, from 2009, records a decision of the fifteen-member Security Council in official form. The collection's copy follows the record held by English Wikisource. Inside the act, the preamble does the explaining and the operative clauses do the obliging. Both parts survive here, giving the decision its full context and its full force.
un-sc-res-2076:
M23's seizure of Goma drives Resolution 2076 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 20 November 2012. The rebel group had taken the city after fresh attacks in North Kivu. Reports said outside support kept flowing to the rebels. Crowds of displaced people were growing again across the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that M23 leave Goma at once. The group must halt all advances, disband, and lay down its arms for good. All outside support to M23 must stop now. The sanctions committee should review two named M23 commanders for listing at once. More targeted sanctions are under active consideration. The Secretary-General must report within days on the claims of foreign backing.
un-sc-res-276: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 276 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1970. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-476:
Jerusalem's status was defended by the Security Council on 30 June 1980. Pakistan, chairing the Organization of the Islamic Conference, had written on 28 May 1980. Israel kept changing the city's physical character, population makeup, institutions, and status. Steps in the Knesset toward a law on Jerusalem caused the Council grave concern.

The Council restated the overriding need to end the occupation of Arab lands held since 1967, Jerusalem included. It strongly deplored Israel's refusal to obey the Council and the General Assembly. All Israeli laws and acts meant to alter Jerusalem's character and status were declared without legal validity. They broke the Fourth Geneva Convention and blocked a full, just, and lasting peace. Such changes were named null and void. Israel was called urgently to drop them, and the Council vowed to examine practical steps if it did not.
un-sc-res-676: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 676 is catalogued here as dating from 1990. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-76: A wire from Batavia is passed on in Security Council Resolution 76, passed on 5 October 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had cabled the Council's president on 5 August. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the armed watchers in Indonesia, the men who kept eye on the truce between Dutch and Indonesian forces. The Council rules, in full, that the wire be sent to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-976:
Angola's new peace operation, UNAVEM III, was created on 8 February 1995. The Lusaka Protocol of 20 November 1994 promised peace after years of war. The ceasefire was generally holding, and the two armies' chiefs had met at Chipipa and Waco Kungo. Yet the protocol's timetable was slipping. Angola's offer of large in-kind support for the operation was welcomed.

The Council authorized UNAVEM III to help the parties restore peace and win national reconciliation. Military and police observers would deploy fast to watch the ceasefire. Infantry units would follow only on the Secretary-General's word that the conditions on the ground were met. A full mine clearance program for the country was named vital. The new force needed a strong public information voice, the Council agreed. The Secretary-General had to report each month on deployment and on the Lusaka Protocol's progress.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1376, adopted unanimously on 9 November 2001, reviews the Congo war's slow thaw. The Lusaka ceasefire was generally being respected, the Council found, though fighting continued in the east, where it told the parties to stop backing armed groups. Some foreign forces had withdrawn, including Namibia's whole contingent, which the Council counted as a real step.

Other states that had not yet begun pulling out were asked to start. The Council took note of the Secretary-General's October report and recommendations, and welcomed a joint meeting held that same day with the Lusaka agreement's political committee. Congo's sovereignty, including over its natural resources, was reaffirmed even as foreign armies still occupied much of its territory.

Emergency relief arrangements for Iraq are kept in force a little longer on 24 April 2003. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that paragraph 4 of its resolution 1472 of March 2003 would remain in force until 3 June 2003. Those provisions gave the oil-for-food machinery flexibility to deliver humanitarian relief after the outbreak of war, and the Council noted the measures could be renewed again.

Haiti's climb back from chaos took a new step in late 2004. A stand-in regime ran the land. Polls were set for 2005, with power to pass to elected hands. The UN force, MINUSTAH, kept the peace. The chief's report of 18 November 2004 drove the talks. Resolution 1576 passed on 29 November 2004.

The force's term ran to 1 June 2005. More terms were meant to come. Armed bands that played at police work drew blame. A swift arms hand-in drive was called urgent. Rights abuses were damned, as was jail with no charge for one's politics. Donors were told to pay pledges made in Washington that July at speed. Word on the work was due each three months.

Somalia's arms embargo monitoring team is set up once more on 10 May 2006. The country's transitional federal institutions were still struggling to build real national governance. The embargo, dating from 1992, continued to be broken, and the previous monitoring group's term had run out.

The Secretary-General is asked, in consultation with the sanctions committee, to set the Monitoring Group up again to track violations and gather evidence. Support for the transitional institutions and for the African Union and regional efforts behind them is repeated. Somali leaders are urged to keep up political dialogue, and all states are reminded of their duty to respect the arms embargo in full.

Algeria's admission to the United Nations is recommended in Resolution 176, adopted on 4 October 1962 by ten votes to none, with China abstaining. The Council had weighed the bid of Algeria, filed under the state's full formal name. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a brutal eight-year war that reshaped both countries.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit Algeria to membership. The recommendation capped a remarkable reversal: a state whose liberation movement the UN had debated for years now joined as a member. Algeria quickly became a leading voice for colonized peoples in the Assembly, and this short admission text is where that career formally begins.

Afghanistan's international force is renewed by Resolution 1776, adopted on 19 September 2007 by 14 votes to none with one abstention. The International Security Assistance Force, ISAF, had completed its expansion across the whole country under NATO leadership. Taliban, Al-Qaida, and other extremist attacks, including suicide bombings and abductions, were rising, and civilian casualties were a growing concern. Counter-narcotics and security-sector reform were tied to the fight.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends ISAF's authorization for twelve months beyond 13 October 2007 and authorizes its member states to take all necessary measures to fulfil the mandate. It calls on states to contribute personnel, equipment, and funds, and stresses training and mentoring the Afghan National Police and army so Afghan forces can take over in time. ISAF must work closely with the Afghan government and the UN mission, UNAMA, and report quarterly through the Secretary-General.

Guinea-Bissau's peacebuilding office is extended on 26 June 2009, and its upgrade is ordered. Political assassinations had rocked the country that year, showing again how fragile its institutions are. A presidential election was set for 28 June 2009, two days after adoption, and a free and fair vote is treated as the key step back to constitutional order.

The office's mandate is extended, and the Secretary-General is asked to establish a United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Guinea-Bissau in its place, with a strategic workplan. All sides are called on to respect the election result and keep the process peaceful. The armed forces, including their leaders, are urged to stay under civilian control, and security sector reform is restated as a national duty.

The fall of Goma draws condemnation and a withdrawal demand in Resolution 2076, adopted in November 2012. The 23 March Movement, M23, resumed attacks in North Kivu and entered Goma on 20 November 2012. It displaced people and committed abuses including summary executions, sexual violence, and child recruitment. Reports alleged external support to the rebels.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemns the M23's attacks and demands its immediate withdrawal from Goma. It demands an end to advances, disbanding and disarmament of its members, and restoration of Congolese state authority in North Kivu. It demands all outside support cease. It asks the Secretary-General to report within days on the support allegations and on redeploying MONUSCO forces. It intends to consider sanctions against the M23 leadership and external backers under the Resolution 1857 (2008) criteria. The Great Lakes conference's joint verification mechanism is tasked with investigating the support reports.

South Africa's presence in Namibia is declared illegal by Resolution 276, adopted on 30 January 1970. The United Nations had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966. South Africa stayed anyway. It enforced its own laws there and put Namibians on trial in its courts.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's refusal to obey the United Nations decisions on Namibia. It declared that South Africa's continued presence was illegal. Every act South Africa had taken for Namibia since the mandate ended was illegal and invalid. The occupation was said to have grave effects on the rights of the Namibian people. All states were told to avoid dealings with South Africa that clashed with that ruling. A special sub-committee was set up to study how the decisions could be carried out.

The Comoros, an island chain between Madagascar and Mozambique, declared independence from France in July 1975. Its UN application moved quickly. Resolution 376 was adopted on 17 October 1975 by fourteen votes to none. The Council met for its 1848th session that day.

Members recommended the Comoros for membership. The General Assembly admitted the islands the next month. One island, Mayotte, voted to stay French, splitting the new state. That quarrel shadowed the Comoros for decades. Even so, admission confirmed the archipelago's statehood in law. This resolution preserves the moment. A tiny island nation took a seat equal in voting weight to the largest powers in the Assembly.

Jerusalem's fate is the theme of Resolution 476, passed on 30 June 1980. Pakistan, then chair of a bloc of Muslim states, had raised the matter in a May letter. The Council said land seized by force can never be owned by right. It stressed the city's rare place in three faiths. The holy sites, it said, need care and respect above all.

The Council deplored Israel's drive to change the city's shape, its people, its rules, and its status. It voiced grave fear at bills in Israel's Knesset that aimed to lock those changes in law. It told Israel to end its hold on Arab lands seized since 1967, Jerusalem among them. It deplored its refusal to obey past rulings.

Two more months for the Iran-Iraq observer group were granted on 28 November 1990. The group, called UNIIMOG, watched a cease-fire that still held, although no full peace had followed it. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 23 November, had recommended the step. Resolution 676 records the renewal.

The Council extended UNIIMOG's mandate until 31 January 1991, as the Secretary-General had advised. He was asked to report during January 1991. His report would cover his further talks with Iran and Iraq about the observer group's future. Short renewals had become the pattern for the mission by then. Each one kept the observers on the ground for a few more weeks, while the Council waited to see whether the mission should continue at all.

A cable about the costs of military observers in Indonesia reached the Council in 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had written to the Council's president on 5 August that year. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the observers working in Indonesia. Resolution 76, adopted on 5 October 1949, does a single thing with that request. The Council transmitted the message to the Secretary-General. No sums were set, and the Council gave no answer on the request itself.

Angola's peace deal takes shape in Resolution 976, adopted on 8 February 1995. The government and UNITA had signed the Lusaka Protocol on 20 November 1994, and the ceasefire was broadly holding. Military chiefs from both sides had met to move the plan along. Still, carrying out the deal had fallen behind its timetable.

The Council sets up a new peacekeeping operation, UNAVEM III, to help restore peace and national unity. It allows up to 7,000 troops, plus 350 military observers and 260 police observers, with a first mandate until 8 August 1995. Infantry units deploy only once the Secretary-General confirms a real ceasefire, shared military data, and named quartering areas for UNITA forces. A mine clearance program and a UN radio station are backed. The mission is meant to end once the Lusaka goals are met, with completion expected by February 1997.

wallace-geographical-distribution-animal:
Alfred Russel Wallace, co-founder of the theory of evolution by natural selection, published the first volume of his Geographical Distribution of Animals in 1876. Wallace had spent years collecting in the Amazon and the Malay islands. He asked why each region holds the animals it does.

Volume One sets out the rules: how climate, seas, and land links shape where species can live. Wallace divides the world into six great regions, a scheme still in use. His maps and lists turned scattered facts into zoogeography, the study of animals across the map. Collectors and travelers supplied much of the raw data behind it.

Volume Two of Wallace's Geographical Distribution of Animals, also from 1876, puts his system to work region by region. Alfred Russel Wallace had catalogued thousands of species on his travels. Here he applies his rules to the lands of the Old World and beyond.

The volume works through Europe, Africa, Asia, and the islands of the Pacific in turn. For each region Wallace lists the families present and asks how they got there. Land bridges, past climates, and vanished seas all play a part. It completes the founding text of zoogeography. Readers meet the faunas of lands few had seen described before.
zola-his-excellency-1876:
Macmillan issued His Excellency in 1897 as the sole authorized English version, with Vizetelly's preface. Chapter heads run from The Corps Legislatif and Resignation to An Imperial Christening. Passion and Matrimony, In Retirement, and Recalled to Power follow in turn.

Eugene Rougon, the family's political genius, claws toward the top of the Second Empire. Minister and power broker, he masters the backroom deal and its price. Flatterers, mistresses, and favors traded like coin crowd around him. Zola dissects how power truly works with a razor edge. Few political novels match its grasp of influence, ambition, and the hunger that drives public men.
